en: The Bhadrakalpika Sūtra, Scroll One; also titled the Bhadrapāla Samādhi; translated into Chinese as the *Xiánjié dìngyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Concentration of the Worthy Aeon) by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty. Chapter One: Inquiry into Samādhi. **Chapter One: Inquiry into Samādhi** [The Buddha] was staying in the city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were liberated through perfect wisdom. Among them were the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bāṣpa, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Subāhu, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Kapphiṇa, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Cunda, the Venerable Svāgata, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Upananda, the Venerable Sundara-nanda, the Venerable Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Rāhula, and the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, who was the foremost among those who practice asceticism. Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, including Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī as their leader; five hundred upāsakas, including Yaśoda as their leader; five hundred upāsikās, including Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ as their leader; and eight thousand bodhisattvas, including the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati as their leader. At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by this great assembly, expounding the Dharma. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is the name of this samādhi? By practicing and cultivating which samādhi does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain such a state? The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, this samādhi is called the 'Samādhi of the Worthy Aeon' (*Bhadrakalpa-samādhi*). Good son, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and cultivates this samādhi, he will attain the stage of non-retrogression and will never again fall back. Akṣayamati asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of samādhis are there? The Buddha told Akṣayamati: "There are eighty-four thousand kinds of samādhis. What are these eighty-four thousand? Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Having completed three years—specifically the first three years—he had fully provided robes for all, and his work of conversion was complete.
Having donned his robes and taken up his alms bowl, he traveled through Vaiśālī accompanied by a great assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus and eight billion bodhisattvas.

At that time, the World-Honored One, dwelling in seclusion, arose from his chamber with serene composure. The Bodhisattva Prajñārāja and the Bodhisattva Priyarāja, who had been practicing solitary meditation with single-minded devotion, also rose immediately to go forth and welcome the Tathāgata, preparing the site and arranging the various seats.

At that time, the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and humans and non-humans, all gathered like clouds. All those present in the assembly were illumined by the radiance of the bodhisattvas and attained peace and harmony.

All the bodhisattvas and great sages gathered there had their divine wisdom fully developed and had attained dharani; they had already perfected samadhi and were endowed with the five supernatural powers. With their own eyes, they beheld the mental activities of all sentient beings, discerning and knowing all that was thought, whether mundane or supramundane. Free from deluded thoughts, they widely disseminated profound teachings, practicing generosity and maintaining a harmonious mind.

They maintain themselves in morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and skillful means, such that there is nothing they do not transform and enlighten, having attained the stage of non-retrogression.

They proclaim the Dharma out of compassion for all living beings, harboring no malice or harm, and having no longing for gain or offerings; they do not seek food or clothing from the sūtra passages they expound, for they are free from attachment. Having attained the profound *dharmakṣānti* of the non-arising of phenomena, they deliver all who are born, acting as uninvited friends to all;
they let out the lion’s roar throughout the ten directions to receive and inspire others, rescuing all from beginning to end and enabling them to cross to the other shore.

Courageous and fearless, they transcend all demonic activities; they eliminate the hindrances of the aggregates and perform deeds free from obstruction; they realize original purity and harbor no doubts regarding all phenomena; their accumulation of merit and virtue is beyond measure or description.

They have deeply entered the profound, wondrous, and infinite source of the Way; their minds are harmonious and their countenances are joyful as they first offer greetings. Their speech is composed and orderly, and they cast away all expressions of resentment. They abandon hypocrisy and flattery to extol what is upright and true. With boundless mental conduct, they attain noble forbearance (*āryakṣānti*); their eloquence is uninterrupted as they traverse limitless assemblies. Powerful and majestic, their minds are like space, and their meritorious deeds circulate everywhere like a diamond (*vajra*).

There is nowhere he does not enter, and wherever he goes, he never encounters difficulty. He recognizes the countless kalpas through which he has wandered and the skillful means he has taught: that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, like a mirage, an echo, or a shadow; like what is seen in a dream, like the moon reflected in water, or like the core of a plantain tree, a bubble, or foam.
There are countless transformations, and the masses are submerged and drowning with no place to turn for refuge; he rescues them as they wander through the five realms of existence.

He clearly understands the destinies of sentient beings according to their good and evil deeds, manifesting true merit and power in accordance with what their hearts delight in. Always harboring compassion and free from any thought of cruelty or harm, he accumulates immeasurable virtues to adorn the Buddha-lands and fulfills boundless great vows to achieve the infinite realm of all Buddhas.

With a mind of awakening always settled and never forgetting the path home, he returns to praise the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions; having realized the nature of all fetters and the accumulation of dust-like self-conceit, his will delights in sagely wisdom and he finds joy in spiritual powers.

By means of the karma of skillful expedients, they travel through hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; whatever is taught in the ten directions, they hear and see from afar; they are able to practice all that is cultivated by those of wise intelligence; they rain down the nectar of the Dharma to moisten and nourish all beings; and their immeasurable aspiration for the Way is universally complete in every respect.

Their names were: the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsaśrīghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Varṣadhara, the Bodhisattva Śatasahasrasudeva, the Bodhisattva Avataṃsaka, the Bodhisattva Mahātman, the Bodhisattva Jvalanottaptasiddha, the Bodhisattva Prasannaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Anantakalpacaryāpūjaka, the Bodhisattva Samantajñānagarjitaghoṣarāja, the Bodhisattva Dṛṣṭasamyamithyātva, the Bodhisattva Vimalapadmarāga, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhagurucitta, the Bodhisattva Tejorājarāja, the Bodhisattva Caturyojanaprabha, the Bodhisattva Atikrāntadarśana, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānaskandha, the Bodhisattva Prajñārāja, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśana, and the eight great virtuous ones (mahāsattvas) such as Bhadrapāla.

Furthermore, there were eighty billion bodhisattvas, including the bodhisattva Saṃghagandhahasta, the bodhisattva Amitaratna, the bodhisattva Jñānakośa, the bodhisattva Mahāviśuddha, the bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, the bodhisattva Ghoṣarāja, the bodhisattva Vimalamaṇivicitracaryā, the bodhisattva Siṃhakramavighuṣṭasvara, and the bodhisattva Amitapratibhānavaiśāradya, together with such others as these.

Thereupon, the sovereign lords of the trichiliocosm—the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra and Brahmā, the Sovereign Heavenly King, the Great Brahmā Heavenly King, the various Dragon Kings, the various Ghost-Spirit Kings, the various Āsura Kings, the various Garuḍa Kings, the various Kiṃnara Kings, and the various Mahoraga Kings—all went to where the Buddha was. Each offered flowers and incense as worship, scattering them over the Buddha, and then withdrew to sit to one side, some sitting and some standing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy, beholding the assembled multitude, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to ask a question; if you grant me leave, I shall venture to set it forth."
The Buddha said, “Ask whatever you wish to inquire about; the Buddha shall explain each matter in detail.
King Nanda then asked:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly maintaining the mind of the Way, severing all that is unrighteous, practicing equal karma, and eliminating the various fetters?
One cultivates three modes:

first, walking meditation; second, standing; and third, seated concentration. By transforming those who are undisciplined and transcending them through these means, one causes them to be diligent and free from defilement."
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s accomplishment and fulfillment?

It is to clearly understand the mental natures and conducts of sentient beings; to always speak with utmost sincerity and enter into the activities of all Buddhas; to refrain from dispute or contention; to accord with the voices and speech of sentient beings while entering into the wisdom of ultimate truth; and to now, in the present world, behold all Buddhas of the ten directions without any obstruction.

Having seen the true and wondrous Dharma, they fulfill the vows of the Buddhas, the Most Holy Ones; out of compassion for worldly phenomena, though they move within the mundane world, they are forever without attachment. They practice dhyāna and samādhi with single-minded concentration, yet they do not arise from this teaching, nor do they attain extinction through the dharma of nirvāṇa.

Without failing to fulfill the supreme vows of all Buddhas, they do not become weary or desist midway, nor do they again seek the path of the Pratyekabuddha, nor do they regress or fall away from this vehicle to attain parinirvāṇa.
He cultivates the mind in immeasurable and limitless wisdom; his heart is never distracted as he enters various and manifold realms and performs boundless deeds.

Should there be any questions, he fully elucidates them with eloquence and wisdom. He gathers in immeasurable pure Buddha-lands and attains the noble realization of wisdom that leaves nothing remaining, transforming and enlightening sentient beings with a mind free from attachment.

Without harboring the notion of a person while proclaiming the sūtras, one does not dwell in perversity when manifesting nirvāṇa; yet, without entering ultimate extinction, one practices to attain the Way. Furthermore, one has no reliance as if there were something to be cherished, but yearns for internal practice to abandon both existence and non-existence.
"Today, O Great One!
May you look upon me with compassion. Although my nature is not clever, I dare not fail to once more entreat you to deign to proclaim [the teaching] out of your grace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy (Nandirāja) uttered this verse in praise:
"Having consulted the Exquisite Moon, the Savior of the World proclaimed this radiance:
the conduct of all Bodhisattvas, leading gradually to the attainment of fulfillment.
Entering into the infinite assembly, all devas and humans delight in the Dharma."
Hearing the practice for attaining the supreme path, countless people resolved their minds.
Believing in and delighting in the subtle merit, they asked about the one of universal renown who has crossed over;
he whose mind possesses immeasurable fame and wisdom saw the victory and realized the realization beyond remainder.
Proclaiming throughout the ten directions the practice of conduct, you honor the merit of liberation;
the Buddha’s achievements are peerless, for the Great Sage teaches the path of wisdom.
Seeing that worldly beings are bound in the darkness of defilement, quickly manifest the radiance of the Dharma-light.
Swiftly beholding the three thousandfold world-system, they practice the Way and preach thus.
Their marks and signs are like a multitude of flowers; they uphold the Way with immeasurable voices.
Their samādhis are equal to Mount Sumeru—such is the conduct of the bodhisattvas.
Peerless and without guile, free from the self and the three stains, most tranquil and praised by the multitude, I ask about the conduct of the Honored One among Men.
His intent is firm, his speech harmonious and sublime; what he teaches is complete and without omission.
The Noble Holy One burns away the dust, just as the Buddha’s Way has taught me.
I take refuge and enter the Buddha’s Way; day and night I am diligent without deviation.
Hearing this supreme Dharma that accords with truth, I shall always remain upright according to the instructions of the Way.
If one maintains a mind of constant concentration, with supernormal powers, eloquence, and wisdom,
one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions and asks the Sages how they attain tranquility.
Preaching wisdom beyond compare, one understands countless gateways of meditative absorption.
Because what you have taught is tireless, you inquire about the practices of the ten directions.
You do not ask about entering states of bliss, nor do you consult on the limits of the spheres;
O Wondrous and Victorious One, Crown of the Great Sages, you proclaim only the practices of the ten directions.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Your inquiry is most profound, out of compassion for all beings. There is a samādhi called "Comprehending the Source of All Dharmas.

If a bodhisattva practices this samādhi-concentration, they will attain these meritorious virtues and immediately reach this state of practice. Their majestic spiritual power will be sublime, and they will fully accomplish two thousand one hundred matters of the *pāramitās*. They will master eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi and eighty-four thousand gates of *dhāraṇī*, embodying and understanding sentient beings so as to enter universally into all modes of conduct. Thus, they will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said,
“King Priya! What is called the samādhi that realizes the fundamental nature of all dharmas?”

If there is a bodhisattva who practices the six firm dharmas, whose physical, verbal, and mental kindness accord with their speech and actions, who does not contradict the Three Vehicles nor fail in their essential vows, who understands the practices of the Three Vehicles, and who reveals to the people the karmic deeds they have performed—both their words and their deeds being thus consistent.

Their physical conduct is pure and their speech is gentle like nectar; their mental reflections are clear and bright like the light of the sun. They constantly practice compassion and always harbor a mind of loving-kindness; they harbor no harmful intent and never abandon great pity. They have no attachment to anything and do not crave sensual desire; their physical actions are luminous and pure, and their will delights in what is appropriate for the Dharma. They do not lose their steadfast faith and honor utmost sincerity; they do not forsake their own vows nor those of all beings.

"Distinguishing and yet extinguishing conceptualization, he does not seek ultimate extinction; he delivers sentient beings according to their original conduct, clearly understanding both transgression and merit without disturbing the mundane world. He never craves his own body nor exerts himself in worldly pursuits; out of compassion for the suffering and afflictions of the masses, he desires to deliver them, encouraging all to bestow peace and not to create peril."

He transforms those who are conceited so that their arrogance is subdued; he causes the indolent to become diligent and advance in the teachings of the Way; and he practices the Dharma-treasury of unsurpassed wisdom.

He does not establish the notion of a person, his mind is free from obstruction, and he does not reckon what he possesses, thereby uprooting all fundamental attachments. He severs the bonds of worldly affairs, his will is fixed on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and he analyzes all conceptualizations without harboring any expectations. He does not abandon meditative absorption (*samādhi*) but constantly seeks wisdom; he distances himself from worldly talk, his will is solely directed toward reaching the state of abiding, and he expounds upon supramundane deeds without mundane thoughts.

One’s mind shall not be negligent or forgetful, eliminating all obscurations; constantly contemplating the sutras and the Dharma with an undisturbed heart, one enters what is appropriate without losing propriety. Establishing the dharmas of practice, one understands the world, remains free from transgressions or debts, and perfects all karmic deeds. Through the practice of the six perfections, one abandons lack of faith; harboring much sincerity and trust, one is devoted to the Buddha-way. Constantly mindful of the Buddha and the Dharma, one diligently repents of faults; delighting in assisting in merit, one bestows it upon sentient beings. Because of this, one exhorts all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma, and one should praise the Sages without flattery or deceit.

Accumulating merit and virtue with constant diligence, their minds never wearying or abandoning their practice of diligent cultivation; they follow the path of deeds and the Bodhisattva Dharma, delighting in giving and cherishing all beings with compassion; always harboring a vast intention to seek the cessation of karma, they do not fail in the perfection of restraint, remaining compliant with the teachings.
Their body, speech, and mind are pure and undefiled.

With such sincerity, they follow the teachings upon which they rely without transgression or neglect; they do not dwell in the realm of desire, nor do they lean upon the realm of form, but remain tranquil within the formless realm. They place their faith and joy in the reliable fruits resulting from their practices, firmly abiding in the Mahāyāna without ever regressing.

Entering into places of ignorance and darkness, if one dwells in a mind of stinginess and does not practice this, one should instead offer worship with an impartial mind, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they are free from flattery and deceit, do not deceive the Buddhas, harbor no harmful intent toward the various Bodhisattvas, and refrain from disrupting the holy work with words of falsehood.

"Seeing those who are diligent or those who are indolent, one maintains no dualistic mind; one does not envy the offerings given to others, fulfills great vows, and abandons thoughts of arrogance and anger. One eliminates ignorance through the rectification of foolish, perverse, and deluded conduct; one constantly examines oneself and does not speak of the faults of others, feeling shame and self-reproach for falling short of the Buddha-dharma."
Practicing the Way with a focused mind, he further knows contentment; having renounced his kin, he is weary of decay and decline, and does not strive for gain or offerings.

If he obtains anything, he shares it with others; he does not violate the precepts, nor does he indulge in the faults of common sleepiness. He is able to constantly endure coarse speech, always being cautious with his words and perpetually establishing the transformation of the Path. He praises and chants the virtues of diligence, always maintaining a joyful and harmonious mind, and draws near to and associates with those who are liberated.

Diligently and frequently inquiring after the practice of dwelling in seclusion, he did not abandon solitary retreat and constantly observed the limits of proper conduct. With meritorious virtue, he delighted in practicing the meaning of emptiness; he did not crave conditioned phenomena, did not rely on the aggregates of the body, did not take pleasure in the various elements, did not accept the sense bases, did not set his will upon wealth or profit, and did not dwell within sensory realms. Having removed all inverted views, his mental activity became firm and strong; he cultivated the practices of the noble ones, contemplating the luminous nature of the mind’s source, and attained the ground of universal stillness where all conditioned activities come to rest.

Giving without expectation, precepts without conceptualization, patience without mental construction, diligence without loss, meditative concentration without arising, and wisdom without guidance—by honoring the true and correct Dharma, these perfections (pāramitās) lead one to enter the abode of equality. Not praising one's own virtues and not disparaging the merits of others, neither relying on birth-and-death nor attaining nirvāṇa: this is liberation.

"Having extinguished the passions of love and established the ultimate truth, his face is always serene and joyful; he abandons all looks of anger and is the first to offer greetings. He respects those who are old, young, and of middle age, constantly consulting and praising them with a sincere heart. Cherishing benevolence and kindness, he is free from any intent to harm and does not dwell on idle speech."

They constantly extol the practice of tranquility and detachment; wherever they are, they act with harmony and accord, reconciling those who are divided and maintaining equanimity toward both enemies and friends, free from hatred or attachment.
They seek dhāraṇī and compassionately regard all sentient beings as they would their own father, mother, body, child, or teacher and preceptor—no different from these venerable elders.

They honor the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, filling the space before them as they move with the wind; they serve the Tathāgatas, delighting in their excellence and purity. They harbor no cowardice, revering the Triple Gem; wherever they dwell or travel, they accumulate no possessions. They limit their clothing and food, not being greedy for body or life; their nature is ever pure as they constantly practice begging for alms. They do not abandon contentment or forsake the assembly; they have no longing for household affairs nor do they take pleasure in leaving the community. They do not engage in ornamentation and are free from hypocrisy; their speech is lovely, such that all who hear it rejoice. They exhort and assist the multitude to resolve upon the Way; they are without delusion in their conduct, practicing in accordance with the teachings, and repeatedly praising the Buddhas, the Most True Ones.

Cultivating the path of the Dharma with the mind, one reveres the noble assembly; honoring and following wisdom and clarity, one practices to follow the attainment of knowledge. Protecting the meditative contemplation of the assembly, one transforms others through diligence; constantly proclaiming the Way and its Virtue, one perpetually accords with and practices the Dharma. Believing in the root of merit, one transforms sentient beings; delighting in earnest faith, one lectures and guides them from all sufferings. With pure deportment, one always establishes great benevolence; possessing a sense of shame, dread of blame, and modesty, one casts off evil people and the company of the unvirtuous.

They cultivate ultimate karma, resolve upon the gates of liberation, and seek the conduct of the noble ones. They uphold the four foundations of mindfulness, practice the equal severance of afflictions, arouse the faculties, cultivate the powers, observe the factors of enlightenment, do not abandon the path of practice, and cross over into nirvana.

“Radiant in all that they perceive, their minds are free from longing or conceptualization; they delight in the scriptural teachings and do not violate the purity of the monastery; they are without shame or remorse, free from inversion and thoughts of desire, and aspire to the conduct of a bodhisattva.”

The Buddha-way is vast and boundless; one who is weary of and detests deviant practices eliminates the evil karma accumulated over countless kalpas of the past, cultivating the body to be pure and untainted, with a mind of tranquility and conduct in accordance with the precepts, honoring and upholding the weighty teachings without flaw.

In their conduct, they discard what is untimely according to the occasion; they clearly understand how to act appropriately in coming and going and social interaction; they are filial toward their two parents; they further know the proper measure for clothing, food, and requisites; and they master supernatural powers while maintaining a lucid and settled mind.

Without disparaging right practice, they deliver sentient beings; they receive and uphold the sutras proclaimed by the Tathāgata; they protect and accord with the purity of the assembly while removing its defilements; they guide the sons of the Buddha and bestow upon all bodhisattvas the dwelling places of the Buddhas.

They cultivate manifold wisdom through the practice of benevolence and harmony, delighting in honoring the true and correct. They exhort and transform all beings to resolve upon the guidance of the Way; they take great pleasure in the meaning of the Path and protect the three periods of time. They contemplate the pure karma that serves as the source for the majestic purity of the rewards of the Buddha-lands, and they constantly delight in attending to their own faults as if honoring their two parents, attaining *dhāraṇī* to serve as their sphere of contemplation.

"Attaining samādhi is the bathing pool; the pure and white dharmas are the mother who gives birth [to it]; by attaining firm abiding in all unconditioned states, one focuses the mind in concentration."

Though there is that which is delivered, it is as if nothing were delivered; there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither signs nor signlessness. The guidance and transformation he follows likewise lack any manifold excellence. He establishes Buddha-lands through the attainment of *dhāraṇī*, and his speech is as clear and pure as that of all the Buddhas. He crosses over the realm of Māra with martial valor, slaying the various defilements and eradicating all that is unwholesome. His vow for pure radiance cannot be destroyed by Māra, and the wisdom of the Path he proclaims is inexhaustible, beyond what the world can praise.

It cannot be known by the various heterodox practices of outsiders; it transcends the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. It is that which all should take refuge in and rely upon to establish omniscience, understanding the destinies of sentient beings and guiding them toward the true reality.

Delighting in and rejoicing in the Dharma, he desires to awaken sentient beings; for those who take pleasure in manifold defilements, he causes them to aspire toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), guiding them across to the other shore by means of the ship of the Dharma.

Carrying them on rafts to rescue one another, he takes pity upon the various devas and proclaims the single Dharma. In whatever place he stands, he is free from all deception or fraud; desiring to give, he purifies his mind to bring joy through transformation, and he causes those addicted to frivolous play to abandon it and devote themselves to the path of the Way.

If one desires extensive learning, maintains reverence, humility, and compliance without indulgence, attains samādhi concentration, and whose aspirations and conduct are lofty and subtle, surpassing Mount Sumeru;
who delights in the five faculties, observes the non-existence of all phenomena, and with a mind fond of diligence dwells in the stage of non-retrogression—this is called the patience of non-arising.

"This is what newly initiated bodhisattvas should practice and uphold. You noble sons, grasp the banner of wisdom and strive to seek the Most Honored and Holy One. Like valiant warriors who realize there is no self, abide in omniscience; universally understand those sentient beings who are to be delivered and liberated; be praised by the devas, revered by the nāgas and spirits, and served by the people; and swiftly establish various kinds of meritorious deeds."

All those who have not yet attained realization take refuge in them together; all the Bodhisattvas join in praising them; and all the Lords of Dharma proclaim their teachings in unison. With their faculties stilled and stabilized as their citadel, they guide and benefit all beings through skillful means. Having attained refined contemplation, they resolve the doubts of the multitude, severing all hesitation and removing the dust of affliction, thereby delivering and liberating countless sentient beings.

"If there are those who are ill, one shall provide them with various medicines to treat their ailments and eliminate their sores and pains; always delighting in contemplation and possessing great diligence, one shall establish fearlessness and desire to roar like a lion, entering into analytical eloquence to expound the principles of meaning, manifesting transformations through supernormal powers, delighting in hearing the manifold teachings, and purifying the eye of the Path to illuminate the way to Nirvana."
Abandoning all evil destinies, they cross over the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, establishing all Buddha-lands.

They give rise to such illusion-like samādhi, sit upon the lion throne, and fully accomplish the state of *anābhoga* (the effortless). Never forgetting the root of all virtues, they transform and gladden those who are indolent, uprooting their various desires and perversions; they establish diligent cultivation and mindfulness to rescue the lazy, leading sentient beings through the equal transformation of the Three Vehicles. Casting aside their worldly occupations and all possessions, they possess all-knowledge and attain immeasurable gateways to govern the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

"Regarding the laws and teachings, they understand and penetrate the practice of emptiness, thereby severing disputes and litigation. They cherish faith in the unsurpassed vows of the Buddha-way; though amidst manifold thoughts, they harbor no perverse conceptions. Viewing the three periods of time with equanimity, they do not fall into erroneous views. Through skillful means, they universally enter all things, exalting the Great Way and never treating those seeking deliverance with contempt."

The Dharma Master Yue was like a calf that never tires of its mother; though he followed the Dharma Master, he did not crave gain or offerings. He observed the preaching of the Dharma without showing contempt for the assembly, never interrupting the gift of the Dharma, and responding to questions with benevolence and harmony. He revered the Three Jewels as his foundation to resolve the nets of doubt for the multitude, serving with such earnest diligence that he never ceased or desisted, ultimately never failing in the noble and enlightened work.

"By relying on the gates of liberation, with harmony, joy, and meditative concentration, they digest all defilements so that the mind has no attachments; they contemplate what should be contemplated and promote the three matters of the bodhisattva deeds, using these three matters to manifest for the assembly the sweet flavor of the Path."

If one wishes to manifest transformations and proclaim the work of the Way with a voice like thunder, instructing and guiding those in birth-and-death through the twelve links of dependent origination, opening the gate of cessation toward the gate of Nirvana, and entering the broad path out of compassion, their body shall be secure and their mind forever free from affliction.

Beloved by all the sages, he has never deviated from [the truth]; firm and impartial, his Tathāgata-merit cannot be turned back; he cultivates the root of virtuous qualities to eliminate misfortune; he demonstrates the source of all goodness and trains in noble wisdom; relying upon these, he perfects the karma of radiant clarity.

"In the marks and signs of his conduct, he does not deceive himself; he follows and cultivates the Buddha-way, illuminating the category of wisdom; he expounds upon the Buddha-lands and engages in inquiry and response, such that in the face of boundless difficulties, he gives rise to the pure and white dharmas."

Without wearying of the Buddha-way and without abandoning those of slight wisdom, they associate with those who find it difficult to learn, treating them with love, respect, harmony, and unity. They proceed with a courageous and precious mind, remaining steadfast in their practice; whenever they wish to speak, they protect the general discourse, being joyful in its various aspects, and they manifest all karmic retributions to sentient beings so that they may not commit transgressions.

Thoroughly understanding all dharmas and practicing skillful means, his mind dwells upon auspiciousness and what he perceives is examined with precision; constantly reflecting upon himself, he brings joy to others, tears asunder the net of afflictions, and eliminates ignorance.

Detaching from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), eliminating all consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), reaping name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), pacifying the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), severing all sensations (*vedanā*), cutting off painful and pleasant feelings (*sparśa*), dissolving craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and relinquishing that which is grasped.
Exhausting all that exists, he uproots the source of harm and transcends old age, sickness, and death; he forever disperses suffering and affliction so that no further obstacles remain.

Having already abandoned suffering and transgression, his mind is free from attachment; his practice is thorough and pervasive, providing eternal relief from the three calamities. His contemplation is untainted as he proclaims the scriptural canons; walking alone like a hero, he bathes away all defilements and eliminates craving for the body.

Hearing the Dharma, they uphold, gather, and govern all teachings; studying the Way without weariness, they enter the source of all virtues and never turn back. Accumulating immeasurable merit and the true meaning, they embrace the Buddha’s light and manifest the eye of the Dharma. They praise the noble assembly and subdue those of external paths; they extol the instructions of the Dharma and practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva. Without indulging in worldly play, they utilize their days for transformation and benefit, causing them to distance themselves from both sin and merit, so that their study and practice are like the sun.

"Reverently honoring kings and guiding the multitude of sages, they accumulate causes of purity to bring about the fruit of immortality; their conduct and deportment allow them to know their past lives, and wherever they are born, they always remember them without forgetfulness."

Feeling weary of and detesting the teachings of the foolish, they take pleasure in the true and correct merits of all Tathāgatas and establish them; through the dharmas and teachings upheld by immeasurable paths of merit, they turn toward omniscience.

If one proclaims [the Dharma] so as to bring about abiding in it, transcribes its scriptures, abandons all fear, does not fall into extremes, remains firm and unshakable, and delivers discourses, then all the world shall together recite them.

"All Buddhas of the past have fully expounded this Dharma and have always remained close to it; all Buddhas of the present and all Buddhas of the future shall likewise fulfill their vows and attain supreme merit, entering into the conduct of all sentient beings."

Manifesting the Vehicle of the Śrāvakas and appearing as those of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, they uphold the Buddha-dharma without ever forgetting any gateway of practice; do they thus give birth to Buddhahood?

They proclaim the true and correct path to swiftly achieve right wisdom, inquire into the virtues of the Buddhas to provide protection throughout the three periods of time, and transform the silent perils of affliction. Having attained skillful means, they distinguish the elements of earth, enter the samādhis of the elements of water and fire, establish the element of wind, and further, through the element of space, reach the gateway of liberation.

With pure, empty, and seed-like wisdom, they guide and benefit the three realms; harboring no afflictions, they eliminate all fetters until none remain. Casting off all attachments, they submerge the various hindrances so that the mind becomes serene and tranquil. They clearly cultivate bodily conduct and dwell in eternal peace, while also understanding the actions of others and the states in which they abide, whether in existence or cessation.

"If one expounds written words without relying on verbal expressions, casting off the notion of self and having the mind already detached from all such dependencies and desires, then though remaining amidst them, one observes them as a dog smelling [filth]; entering into the subtle and gradually awakening from the exhaustion of manifold labors, one crosses over the various torrents without destroying the factions of others, skillfully advancing in the Dharma of the Path without any attachment."

Reverently honoring the good teacher, abandon the fault of drowsiness and cross beyond all obstacles; sever doubt, dispel lustful desire, and cast off indolence. Protecting against the notion of self, act as a luminous guide for sentient beings; do not fixate on life, nor greedily seek after dharmas. Do not speak excessively; let your words be pure and harmonious, and always contemplate with clarity that you ought to practice with urgency.

"In practicing the Way of benevolence and clarity, one need not give rise to deliberate thoughts; one delights in dwelling in seclusion yet moves among the multitude, harbors no cowardice and seeks not the faults of others, but reflects upon one's own conduct and constantly upholds the Buddha-way."

One should abide in equanimity; before long, one will dwell in a single land, relinquishing all that is craved so that one’s state becomes imperial peace. One extinguishes the manifold darkness of the body, and the mind is neither weak nor inferior. One cultivates skillful means to nourish the intention, yet remains free from conceptual thought, not seeking liberation through the attachment of consciousness.

The mind is constantly focused on giving rise to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); it equally observes loving-kindness, extends compassion and grace, always practices sympathetic joy, and gladdens others with a serene countenance and a joyful expression through the Dharma.

"Relying upon your compassionate protection to rescue those fallen into harm, you constantly deliver people through the causes of precepts and prohibitions. Entering into samādhi, you penetrate all dharmas with this wisdom; you master written characters and thoroughly investigate them through reflection, thereby unraveling all fetters so that beings may be free from fear."

Entering into all sounds and voices to attain beneficial meaning, they constantly delight in expounding the Dharma as it is bestowed; they rejoice in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, never wearying of solitary retreat; their resolve is fixed upon the Path, without distinction of high or low.

Not lacking in any dharmas, he proclaims and accords with them, never deceiving sentient beings; his resolve and delight are firm and steadfast, thereby achieving fulfillment; he practices with diligence day and night without ceasing or slackening—this is called the Samādhi of Correct Concentration that Realizes the Source of All Dharmas.
When the Bodhisattva practices this, they enter universally into the realms of all sentient beings and honor all-knowledge.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Practicing purity, The great path of the Sages, With a mind of faith and joy..."
Free from delusive karma,
with self-awakened intent, this essential eloquence is the samādhi of abiding in giving.
It subdues all māras, removes all defilements, and severs the causal conditions of birth-and-death and desire.
Wisdom and renown, wealth and virtuous merit, protecting the three realms—
this is the perfection of deliverance.
Of noble and wise lineage, he eliminates worldly attachments and delivers all from suffering.
This samādhi praised by the Buddha is the dwelling in giving, entering the subtle and wondrous gateway of the primordial limit.
Through clear realization, one is free from anger and resentment; severing all suffering and affliction, one enters eternal peace.
This samādhi is the practice of all Buddhas; it is the liberation within the mind, the flower of awakened intent.
It is the abiding of all who dwell in peace, the garland of awakened mindfulness—to speak of this is supreme.
Samādhi is the concentration;
the flowers of awakening, The gate of liberation and illumination, like the full moon, Outshining the multitude of stars.
The light of the Way pervades the three realms; This Dharma transcends all, and thus it is praised as being like the moon.
With the threefold penetration as medicine, one brings about purity;
dwelling in seclusion beneath a quiet tree, one abandons gain and offerings as well as flattery,
and through the accumulation of practice, seeks this samādhi.
Not concealing one's virtues, not seeking profit, praising the qualities of one’s own body;
wearing the three robes, always begging for food, personally seeking this— practicing samādhi.
Questioning the wise, constantly sighing in solitude, consulting and lecturing upon them,
and practicing the essentials, one swiftly attains this samādhi concentration.
Sentient beings alike, weary of all flavors, distance themselves from the assembly and delight in stillness; they constantly seek this sublime samādhi.
Do not be fawning or deceitful; aspire to this treasury, rely on shame and remorse, and savor the taste of liberation.
Rest upon the meditation seat, dwell in contemplative stillness, delight in non-self, and always remain joyful.
With the mind ever at peace, endure the insults of others as if they were echoes in the void;
remaining in true practice, let the heart harbor no resentment.
This is samādhi—know this through faith—and understand the retribution of both sin and merit.
Do not practice perversity or the karma of the evil realms; constantly cultivate emptiness, the source of the noble ones.
Diligent day and night with the power of vigor, attain samādhi and reach the gate of wisdom.
The path that is without benefit, the mind set on equanimity, the truth of the Way,
and the establishment in non-arising; beholding the meaning of the Dharma— those who practice this are the objects of the Buddha’s compassionate regard.
2. Chapter on Conduct. Chapter Two. The Buddha said:

"This Bodhisattva King of Joy, having attained this Samādhi of the Fundamental Nature of All Dharmas, understands that all dharmas are free from inversion; because all dharmas are immovable and cannot be tilted, his practice and aspirations aim at rescuing and liberating those in the five destinies. He subdues and transforms all Māras so that they submit naturally. He is loved and respected by the people and sentient beings of the world, and revered by the wise, seeking to fully elucidate all dharmas as well as what is non-dharma."

His virtue and wisdom are as bright as the full moon among the multitude of stars; having long dwelt within birth and death, he is known by all sentient beings. He exhorts and transforms all, his will and nature being pure, and having relinquished all that is grasped, he is protected and sustained by the trichiliocosm.

Having attained the stages of the Way, he discerns non-self and realizes there is nowhere to which one can return; seeing the three realms of suffering, he transforms and guides them as a protector of sentient beings, attaining reverence and humility without becoming self-important.

Transcending all aggregates and hindrances, they clearly understand what the Buddhas have proclaimed; they expound upon the appropriateness of the timing for nirvāṇa, thereby further attaining the thirty-two marks of a great man.

"Whether there is gain or loss, suffering or pleasure, fame or insignificance, praise or blame—by understanding that these eight worldly dharmas are all devoid of attachment, one rescues all sentient beings and consoles them with the nectar of immortality. One manifests parinirvāṇa to awaken all, removes their burning afflictions, and severs these hindrances. Never clinging to or being deluded by the six sense faculties, one enters the gate of the sixteen-syllable dhāraṇī and recognizes its destination; being able to proclaim this, one thereby attains dhāraṇī."
"What are the sixteen? First is called 'non-existence';
second is called 'crossing over'."
Third is practice;
fourth is non-practice;
fifth is upholding.
Sixth is obstruction;
seventh is activity;
eighth is solidity.
Ninth is power;
tenth is birth;
eleventh is integration.
Twelfth is exhaustion;
thirteenth is obscuration;
fourteenth is cessation.
Fifteenth is abiding;
sixteenth is burning.
These sixteen matters constitute the teaching of written words.

If one’s practice of understanding consists of the teaching of these sixteen syllables, they will attain the stage of immeasurable *dhāraṇī* gates; they will understand all phenomena and attain mastery, discerning and seeking the wisdom-intent of all sentient beings; they will eliminate all worldly afflictions and proclaim the Buddha-way everywhere, receiving great power and penetrating the true Dharma; they will deliver and transform the masses, guiding them toward benefit, their voice harmonious and elegant like that of a phoenix, until they attain the stage of universal abiding in equanimity.

He utters the lion’s roar with sublime majesty; through the perfection of patience, he is fully endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Transcending the realm of Māra, he is completely proficient in the sounds of lamentation and the voice of the Truly Real (*tathatā*). Having abandoned self-conceit, he attains forbearance; he realizes the profound and abstruse meanings, and there is nothing non-virtuous in his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Wherever he goes, he proclaims the unsurpassed Dharma; he gathers all essential sūtras, his power being difficult to equal. He discerns the gateways to the path of all dharmas and knows the destinations to which the conduct of sentient beings tends.

“Recalling the countless kalpas he has traversed, he constantly upholds all dharmas to extinguish every ailment; having purified and removed the web of fetters and severed all doubt, he swiftly attains perfect enlightenment and is praised for his radiant manifestation. Universally entering the noble wisdom of all dharmas, he is able to use skillful means to extract the heat of affliction, preaching all dharmas while personally practicing them.”

"Clad in the food of ambrosia, he tears asunder all doubts; abandoning his own dwelling-place, he manifests unsurpassed compassion to cover all sentient beings. Mindful of his past lives and the places where he was reborn, he is resolved upon the virtue of Nirvāṇa to enlighten the ignorant and foolish. He understands the destination of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and attains supreme wisdom; he gathers all perceptions and establishes them in their proper abodes. Without losing the stages of the Path, he transcends various transformations; he penetrates all sounds and voices while setting aside all [worldly] attachments. Wherever bonds are untied, he brings fulfillment to the Buddha-fields."
"Remaining detached from the five aggregates without conceit, one swiftly understands all verbal expressions; for this reason, one subdues Māra and abandons all non-Buddhist teachings.

One beholds the present Buddhas in incalculable lands throughout the ten directions, hears the Dharma they preach, and upholds it without forgetting; thus, according to one's vow, one attains this samādhi and finds therein self-delight."
If there is a bodhisattva who attains this samādhi, one should say that they have reached all-knowledge (sarvajñā). Why is this?

Because by means of this concentration, at the very moment they resolve their minds, they become a successor in their final birth and attain supreme perfect enlightenment; from one they give rise to two, from two to three, and from three to four—immediately upon resolving their minds, they attain the Way of the Buddha.
"Why is this? Furthermore, this samādhi is itself omniscience.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Immeasurable and beyond instruction, he is without equal;
his origin has no point of return, for he is liberated from all realms of existence.
Subduing and transforming without attachment, his supreme excellence is boundless.
Upholding this sublime model, the wondrous conduct of the ten directions;
abandoning strife for the sake of joy, with a mind weary of the dust of manifold defilements;
supremely delighting in the truth among men, his speech is exceedingly fluent.
Supreme in following the merit of Asaṅga, he has cast off the darkness of birth;
upholding this Dharma, he establishes it throughout the ten directions.
Thoroughly understanding and transcending all explanations, he exhorts others with joy toward the further shore.
Honored and revered by gods and men, his acts of giving and relief are foremost.
Through the *pāramitā* of all practices, he courageously proclaims virtue;
by cultivating and upholding the scriptural verses, he reaches the stage of the Ten Powers.
Having abandoned the distractions that hinder coming and going, one is then able to reach fundamental non-being;
according to what the mind desires, one transforms and enlightens the multitudes.
Attaining the practice of traveling the true path, wherever one dwells, there is no defilement.
By means of this, the eye of giving is clarified; his conduct wanders where there is no wandering.
His will is firm and filled with compassion; he regards all people as his own infants.
Wherever the Honored One among Men goes, he exhorts and instructs others regarding their various evil deeds.
Forever free from destruction, he roars with confidence amidst the assembly;
thus establishing his practice, there is none among the multitudes who equals him.
He attains protection throughout the ten directions, as well as for all others who have not yet reached it.
Exhorting people to joy without limit, they long cultivate tranquil concentration.
Renouncing their household affairs, they promote the Dharma like nectar;
upholding this sutra, they return to supreme virtue.
Having accumulated many meritorious deeds and instructed countless people, you have exhorted and gladdened the ignorant masses; never for long did you indulge in play or indolence.
You have clearly understood the six realms of existence, and through tranquil excellence, you have awakened to what is good.
Delighting in harmony and bringing peace to all, he abides in these meritorious practices.
Attaining extraordinary renown and glory, like the moon moving through the dustless sky,
he delivers the multitudes of devas and humans, standing before them without fear.
His fame flows everywhere, supreme; he bestows the most excellent nectar.
Practicing what ought to be practiced here, he swiftly attains the Way of the Buddha.
Abiding in that which is appropriate to dwell in, he is present before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He proclaims that which ought to be taught, in order to transform all devas and humans.
What he expounds is most subtle and wondrous; he also proclaims the practice of the Ultimate Truth.
By reverently cultivating these practices, one shall always delight in the Dharma of the Deathless (Amṛta).
Having subdued the power of Māra, he establishes others in benevolence and harmony;
transcending all realms of suffering, they return to the Buddha’s true path.
Reaching the ultimate state of excellence, they abandon the circuitous ways of worldly existence.
"Practicing courageous skillful means, one achieves and maintains virtuous qualities.
The Buddha said:

"If there are bodhisattvas who study this samādhi, all Buddhas of the ten directions will protect them. With wisdom they illuminate their minds so that they become clear and enlightened, not being obscured by the hindrances of the aggregates (skandha-nīvaraṇa). They attain supernormal powers (abhijñā) through which their vision is infinite; the assembly of bodhisattvas all together nurtures them, enabling them to achieve the stage of being 'born only once more' (ekajātipratibaddha), while the multitude of śrāvakas come from afar to praise them."

"Desiring that [this work] be completed early so that the ten directions may receive deliverance, I have petitioned the King of the Brahmā Heaven, who presides over the seventh heaven and possesses all Brahmā attributes, to personally provide protection from afar and dispatch the hosts of devas to come and offer their compliance."

Śakra, the King of Gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, possessing merit from past lives, recognizes those who study this samādhi with utmost sincerity; he dispatches various devas and humans to descend and provide protection, ensuring that their practice remains peaceful and secure, free from any unauthorized interference.

The Four Heavenly Kings shall personally attend to him and dispatch their subordinates to protect the Dharma Master; for four thousand li around, they shall ensure that no one seeks to find an opportunity to harm him, so that the True Dharma may be expounded and recited in peace and tranquility, transforming and enlightening all beings within the five realms of birth and death.
The fourfold assembly revered him, making offerings without weariness and listening to his teachings without fatigue.

When he preached the sutras for others, he gained the minds of his fellow students so that they were all at ease; each found their own place and harbored no resentment. Even if someone conceived a jealous heart and wished to cause disorder, they were unable to do so.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva constantly practices patience and maintains a mind of benevolence and harmony; if someone becomes angry toward him, he does not dwell upon that person's evil. If there is an adversary who comes intending to cause harm, he does not contend with them but simply avoids and departs from them so as not to meet. Even if they encounter one another on the road, it is as if they have not seen each other at all.

With compassionate thoughts, cause all those throughout the ten directions to take refuge in the Buddha; do not harbor evil intentions or slander the Dharma Master. Contemplate that the Dharma itself is without fault, but rather pity those individuals who, harboring poisonous hearts, fall into the perils of the three miserable realms of the evil destinies.

Their foolish delusions give rise to transgressions and harms that in turn endanger their own persons, just as when trees rub against one another in a rising wind and suddenly produce fire that burns their own forms; like a venomous snake whose poison increases day by day until it harms its own body; or like iron that produces various impurities which bury its own form.

Shrouded in the darkness of folly, their minds remain closed and unenlightened; they do not contemplate the kindness of the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, but instead give rise to harmful intentions and act in opposition to their teacher. Driven by greed, envy, and jealousy, they seek to endanger and destroy him, allowing themselves to indulge in arrogance for a time, heedless of the great calamity that awaits—a truly piteous and tragic state of affairs.

The devas, ghosts and spirits, celestial deities of the void, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas all went to pay homage, prostrating themselves and taking refuge; they never grew weary of wishing to see him and repeatedly came forward to welcome him. They listened to and received the sūtras, inquiring into their meaning and attaining understanding; they contemplated and practiced them without ever becoming indolent or weary, for all the spirits loved, revered, served, and made offerings to him.

He honors morality as a filial son grieves when parting from his parents; though years have passed, his longing remains insatiable. All the celestial deities, spirits, humans, and non-humans cherish and revere his boundless and ultimate virtue; this is all brought about by the Bodhisattva’s diligent and sincere cultivation of this samādhi of loving-kindness and compassion, and it is for this reason that he possesses such merit.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Joyful King:

"If there is a bodhisattva who accumulates merit and virtue, transforming and enlightening countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, such that they are filled with joy and exultation—this is no different from [the former case]. Without engaging in frivolous laughter, one thereby attains extraordinary merit and renown; one's fame and virtue become far-reaching, and one is praised throughout the ten directions!"

His conduct is as immovable as Mount Sumeru; his brilliance is like the sun and moon, universally illuminating the world; his virtue is as weighty as the earth, giving birth to all things; his Way is honored and his station is high, giving rise to all the categories of the Path—this is the treasury of the Bodhisattva Dharma of the six perfections of the utmost limit.
The mind is like space, free from attachment; it traverses the three realms alone, without hindrance.
It is like a bird flying through the void leaving no tracks, and like a lotus flower unsullied by dust or water.
The Buddhas of the ten directions all cause bodhisattvas to practice this samādhi.

Now the Buddha proclaims it for you; you must be diligent and harbor no doubts. Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or even ordinary people among the ninety-six arts and sixty-two views, or crawling insects, wriggling creatures, those that move by feet or breathe—humans and non-humans alike—who study this samādhi or hear of it with joy, each shall obtain their wish, and thereafter they will surely attain this samādhi.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The Buddha’s True Dharma is ever radiant; it is the joy of the faculty of faith and the foremost wisdom."
Walking like a rhinoceros, free from the notion of self, one maintains this tranquility, the wondrous samādhi.
Attaining mastery and awakening to patience, one covers the three periods of time as if with a canopy.
Establishing transformations for countless people, they practice this wisdom like the ocean.
They eliminate the self and the afflictions of toil, proclaiming the Buddha-way and leading all to nirvana.
By severing defilements and transforming the three periods of time, one swiftly practices; this is tranquility.
Recognizing the body and life, as well as others, one sets the mind upon the path of all Buddhas.
Establishing mindfulness, one attains all karmic results and this wondrous samādhi.
Providing much guidance, one governs the primordial limit, constantly preaching peace and extinguishing suffering and affliction.
The transformative gift, the flavor of ambrosia— To practice this is the lineage of the Buddhas.
Delighting in supreme clarity, with radiant words, Its renown spreads abroad as universal merit.
Amidst the assembly, he is most majestic, like the full moon in the height of autumn’s brilliance.
His retinue, wealth, fame, and virtue— all that exists within the cycle of birth and death—
is known by the Buddha.
His eloquence is like the king of waters; having practiced samādhi, he has attained this merit.
The Dharma is natural and devoid of self; before long, he will master it and expound its meaning.
Thus throughout three thousand worlds, practicing the True Dharma, this is samādhi.
Contemplating and calculating,
throughout three thousand worlds, sentient beings fill them as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If one trains in and takes refuge in the path to the Deathless, the wisdom attained therein will surpass this.
Poison shall not take effect, nor shall sword or fire;
there shall be no danger from insects or snakes, nor fear of the staff; neither kings nor rākṣasas can cause harm.
With a harmonious mind, cultivate this diligently; you shall not lose your wealth, nor perish your family;
you will have no illness or sorrow, and no calamity or affliction.
If one upholds these four lines of Dharma, one's eyes will not go blind and one's hearing will not fail.
If there is study, contemplate this; if you constantly revere it, [you shall attain liberation].
This dhāraṇī, practiced with diligent application, is this samādhi.
If there are those who wish to quickly achieve the Way and delight in the foremost field of merit, they should study this, the root of the sūtra.
All things arrive at, yet are silent and non-existent.
Chapter Three: The Four Matters. "There are four matters by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi."
What are the four?
First is giving: bestowing gifts upon all without harboring expectations for reward.
Second is upholding the precepts: refraining from violating any prohibitions with the resolve to attain the Great Way.
The third is to always maintain a heart of compassion, regarding enemies and those one holds dear with no dualistic mind;
the fourth is to observe all classes of sentient beings within the three realms as being entirely one's own kin, never regarding them as outsiders.
These are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi. What are the four?
First, constantly practicing great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;”
Second, they constantly practice great compassion; seeing the suffering and affliction of sentient beings in the three miserable realms, they shed tears for them, desiring to rescue and deliver them.

Third, observing that the masses are deluded, transmigrating through the five destinies without being able to free themselves, they reveal the correct path so that their will and virtue may emerge spontaneously.

Fourth, examining how the three flows of existence revolve from beginning to end without ever ceasing, causing physical pain and mental distress, they take pity on them and proclaim the root of sin and merit, and the root of birth and death which is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva attains this concentration.
What are these four?

First, it is to observe how sentient beings are deluded by various heterodox views and the sixty-two false perspectives; they hesitate and brood, falling into the net like a bird throwing itself into a trap, failing to realize their own destruction while coveting trivial gains.

Second, it is to observe the ninety-six kinds of paths of confusion where beings create their own ignorance and darkness, like moths flying into a lamp’s flame; once submerged in the three miserable realms and cycling through the five destinies without end, they cannot free themselves, and only the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas can deliver them.

Third, it is to observe those who use external spells and incantations to harm others; the Bodhisattva takes pity on them, for it is like a madman drowning in water and only then feeling regret—by that time, what can be done?

The fourth is: like a hunter shooting at flocks of birds or using nets to catch fish, they accumulate a vast cover of transgressions and fall into the three evil realms for countless billions of years. [The Bodhisattva] abandons the peace of their own body to go and rescue them, proclaiming to them the afflictions of sin, merit, birth, and death; demonstrating the karma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), or further revealing the unsurpassed, right, and true [path] so that each may attain peace.
This is the fourth.
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi. What are the four?

First, one creates an image of the Buddha seated upon a lotus flower, whether by carving it in relief, painting it on a wall, silk, or cotton cloth, making it upright and beautiful so that the multitude may rejoice and thereby obtain the merit of the Way.”
Second, to take this sutra scroll and transcribe it upon bamboo, silk, or fine white cloth, ensuring that the characters are aligned and upright from top to bottom;

third, to recite this sutra day and night with diligence, not abandoning the text until it is mastered and fluent, so that there is not a single stumbling block and listeners may attain understanding;

fourth, to uphold this samādhi and distinguish the beginning and end of all Buddhas point by point to expound their meaning for others, skillfully opening up the unsurpassed, right, and true path for bodhisattvas, causing all beings to consult and receive it together, giving rise to no doubts, and each attaining enlightenment and penetration.
"These are the four.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having heard this sutra, one delights in supreme virtue; if there is a person..."
Seeking this path, how excellent is its study! By means of these four lines, one attains the lineage of the Ten Powers.
The King among Men, together with sixty *koṭis*, dwells securely therein.
They shall always protect these students who are able to recite this samādhi;
having already heard it and being able to believe and rejoice in it, these people shall achieve perfection.
Not doubting the Way, they all see it equally; there is no birth or death.
Practicing the Buddha-way, they obtain this hearing; they delight in meritorious achievements and do not grow weary.
By copying and upholding this sutra, maintaining mindfulness and awareness for hundreds of thousands of eons,
one will attain eloquence and excellence, reaching the state of a Buddha.
He spoke thus of this most settled state of mind; Prince Candra heard it in detail,
abandoned his kingdom, became a śramaṇa, and applied himself diligently day and night to hearing and receiving the Dharma.
In their final existence, as their lives draw to a close, they shall immediately be reborn in the lands of other Buddhas—
lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and even more than that— where all the devas offer worship to the Buddhas.
Following his guidance, he heard of the samādhi and, within three kalpas, attained the path of Buddhahood.
Taught and transformed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara—the Jewel of No Weariness—he heard this and obtained the fruit of virtue; therefore, one should hear it.
Do not be indolent.
For the sake of the ten directions, you are constantly to be saved; now I entrust myself to you with earnest persistence.
O virtuous and worthy one, your speech is gentle and harmonious; this increases the Dharma and is a precious treasury of the Path.
Chapter Four: On the Dharma-Master. The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"In the distant past, incalculable and immeasurable kalpas ago."
At that time, there was a Buddha named Vimalavyūhagarjitaghoṣasvaramajus-tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

During the era of that Buddha, there was a Dharma-preacher named Aparimitaguṇavaiśāradyadhvajavikurvaṇasvara. He had previously heard the Tathāgata preach this samādhi-concentration; having studied this samādhi, he explained its applications in detail to transform sentient beings, delivering countless billions of devas and humans alike.

There was a prince named Viśuddhapuṇyavipākasvararāja who, upon hearing this samādhi, felt great joy in his heart. He then covered the Dharma Master with hundreds of thousands of exquisite, fine garments and spoke these words:
"May all sentient beings throughout the three realms who are in distress be universally enabled to attain and establish themselves in this samādhi."

By virtue of these roots of merit, he beheld as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eighty billion Ganges Rivers; he established various practices to honor the Dharma of equality, and in the presence of those Buddhas, he heard this samādhi.

Having proclaimed them all, they were all able to endure and uphold this meditative concentration; in whatever place they were born, they always remembered their past lives, and in the Buddha-field of Immeasurable Virtue and Purity, they attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
"The Prince named King of Pure Merit and Multitudinous Voices is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
The Dharma Master who taught and liberated sentient beings is the Tathāgata Mahācandra."

The crown prince made offerings to and took refuge in the Dharma Master Debian-chuangying-bianyin, who was immeasurable in virtue. Consequently, for seventy thousand kalpas, he was able to exhaust all veils of sin by virtue of hearing this exposition of the samādhi. For the sake of the prince, [the Dharma Master] removed his exclusion from the monastic community, cleared away all hindrances, and expounded the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*). In every place where he was born, he attained the practice of the dhāraṇīs of immeasurable gates; at the very moment he resolved his mind, even in the space of a finger-snap, he was never apart from the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha said:
"At that time there was another Buddha, named Maitrānana-vimalacandramukhagarbha-tejas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world and preached this samādhi."

There was a son of a householder named Yaśovimalavipulacitta. Having heard this Dharma being preached, he renounced his household affairs out of faith and went forth as a śramaṇa. He abandoned seventy thousand court ladies and such vast treasures—four treasuries of precious jewels and various rare gems—that if they were spread out upon the ground, they would cover each of the three million one thousand eight hundred pleasure gardens. Without ever lifting his feet to step heedlessly upon the earth, and without setting his heart on worldly things, he renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship to practice the life of a śramaṇa.

Having already been a śramaṇa for sixteen thousand years, he has practiced walking meditation with single-minded focus, constantly cultivating diligence without ever ceasing, never once giving rise to a thought of indolence.

Except for the time he took his meals and washed his hands and mouth with those around him, he never slept; he was always self-awakened and did not sit down even once throughout the entire sixteen thousand years.

Immediately, they all received the Dharma taught by the Buddha; they recited it until they were thoroughly proficient, their voices harmonious and elegant, and they attained the dhāraṇī named "Universally Entering All Sounds," causing everyone to bow their heads and pay homage to the Buddha.

A multitude of sixty-six *koṭis* of devas followed him to receive his teachings and served as his attendants; with physical and mental diligence and at all times maintaining composure, they did not neglect their cultivation as they attended upon the Tathāgata.

Now, manifesting in the southern direction, he has attained perfect enlightenment, named Sarvaguṇavyūha; his world is called Guṇaprasanna, and therein, upon that land, he has achieved supreme, right awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I recall a past life, Countless eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
When there was a Buddha named Vyūhaprabhāsa, The Tathāgata Thunderous Roar."
There was a bhikṣu who upheld the Dharma; at that time, while seated upon the lion throne, he expounded this samādhi.
When the prince heard it, he offered excellent, fine robes as an offering to the Dharma Master.
Universally beholding all the Honored Buddhas, one attains the state of Buddha Amitābha.
Whatever offenses were committed in previous lives, whatever transgressions were committed in the past,
upon hearing this flavor of wisdom explained, they are all exhausted without remainder.
There was a Buddha named Vimalacandra who preached this samādhi;
hearing of it, the son of a householder revered the Honored One and left the household life.
For sixteen thousand years, he devotedly practiced and promoted this samādhi.
Never again shall I fall into sleep, nor dwell in indolence;
having attained this noble and holy path through hearing and receiving the teachings,
I shall no longer take pleasure in returning to the household life, nor shall I long for affectionate ties.
They behold incalculable Buddhas, from whom they receive instruction and counsel;
they enter entirely into all the practices of the Path and swiftly attain the Way of Buddhahood.
All their vows are fully perfected, and their names bring joy to the hearts of men.
When the time comes to attain the Way of the Buddha, who would not diligently apply themselves to this task?
In future ages, having heard this Seal of Wisdom, they will find no security even in wealth or worldly affairs;
they will leave the household life without any craving.
Whether reviled or beaten, or even slandered and attacked,
may they each hear and know the Dharma and proclaim what the Buddha has taught;
though encountering hundreds of thousands of calamities and afflictions, may they be able to endure the hardships of sensual desire.
Observing the afflictions of worldly toil, he himself declared that he had attained the path of Buddhahood.
Seeing the Buddha within a dream, he rejoiced, thinking,
"I am truly awakened," and took delight in this and the Dharma, for he no longer doubted the path of the Buddha.
Relying on the pursuit of sounds and benefits, yet hearing this sūtra,
one will naturally enlighten and transform one’s own mind, and before long attain the Way of the Buddha.
Hearing the essential principles of this sūtra and learning of various practices, one shall achieve this.
Free from all further obstructions, his dwelling is like empty space.
Thereupon, having gone forth, he received countless offerings;
yet because of the impurities of his kinsmen, they gave rise to thoughts of slander.
Sharing in calamities to eliminate the karma of affliction, one maintains the mind by relying on what has been heard;
yet others, conversely, treat me with contempt.
Having attained the vision of the perfected light, I shall make offerings to the Great Holy Lord.
In his walking, he was filled with self-surprise, thinking he had attained the Way of the Buddha.
Those who are sycophantic and deceitful remain far removed from the Path;
they harbor grief and anxiety again and again because of their habit of disparaging others.
If there are those who hear this sutra, they shall know they have attained the Buddha-way;
before long they will realize perfect enlightenment and behold Amitābha.
Those who rely on inverted views are likewise far removed from the Way.
If one does not accord with the fundamental, the Buddha will not bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
Observe this son of a householder: having bestowed his treasury of wealth and jewels, he subsequently went forth into homelessness and wandered from house to house for alms.
"From Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, I once heard this meaning:
'One should diligently and reverently practice such a samādhi as this.
Thus spoke the Buddha."

"When a bodhisattva practices the Way, they protect the ten directions with great compassion and transform others who have not yet attained realization. By means of the six perfections, the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, and the six supernormal powers, they employ skillful means to transform the various classes of sentient beings. Those thus delivered are without limit, and they are made to dwell in long-term peace and security. Each abandons their household affairs to cause the Dharma to flourish; they rain down ambrosia and proclaim the scriptures, just as a skilled physician uses medicine to treat the masses, completely eliminating the three combined ailments of wind, cold, and heat."
The mind has four ailments:
first, lustful desire;
second, anger and hatred.
The third is delusion and darkness;
the fourth is the notion of self.
By using the correct meaning of wisdom to reap these four ailments, they are entirely eliminated without remainder, leading to the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.

Just as when the sun rises, all darkness is extinguished and its departure is unknown, so too does the Great Sage, through the wisdom of skillful means, radiate a great brilliance that illuminates the triple world; the five aggregates, the six decays, and the twelve links of dependent origination are naturally extinguished, their destination unknown.
Just as the moon in the darkness naturally brings light that dispels the many glooms of the night, so it is with the Bodhisattva:

through the illumination of the wisdom of the Way, he dwells within the realm of birth and death; though the defilements of the three impurities exist, his mind remains unattached. He transforms and enlightens those subject to the endless sufferings of beginning and end, attains the samādhi of non-arising, and delivers all beings.

Just as the great ocean produces all manner of rare, precious, and extraordinary jewels, such that those who enter it to gather them find no lack and each returns fully satisfied, so it is with the Bodhisattva:

entering the ocean of the Mahāyāna, they select and take up the profound and wondrous teachings of the *kumārabhūta*, adorn and purify the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the gates of the three liberations, and traverse the three periods of time to rescue and relieve those in peril and distress.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King rules over the four realms of the world and is venerated by all beneath heaven, so it is with the Bodhisattva:

he circulates through all instances of birth, old age, sickness, and death; possessing the four immeasurable minds, he transforms these four ailments until they are forever eliminated without remainder, so that their decay and extinction from beginning to end are suddenly and utterly exhausted, such that their whereabouts can no longer be known.
