"Just as a ferryman ferries people back and forth without end, so too, with the casket of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka dhāraṇī, one expounds the true nature of the profound and essential Dharma, traveling through incalculable kalpas without weariness."
Just as parents give birth to and raise their child until they have grown up and attained adulthood, so it is with the Bodhisattva:

through the power of skillful means and wisdom, practicing great compassion, they exhort and transform the ignorant and deluded, causing them to resolve upon the Way. Through the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, and the six perfections, they employ expedient means that reach everywhere throughout the ten directions. They fulfill the ten stages and the state of being one birth away from Buddhahood, attaining unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment—the most supreme awakening—to deliver all beings drowning in the cycle of birth and death, making their minds serene and enabling them to turn back the current and reach the source.
It is just as when a tree is planted and gradually develops roots, sprouts, stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit until it becomes lush; so it is with the Bodhisattva:

from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they attain a joyful mind, and body and mind find rest, free from the afflictions of the five aggregates and the three evil realms, and the sufferings of the eight difficulties. They fully perfect the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—and, regarding that which is unborn, they never rely upon anything and are entirely free from manifold conceptualizations. No longer do they perceive the origin of "self," "person," "body," "life-span," existence, or non-existence; wherever they manifest, they provide extensive salvation for those undergoing birth, old age, sickness, and death throughout their existence in the world.

Abiding in the six dharmas and employing skillful means according to the times, they guide and benefit sentient beings, ensuring they are not led into confusion or obscured by the darkness of ignorance and the coverings of transgressions. Pure as space and undaunted by any hardships, their supreme wisdom is the medicine of immortality, used to heal all the calamities of birth and death.

"It is just as if a householder had many sons, for whom he built ten-storied high pavilions, so that the princes might play upon the pavilions, performing various musical entertainments to delight those who come up and down to observe them."

The World-Honored One, thus employing unobstructed loving-kindness and boundless great compassion, practices skillful means to transform and guide the various classes of sentient beings within the triple world. He reveals the stages of the path, from the beginning of the initial resolve through the entirety of the ten abodes; all who see him rejoice and do not fail to set their minds upon enlightenment. Rising from the first abode, they practice the bodhisattva path, distributing relief to the destitute and bestowing the seven riches upon those in the triple world who are impoverished in the Way. Through the precepts of universal wisdom and true reality, they firmly abide in the boundless wisdom of the bodhisattvas.

Without seeking realization midway, one studies benevolence and harmony, with a mind of sincere faith in the Triple Gem, entering into infinite compassion. Establishing inexhaustible pity, one is endowed with the four immeasurable minds; having fully possessed these four, one achieves the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Once the five powers are perfected, one is fully equipped with the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); having reached the culmination of the six perfections, one attains the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Having attained this patience, it is called the second stage.

The third is the patience of resonance (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*): understanding that all resonances are fundamentally empty and quiescent, and that the sounds of the three realms are all void, unreal, and lack even a single true reality. By comprehending this meaning, one gradually enters the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), fully realizing that the three realms have no root and the five destinies have no origin.

One who realizes this wisdom attains the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Entering into all that arises, their mind is without arising; like empty space, it is without hatred or affection. Thereby they receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); having received the prediction, they attain the present concentration and behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.

"It is like a person with clear vision whose eyes are pure and transparent; at night, when the sky is cloudless, they observe the stars and, looking up toward the sky in the east, west, south, and north, they know the positions of all the infinite stars."

In this way, the bodhisattva attains present concentration and beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions; he fully knows their locations, their names, and their teachings, as well as the number of their bodhisattva disciples and retinues, and the number of those delivered through their preaching of the Dharma.

Arising from samādhi, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of others, practicing the wisdom of the various emptinesses. Those who hear what he teaches all give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. From this point on, he accumulates practice and correctly governs the land; he instructs and transforms sentient beings by perceiving their fundamental natures, administering medicine according to their ailments so that they may take it and practice it, and he guides those with superior, middling, and inferior capacities, each bringing them to their proper place.
"It is like a noble universal monarch who has many sons whom he appoints according to their talents: some become crown princes, later established as sovereigns to govern the four continents;
some become great ministers, attending at his side to protect him;
and some become envoys to proclaim the king’s commands."
In this way, the Bodhisattva transforms all beings, guiding them according to their superior, middling, or inferior capacities.

He may manifest the unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment of a Bodhisattva, explaining the wisdom of the fixed nature of the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*): whether a Buddha appears or not, the dharmas abide as they are. Those whose minds do not enter deeply will not understand this teaching.
Or he may manifest as a *pratyekabuddha* to entice them forward; only upon reaching infinite wisdom do they attain holy clarity, for fundamentally there is no duality.

It is like the many streams of water that converge and return to the ocean, merging into a single flavor. Seeing the terrors of birth and death within the three realms, and the calamities of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, they fear suffering and loathe their bodies, seeking instead the state of a *śrāvaka*. Therefore, [the Buddha] proclaims for them the hardships of birth and death, which revolve without end, circling through the five destinies without finality.

They sighed with admiration and praised the bliss of Nirvana—neither born nor aging, neither ill nor dying; neither hungry nor thirsty, neither cold nor hot; without enmity or fetters; neither opening nor closing, without sorrow or joy; without high or low, neither continuous nor severed; without coming or going, without union or dispersion; eternally free from all hardships and in accord with the Way. Thus, by chanting upon the paths of difficulty and ease, suffering and peace, they led those who study non-action forward step by step until they reached the Great Way.

Just as the four great rivers enter the sea and become of one flavor without any distinction, so too do the three vehicles ultimately reach a single point of fulfillment: the unsurpassed, right, and true, which is boundless and fundamentally pure. Upon reaching the tenth stage, it is called "Valiant Subjugation."
Why is he named "The Brave Subduer"?
It is because he is like a fierce general leading a great army, who brings all his troops to subdue formidable enemies, such that none fail to be humbled and brought under control.

When a bodhisattva thus attains the Samādhi of Valiant Subjugation, they circulate above the existence and non-existence of the three realms. With the Way illuminating the mind, there is nothing that does not penetrate through; each being returns to them and all resolve their minds upon the Way. Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, they subdue the hosts of Māras and deliver beings throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva practices great loving-kindness, Constantly self-disciplining his own mind, And transforming other sentient beings;
Those whom he brings to liberation are always at peace.”
As medicine cures wind, cold, and heat, so the Bodhisattva eliminates the three poisons;
as the rising sun exhausts all darkness, so he guides and transforms beings to eliminate their entanglements.
Just as a householder’s ten-storied pavilion ascends higher with each successive floor, so too does the Bodhisattva progress through the ten stages of abiding.
Just as a tree gradually grows and flourishes, so too does one who has set out as a śramaṇa from folly achieve the likeness of the Way.
Though he bears the heavy burden of benefiting sentient beings, his mind remains attached to kinsmen and relatives, and his heart finds pleasure in the household life.
Not by merely hearing the pure Dharma, nor by failing to leave the household life and observing no precepts, can one achieve the path to Buddhahood; this is the study of non-negligence.
If, in the final age, one studies this and succeeds in hearing this sutra, [one shall attain it].
For the sake of gain and offerings, they seek fame by practicing slander.
Before one's face, they bow their heads in salutation and exclaim, "How excellent!
But once they have departed from that person's presence, they immediately speak of their faults.
Feigning sorrow, she shed tears of rain; returning to herself, she contemplated her own body.
Then, amidst the assembly, she spread rumors of his evil conduct:
that he did not wish to honor his teacher nor obey the commands of his venerable elders.
Seeking superiority for oneself, one calls the chaotic state of stillness "purity.
Desiring to destroy the merits of others, one boasts of one's own boundless achievements;
knowing another is honored, one harbors jealousy, envying them for receiving offerings.
With flowers, incense, and robes, with music, banners, and canopies,
one may make offerings to the Buddha’s relics and claim to have seen the Buddha;
yet if one hears this sutra, that alone constitutes true worship.
Renouncing all pleasures, one should constantly practice this essential conduct.
For the sake of honoring oneself, one must be able to abandon these hindrances;
one should revere the sutras just as Subhūti did.
Abandoning and disregarding craving for life, always practice dwelling in seclusion;
diligently cultivate these sūtras of the Path, for your lifespan in this world is drawing to a close.
Now I address King Nanda: hear what has been practiced in these deeds.
Knowing within themselves that they have subdued their own minds, they profess faith and act in accordance with it.
Yet they constantly slander the Buddha, questioning whether his words are true or not;
though they stand among the fourfold assembly, they still claim their own views to be the ultimate truth.
Those whose occupation is the greed for gain and offerings do not delight in the Buddha’s true path;
such as these, who seek only honor and respect, are very far from liberation.
My great supernormal power now manifests its mighty influence here.
All have attained the Way by guarding the prohibitive laws and practicing them with devotion.
Upholding the supreme dharma of the precepts, they act as if they were ignorant and incapable;
having completely abandoned greed for profit, they cultivate tranquility in secluded dwellings.
Now the Buddha establishes this; what the Buddha has spoken is not in vain.
In the future, during the final age, this sutra shall abide where it is.
One shall encounter immeasurable radiance and again behold the Awakened One, the Unwrathful.
Sixty-two billion Buddhas, together with their assemblies, all beheld this;
the Buddhas all entrusted it to him, and thereafter protected this Dharma.
Having been certified by this sutra, they thereafter jointly guarded and sustained it.
"At that time, as fine rain and subtle flowers fell, the devas and humans of the three thousandfold world system all sighed in wonder because they had heard this Dharma.

At that moment, thirty thousand Bodhisattvas, including the Bodhisattva King of Joy, heard what the Buddha had said; their eyes filled with tears, and in reverent awe their hair stood on end. They extended their right arms, rose from their seats, joined their palms, and with one voice addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! In the future, during the final age of the five turbidities and evil world, we shall not slight the Dharma-preachers.

If there are those who are disrespectful and wish to destroy the All-Knowing One of Universal Radiance; when the Dharma is about to perish and their learning and knowledge are meager and insufficient; when the pure and righteous Dharma is on the verge of extinction; out of fear for the impermanence of the Dharma and at a time when the Dharma is in chaos—we shall sacrifice our own lives to protect this scripture of the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing wisdom, ensuring it is propagated and established forever, and that they may dwell in solitude and study with single-minded devotion.”
With a single mind as steadfast as a rhinoceros, you should receive and protect such a sūtra as this.

Regarding the various treasuries of the Tathāgata’s ultimate path, those who study wisdom and the seals of all eloquence, and who clearly understand the root of immeasurable virtues, should seal them with the Dharma-seal of transformative instruction.

Those of the lineage of dhāraṇī subdue the hosts of Māra’s officials and understand the meritorious deeds performed by those of all-knowledge. They receive and uphold this scripture, recording it upon bamboo and silk.

If they are in the hells for the sake of all beings, they endure all suffering and affliction without weariness; because of this samādhi, they circulate through the difficulties of the three realms and five destinies without becoming exhausted.

Practicing the four immeasurable minds—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and bestowing the four kinds of benevolent giving, he acts with humanity and love to benefit others. He equally benefits and rescues those who are ignorant and deluded throughout the ten directions, causing them all to resolve upon the Way. Thus, those in the hells find rest, hungry ghosts are satiated, and animals are liberated to be reborn among gods and humans.

The minds of devas and humans opened to the Dharma, delighting in it; those in the five realms of existence attained understanding of the mind and came to believe in and revere the Triple Gem, no longer craving worldly glory. They observed the three realms as being like illusions, echoes, mirages, plantains, dreams, bubbles on water, and froth. Realizing that all phenomena are entirely devoid of true reality, they all resolved to attain the Way, desiring to deliver the beings of the ten directions from their perils and hardships.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva King Joy, with a heart filled with both sorrow and joy, spoke these verses:
"Because I have understood this karma, And because my mind delights in the meaning of the Path, I do not disparage such luminous wisdom; I offer praise to the Protector of the World."
Sacrificing their own bodies and lives, they seek this supreme path of the Buddha;
in the fearful worlds hereafter, they maintain this samādhi-concentration.
Even if for incalculable kalpas they should dwell within the hells, [they shall not fall].
Delighting in upholding this samādhi, one should always endure such suffering.
One should invite all sentient beings and preach the Dharma without expectation of reward;
one should give away all manner of wealth and practice compassion toward all living beings.
Even if one’s body, life, flesh, marrow, bones, blood, and veins were to be severed,
one would never practice indolence. In whatever place one is born in future lives,
one will habitually dwell in seclusion, having renounced all possessions.
May compassion pervade all classes of sentient beings, providing medicine to those who are ill.
Having never studied such a practice, which would be like returning to the ways of the heterodox,
one should cultivate these true mantras according to the instructions within this sutra.
Always practicing with heedfulness, following the Buddha’s instructions,
and enduring all for the sake of sentient beings— we are your companions.
Whether dwelling alone or in a crowd, wherever we stay, we have nothing to fear.
"Without craving for gain or offerings, proclaim the sublime path of the Buddha.

When the Buddha preached this sutra, seventy *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of sentient beings who had come from incalculable Buddha-lands all attained the stage of non-retrogression upon hearing this scripture, and shall surely realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, ten thousand bodhisattvas all attained this samādhi concentration; they each made a solemn vow that in the future final age, they would serve and make offerings to the Dharma masters.
Thirty *koṭis* of devas and humans have all attained the stage of non-retrogression and shall realize perfect enlightenment;

sixty *koṭis* of devas and humans have attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; and eighteen hundred million people, including these four assemblies, have given birth to the Dharma-eye, such that the evils of the three miserable realms have been entirely extinguished.

The Buddha emitted rays of light that illuminated the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extending from the Avīci Hell below up to the Ultimate Realm above.

All sentient beings in the Heaven of the Thirty-three attained peace and security, free once more from all afflictions; from those rays of light, there spontaneously manifested countless billions of trillions of pure jewel lotuses.
Upon each and every lotus sat a Tathāgata, and their retinues who had gathered for the assembly were likewise identical, without any difference.

Beside each of these Buddhas stood a Bodhisattva named Pramuditarāja, kneeling with palms joined, exhorting the Tathāgatas to preach this samādhi-concentration. All these Buddhas transformed countless, incalculable, and boundless assemblies of sentient beings, causing all those beings to fully realize the limitless, to be free from all obstructions, and to attain equal enlightenment.
Chapter Five: The Offering of Dharma. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"Do not regard the offering of robes and food as the foremost way to serve the Tathāgata."
If one wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, one should serve him with the offering of the Dharma. Why is this?

In the past, incalculable and inexpressible kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Golden Dragon Resolving Light (*Suvarṇanāga-viniścaya-prabhā*). His lifespan was immeasurable, his land was named Immeasurable Purity (*Anantaviśuddha*), and the assemblies of his followers were beyond calculation.

There was a Dharma master named Infinite Jewel Sound who, practicing in the final age of the degenerate world, studied this samādhi among the common folk; all the other bhikṣus collectively ostracized him.

At that time, that Dharma Master, harboring no cowardice and not being greedy for his own body or life, again applied himself with diligent vigor to expounding this samādhi; he entered the mountains and partook of various fruits.
At that time, the devas from the heavens of the Four Great Kings up to those of the twenty-fourth heaven, Akaniṣṭha, all came to listen to the sutra.

Then, countless multitudes all thought of him together; their hearts were filled with longing, regret, and sorrowful yearning to see him, wishing to hear his fame and listen to the sound of his Dharma.

At that time, there was a king named Sarvasattvānanditarava, who was a wheel-turning sage-king (cakravartin). He went to where [the Dharma teacher] was to hear this samādhi; having heard it, he rejoiced in the Dharma teacher.
The king said to the bhikṣu:

"Propagate [the teaching] freely without harboring any fear; I shall personally dispatch people to guard you and station thirty thousand men at your side. Do not let this deter you from doing what is right for you; I shall provide protection, for that which the Buddha has spoken is extremely difficult to hear."

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King dispatched his thousand sons—each brave, eminent, and capable of matching a thousand men alone—to guard him. Thirty thousand people provided him with all manner of delicious foods as offerings; they bestowed peace and security upon him according to his needs, always maintaining a harmonious mind free from any intent to harm, and providing everything he required so that he was fully satisfied.

Having established the power and majesty of his spiritual authority, that Dharma Master expounded this samādhi for half an eon; by means of these roots of virtue, all were brought into complete harmony.

The king’s princes and their retinues, after another eighty kalpas, beheld sixty billion *trayastrimśat-nayuta-koṭi* Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; from all these Buddhas they attained this samādhi and, according to their heart's wishes, received and took up Buddha-lands.
"King of Joy!
If you wish to know whether the Dharma Master of that time was anyone other than this person, do not entertain such a thought; he is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha."
At that time, the king named Aśoka-ruta was none other than Akṣobhya Buddha;
his thousand sons were those who appeared as the thousand Buddhas during the Bhadra Kalpa.
The Buddha said,

“King Nanda! Those thirty thousand people who were then appointed by the king to serve as attendants to that Dharma Master are none other than these thirty thousand bodhisattvas, King Nanda and the others, present here now.”

At that time, the planting of merit will yield its fruit here according to one's wishes, bringing about peace, harmony, and the provision of offerings for this samādhi and the practices of all bodhisattvas.
Therefore, Rejoicing King Bodhisattva!
"Those who wish to study and attain this samādhi should receive, uphold, transcribe, recite, and explain it in detail with reverence and diligence, and practice it with a sincere mind.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to bestow peace upon all sentient beings, And to be fully endowed with the treasuries numbering in the billions,"
For those who give rise to the mind set on honoring the Way, the merit and blessings thereof are beyond comparison.
Even if one were to cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to achieve the path of a Pratyekabuddha and provide them with complete offerings for an entire kalpa,
that merit would not equal the merit of giving rise to the mind of the Way.
If one were to cause all sentient beings to attain the Buddha-way and provide for them according to their needs for an entire kalpa,
yet there be someone who resolves their mind upon the Honored Way, this merit would be far greater and beyond comparison.

If there are those who aspire to seek all Buddha-dharmas, yet do not give rise to the resolve for the Path, it would be better for them to take up these four-line verses; their merit will be equal to that of one who protects the mind set on the Path.
Even if all classes of beings in this world were established in and maintained within the Buddha-way, [the merit of the former would still surpass theirs].
If one hears these lines and receives them with reverence, their merit shall transcend all fear.
Even if for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
one were to fill all buddha-fields with every kind of precious jewel and constantly offer them to all bodhisattvas, to protect even a single verse of this gāthā would be far more exceptional.
This samādhi is inconceivable; if one can receive and protect even a four-line verse, the merit of protecting the Buddha’s Way is such that all beings together could never exhaustively praise it.
At the time of the end of life, countless Buddhas will all spontaneously appear before one;
the Honored Buddhas of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions will arise to protect and uphold these four-line verses.
At the time of their final passing, countless Buddhas come to protect their minds so that they do not forget;
according to their wishes, they receive their rebirths, because they rejoice in this samādhi.
With body ever tranquil and mind harmonious, they proceed to the peace of the sages in the heavens;
not perceiving suffering until they reach the Buddha-way, they encourage and assist others—this is called valorous diligence.

Entering hundreds of thousands of millions of immeasurable gates, with infinite light from the treasury of supreme radiance, I abide in this power and proclaim it: one should diligently cultivate this samādhi concentration.
The Buddhas are able to proclaim this; therefore, through this, one should honor diligence.
While the Buddhas are present, practice with vigor, lest you harbor regrets in future lives.
Then he saw this Dharma held in his hand; pure and harmonious, he practiced it with great purity.
All were my sons, transforming beings boundlessly, upholding the Buddha’s teachings and practicing compassion and benevolence before and after him.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this samādhi, he entered into meditative absorption (samāpatti) by means of that very samādhi.

King Nanda also entered into samādhi and, through discernment, entered into the seventy true dharmas. Having completed this discernment, by the majestic power of this samādhi, eighty-four thousand people within the city of Vaiśālī and another eighty-four thousand people outside the city each thought to themselves:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is exceedingly difficult to encounter; only once in the course of a long eon does a Buddha appear. He is rare to behold or hear, bringing great compassion and great peace to all, out of pity for the devas and the people of the ten directions."
"Now he is in a quiet chamber, absorbed in samādhi; we shall use skillful means to encourage and assist the Tathāgata to arise from this samādhi.
At that time, eighty-four thousand people from both inside and outside the city of Vaiśālī first went to Śāriputra and said to him:

"The appearance of a Buddha is rare, and those who have faith are extremely difficult to find. Human life is hard to obtain, and so is the attainment of the samādhi of the Equal and Perfectly Awakened One. Who among us can awaken him and cause the Most Perfectly Awakened One to rise from his samādhi? We pray only that you will take pity on us and grant us all protection."

At that time, having heard what the people of Vaiśālī had said, Śāriputra rose from his seat and went to where the Buddha was. Standing before the Buddha, he cleared his throat and made a sound, snapping his fingers with all his might and striking his two knees, desiring to awaken the Tathāgata from samādhi; yet because of the Tathāgata’s meditative absorption, he did not know the nature of the Tathāgata’s samādhi.
At that time, Śāriputra went to where Maudgalyāyana was and told him the details from beginning to end:
"The people both inside and outside the city of Vaiśālī desire and pray that the Tathāgata will arise from his samādhi."

Then Maudgalyāyana, by means of his supernormal power, shook the trichiliocosm and, abiding in the Brahma-heaven, uttered a great voice, desiring to awaken the Tathāgata from samādhi, yet he was unable to make him rise.

At that time, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went directly to the presence of the worthy Ājñātakauṇḍinya, as well as Vāṣpa, Pilindavatsa, Mahākoṣṭhila, Kapphiṇa, Rāhula, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Kātyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Upasena, Revata, Kapphiṇa, and the Bodhisattva Maitreya; together with five thousand bodhisattvas, they proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, surrounding the World-Honored One, and each took his own customary position.

The Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, and the Nirmāṇarati devas—along with all the countless gods and humans within the realm of desire—each prepared their ceremonial carriages and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

Each pressed their palms together in reverence and, with hearts filled with sorrowful longing and devotion, they took refuge in the Buddha. The Brahmā devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, up to the Śuddhāvāsa devas—countless sons of gods of all these realms—with one mind bowed their heads in homage to the Buddha, desiring that the Honored One would arise.

Chapter Six: The Perfections (Pāramitās) At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy sat in meditative seclusion for seven days, his mind free from any other distracting thoughts.

After seven days have passed, try reflecting for yourself: when you rise from your meditation and proceed to the high seat, you will prostrate to pay homage to the Buddha and visit all [the beings], seeing various manifested Buddhas along with a multitude of bodhisattvas; then, proceeding before the Buddha, you will join your palms and pay homage to the seat.

At that time, the World-Honored One, tranquil and composed, arose from samādhi; he surveyed the entire assembly, and having surveyed the assembly, remained silent for a while before bowing his head in self-refuge.
Then the Bodhisattva King of Joy came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Dharma of the Way is profound and subtle, beyond reach; the Unsurpassed, Right, and True is beyond analogy. "At this time, as my desire has passed, I wish to ask a question; if you would grant me leave, I shall venture to speak.

"These bodhisattvas have accumulated merit and virtue, cultivated their aspirations, and disciplined their minds; they cherish and yearn for the Buddha-way and the various *pāramitās*, planting many roots of goodness to seek ultimate truth.

others practice the *pāramitās* for the sake of all bodhisattvas."

Thus, with such vast and universal causes and conditions, from the beginning to the end, one studies the catalogues of the Dharma scriptures; earnestly receiving and giving rise to the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the assembly of bodhisattvas, one manifests and exalts the Way and its teachings, speaking only of their essential meaning.
