If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain this understanding, they shall all achieve the extraordinary, profound, and boundless practice of all dharmas; being peerless and incomparable, they embrace the sagely wisdom, eliminate all reliance, extinguish all defilements, and sever all doubts.

These constitute two thousand one hundred [virtues], among which there are specifically one hundred degrees of the Infinite (apramāṇa). They primarily eliminate the four great elements and remove the six decays until nothing remains. Walking alone through the three realms, coming and going and circulating, they enter universally throughout the three periods of time. Just as the sun and moon do not fear the various darknesses, and bring to fruition the myriad things—the hundred grains, grasses, and trees—whose flourishing depends upon the earth, so too do these virtues flourish by relying upon the Dharma.

The Bodhisattva is likewise so with respect to the two thousand one hundred *pāramitās* and these one hundred *pāramitās*. Regarding those two thousand one hundred *pāramitās*, when greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal distribution are each divided into two thousand one hundred, they total eight thousand four hundred; and when each of these eight thousand four hundred is further distinguished by ten items, they total eighty-four thousand. By being able to fulfill these *pāramitās*, one has already completed the eighty-four thousand essential and supreme deeds, and naturally masters the eighty-four thousand gates of *dhāraṇī*. One then penetrates the five hundred distinct categories of noble accomplishments of all Buddhas, using them to delight and transform all sentient beings. Having clarified and perfected all spheres of practice, one initiates [activity] according to the time, providing salvation and peace for all until reaching the ultimate limit of infinite wisdom—the Dharma-body.
Chapter Seven: On Practice. At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy addressed the Buddha once more, saying:

“I have heard the World-Honored One briefly outline the essential points regarding the realm of all Buddhas; however, being naturally dull-witted, I am unable to fathom where the definitive meaning leads. I only pray that the Great Sage will deign to look upon me with compassion.”
How excellent is this virtue!

You should extensively praise and expound upon this essential scripture so that all may understand it; out of great compassion and for the sake of the peace and security of many, you should take pity on the devas and the people of the ten directions, and further disseminate it once more.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well!
Now, for your sake, for all the bhikṣus, and for all the bodhisattvas, I shall explain it again.
The Bodhisattva King of Joy and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: "What are the six matters of the perfection of practicing the Dharma? From time immemorial, one has never before resolved [to attain enlightenment];

thus, one now resolves upon the mind of a Bodhisattva that is equal and truly real. Toward all sentient beings and toward those who have attained equal awakening in the past, one practices giving, upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom. One is devoted to the path of the Buddha, and with a heart of aspiration for the truly real, one never forgets it even for a moment. This is called the perfection of practicing the cultivation of conduct."
These are the six. What are the six matters of the Perfection of Radiance?

To manifest and reveal the Dharma of the path of wise enlightenment; having personally examined one's own precepts, to give rise to the Bodhisattva mind, beginning with giving and proceeding through precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—this is called the Perfection of Radiance.
"What are the six matters of the Worldly Perfection (Lokadānapāramitā)?

To provide offerings to the Buddhas and establish merit and virtue all for the sake of sentient beings; the six perfections are likewise so. To restrain the six sensory desires, to aspire toward the six supernormal powers, to comprehend past karma, and to advance toward the Great Way—this is the Worldly Perfection."
"What are the six matters of practicing the *pāramitā* for the sake of sentient beings?
If one gathers in sentient beings through giving, one thinks to oneself:
'May all sentient beings always obtain peace and security,' and furthermore, one encourages others to enter the Buddha-way."

The six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are likewise thus: one establishes others through the precepts, regarding suffering as empty; one delivers them through the dharma of patience; one rescues them through diligence; one gathers and protects sentient beings with a single mind; one casts oneself into inverted perceptions to attain wisdom; and one encourages and assists the Path, desiring to bring peace to sentient beings and seeking to achieve perfect enlightenment in order to deliver sentient beings. These are called the six matters of practicing the perfections for the sake of sentient beings.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of abiding?
If one establishes one's vows with firm resolve, and the mind of the Way is pure, harmonious, and free from contention, this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

To establish a dwelling in the lands and contemplate the precepts of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñā), keeping one's will fixed on the Dharma without seeking any reward for it—this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
To abide in the Dharma and endure all sufferings while remaining steadfastly established in the essentials of the Way—this is the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
To establish right practice for incalculable eons, never ceasing one's diligence until reaching all-knowledge—this is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To cultivate and uphold single-mindedness, seeking the thought of the Dharma with the desire to achieve the Buddha-way—this is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).

Abiding in the meaning of the Path, one elucidates all dharmas; examining them as they truly are, one attains supreme perfect enlightenment, with a mind free from variation and devoid of delusive thoughts—this is the Perfection of Wisdom.
These are the six matters of the perfection of abiding.
What are the six matters of the perfection of birth-and-death?

To give immeasurably so that it is inexhaustible, to remain within birth-and-death until the attainment of the Buddha-way, and to achieve great wealth and prosperity wherever one dwells—this is the perfection of giving.

By encouraging [the practice] from beginning to end, one is entirely shielded from the afflictions of all disturbances; possessing a lifespan that is immeasurable, one does not meet an untimely death amidst the cycle of birth and death—this is the Perfection of Precepts (Śīlapāramitā).
If one encounters an adversary yet the mind does not give rise to agitation, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without weariness throughout incalculable eons and to carry out the roots of goodness—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To enter meditative absorption through the conditions that give rise to it is called *dhyāna*.

To employ the various *pāramitās* without abandoning them to assist in the Buddha-way, to establish all karmic activities and technical skills, and to cause all things to reach their proper place through ultimate wisdom—this is called *prajñā*.
This is the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) within birth and death.
What are the six matters of the perfection of detachment from the dust of worldly attachment?
To establish the Way and the manifold merits of various virtues, and to do so by means of exhorting and transforming all classes of sentient beings—this is called giving (dāna).

Like a lion, he is like a noble cakravartin king who has eighty-four thousand palace ladies; yet those ladies who deviate from the Buddha-way he never associates with, instead causing them to take refuge in the Three Jewels and eliminate the three hundred defilements. He brings all their labors to a single state, swiftly attaining the arts of the Way, and through these precepts and prohibitions, he compassionately exhorts sentient beings—this is called upholding the precepts.
That which is transcended by ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the removal of worldly toil; following the minds of others without defilement is what constitutes patience (*kṣānti*).
As for that which is attached to diligence (*vīrya*), what is meant by the Perfection of Diligence?
Because they are attached to things, they practice diligence.
Fearing others as one would fear a prince of light, they understand the causal nature of the act of giving and establish them in peace; because they are attached to things, they practice diligence.
What is meant by dhyāna?
It is because of attachment that one practices meditative concentration; by perceiving a self, one restrains and pacifies the mind—this is called dhyāna.
What is meant by practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) because of attachment?
If the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible, and one, out of compassionate radiance, delights in attaining noble insight and encourages others toward the Way and its Virtue—this is called wisdom.
Because these are what they are attached to, they are called the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Benefiting Others?
To transform sentient beings by means of delighting in virtuous merit is giving;
to rely upon a mind of loving-kindness and harbor no intent to harm is ethical discipline;..."
To be able to endure all the subversive teachings of the True Dharma without revulsion or loathing is called patience (*kṣānti*);
if one diligently cultivates supreme practices for the sake of others, desiring to rescue them from peril and distress so that they may all attain eternal peace, this is called diligence (*vīrya*);
if one contemplates the Dharma with a focused mind, accumulating pure merit, this is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
To satisfy and bring fulfillment to all sentient beings through these causes and conditions, and to proclaim the aspiration for the Way—this is called wisdom;
this is called the perfection of benefiting others among the six perfections.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of abiding?
To practice giving by abandoning perversions and not hoping for reward—this is called generosity.
To rely upon precepts and prohibitions as the basis for all wealth and undertakings—"
One practices patience for the sake of sentient beings;
one exerts diligence in all that one abides in;
and one contemplates the scriptures while practicing tranquility.
To dwell within that state with serene composure is called wisdom;
this is the perfection of the six sense bases.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the path?

If one can practice and cultivate the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), such that there is nothing one cannot undertake, this is called giving (*dāna*);
if one does not perceive the limits of body, speech, or mind, this is called morality (*śīla*);
and if one cultivates compliance with the true reality (*tattva*) of dharmas such that there is no contention whatsoever, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If body, speech, and mind do not dwell in contrariety, and one does not set one's will upon trivialities but practices with diligence and without slackening, this is called vigor (*vīrya*).

If one upholds the Dharma with a mind that is focused and single-minded, having no attachments, and delights in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) such that its realization is as thorough as it is true, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To understand that the three realms are empty like illusions, transformations, or dreams, and that the Way has no past, future, or present, thereby extricating and rescuing others from worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
"This is the Buddha-way of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
The Buddha said to King Nanda:
“What is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā)?”
If one does not destroy or sever skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), but transforms sentient beings and delivers them through wisdom, this is called giving (*dāna*).

If one composes five hundred verses of hymns, abandons the ninety-six heterodox paths, eliminates all suffering and affliction, upholds the honorable right view, and transcends to the supreme state of the eternally peaceful land, this is called precept-keeping (*śīla*).

If one removes suffering and distress so that the chamber of wisdom is tranquil, feels weary of sensual desire, diligently cultivates vigor, and successively teaches and delivers one another through the Way, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To practice self-restraint such that one regards all territories, people, elephants, horses, and carriages with tranquility and detachment, seeking the root of suffering and realizing it has no fundamental basis—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To mind one’s own faults while pitying others, thereby bringing about vast peace—like a lute, and subsequently attaining stillness with a firm mind, like a lion, the king of beasts, or like a guide leading a caravan of merchants—this is called diligence.

If one gives rise to a single-minded focus where form (*rūpa*) is not produced, yet issues forth the teachings of the *śrāvakas* and the teachings of the *pratyekabuddhas*, remaining within those activities without passing into final extinction (*nirvāṇa*)—this is called single-minded concentration (*citta-ekāgratā*).

If, regarding all phenomena, one perceives no sentient beings, no self, no person, and no life-span, and practices the path through these six matters by recollecting the Dharma—leaving the household life to train and cut away the ten unwholesome actions—this is called wisdom;
this is the perfection of wisdom among the six matters.
"What are the six matters of practicing and establishing the perfection of wisdom for oneself?
If one obtains great wealth and exhorts oneself [to share it], as well as pitying sentient beings and bestowing relief upon them, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If, whether in the heavens or among humans, one brings about peace and security and provides natural food and drink, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one attains patience, rejoicing in tranquility with a countenance as supreme as a lotus flower, resulting in the ultimate reward of noble and exalted status—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Having practiced the Buddha-way, not looking up to others even while following and cultivating it, standing independently by oneself—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, upon receiving meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one remains constant as if during the destruction or formation of a kalpa, arriving at this land—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Though dwelling in the world, to maintain conduct of sincerity and faith while guarding body, speech, and mind—this is called wisdom;
this is called diligently cultivating the six perfections for oneself.
"What are the six matters for attaining the *pāramitā*?
If one understands that through giving one attains great wealth, and by means of such giving attains the Buddha-way to assist all beings—this is called giving.

If the mind is without attachment, tranquil and serene, and does not give rise to conceptualizations, and by means of such observance of the precepts brings salvation to sentient beings—this is called observance of the precepts."
To not slander the Dharma and to have no heart of malice, never harboring resentment until one attains the path of Buddhahood—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice with diligence without harboring distress or feverish anxiety, cultivating day and night—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
To follow the supreme teaching with the body, committing no transgressions and attaining *samādhi*—this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).
If one practices all dharmas and fully penetrates the fact that all things are non-existent, this is called wisdom;
these are the six matters of the perfection of attainment.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of mindfulness?
If one practices the virtue of giving and encourages the path to deliver sentient beings, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If the merit obtained through body, speech, and mind, as well as the rewards of the precepts, are applied to the Path in conjunction with giving, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one receives all dharmas gathered in the assembly and what is manifested is examined with thorough scrutiny, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one practices expedient means without making arbitrary judgments, possessing wisdom and unimpeded diligence toward both self and others, this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
If one gives rise to meditative reflection, severs [defilements], and receives the auspicious responses of great virtue through consultation, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

Wisdom transcends the other shore, and as the Sage stands supreme above all, he bestows the seal of the Way to nourish the mind; that which he nourishes is the guarding of mental conduct and the proclamation of the Dharma—this is called wisdom.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of mindfulness.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of detachment from the world?
If, through skillful means, one severs all conditioned phenomena and exhorts others toward the virtue of the fruit of the unconditioned path, this is called generosity.
If one seeks the prohibitions and precepts, yearns for the source of the Dharma, and the mind harbors no perverse thoughts, this is called ethical discipline."
If one thoroughly understands impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and comprehending internal and external phenomena delights in this Dharma, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one practices with diligence without a harmful intent, upholding the ancient principles of one’s vows with a mind free from attachment, this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
If, through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not abandon profound contemplation and thereby eliminates worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one does not confuse the twelve links of dependent origination, employs skillful means to remain undistanced from worldly defilements, and transforms others according to their inclinations at all times, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of creating meritorious karma?
To bestow the blessings of the four debts of gratitude upon sentient beings through the karma of giving is called generosity (*dāna*).
To employ the precepts so that the countless classes of sentient beings all receive grace and attain deliverance is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

It is like when fledglings or newborn wild animals fall into a fire; seeing them, the Bodhisattva extinguishes the fire and delivers them from the peril. Because they witness this peaceful rescue and the bestowing of grace, they give rise to the mind of enlightenment—this is called patience.

Furthermore, if one transforms and instructs the multitudes in countless lands, bringing them down to the path according to the times, and practices patience even while in the eight difficulties; or if one’s head were severed and one encountered manifold sufferings, enduring them all without a single thought of resentment arising in the mind—this too is patience.

If one acts with the fourfold kindness (*caturvidhā upakārāḥ*) regarding all that is seen, exerts diligent effort at all times to provide benefit, and reverently follows great benevolence and boundless compassion to transform immeasurable sentient beings; acting as a leader to encourage and assist all, such that this mind’s practice perceives no suffering and guides and benefits the three realms so they may receive universal protection—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If, while not yet having cultivated the source of wisdom, one is diligent in all dharmas without transgression or loss, and possesses the insight of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that realizes the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*)—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*, *samādhi*).

If one is resolved upon a single mind toward all wholesome and virtuous dharmas without neglect or forgetfulness, causing all thoughts to enter the Buddha-way; and according to what they rely upon, instructing them through teaching until they reach the gate of wishlessness and signlessness (*animitta-apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*)—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of the path of rest?

If one takes that which is auspicious and pleasing to the mind—namely, worldly activities—and through such giving enters into right view, gathering merit and encouraging sentient beings, this is called giving.

When the mind rests and the will is set upon the wisdom of the Way, and one practices right speech, right livelihood, right action, and right effort through what has been bestowed, this is called precept-keeping.

When the bodhisattva’s practice of resting in the Way is that which is transcended by the precepts, and he attains the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena without hoping for or conceptualizing a reward, this is called patience.
When the mind cannot be apprehended and the body further exerts itself in vigor without any dependence, this is called vigor.

To cast away perversity and maintain a concentrated mind without distraction, focusing the will with single-minded diligence so as to be free from negligence—this is called *ekāgratā* (one-pointedness of mind).
To gather in the state of non-conceptualization, to uphold the wisdom of the sages, and to deliver others from the perils and afflictions of various troubles—this is called *prajñā* (wisdom).

To practice right view and right intention, to give rise to the One Path, and thereby never to regress—this is called the perfection of the path of the cessation of wisdom (*prajñā-śamatha-mārga-pāramitā*). These are the six matters.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Non-abandonment?
If one bestows gifts upon all through skillful means and gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

If the mind is free from harm and unerring in its pursuit of the Way, reaching ultimate peace and security where no affliction remains—such that when a Bodhisattva descends fully from the Tuṣita Heaven, shaking the great trichiliocosm and attaining a pure and profound land—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one embraces patience as one's inner disposition and establishes the Way that transcends the eight worldly dharmas, this is called patience;
if one exerts diligence to encourage compassion toward all sentient beings, this is called diligence;
if one attains all samādhis of meditative concentration and, without negligence, maintains the four immeasurable minds, this is called single-mindedness (concentration).

By means of the perfection of wisdom, one vows and practices to assist in the accomplishment of all dharmas; there is no appropriate application of skillful means that is not universally provided for—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of compliance?
If one accomplishes the giving of clear wisdom with a unified mind, free from divergent thoughts, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If, through the precepts, one encourages others to leave desire behind, such that their conduct is stainless and pure like water, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one uses a harmonious mind to exhort and transform sentient beings so that they are free from resentment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one employs diligent cultivation of skillful means to remain tranquil, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If one uses gentle medicine, the Dharma, and sacred texts to move heaven and earth, and if through meditative reflection one eliminates all views and the sixty-two doubts, wandering amidst the dust and toil of the world without fear, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one stirs heaven and earth through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), if one’s learning and scholarly inquiries penetrate great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and if one understands the destinies of good and evil, suffering and joy, relying upon and taking refuge in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); thus the bodhisattva perceives fearlessness—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of effort (*vīrya-pāramitā*)?
To personally practice giving and instruct others to give, and further to exhort others to do so; to benefit sentient beings with wisdom and protect them with compassion—this is called giving.
For the sake of sentient beings, to always rely on a mind of loving-kindness, to remain free from negligence, and to sever all evil karma—this is called ethical discipline."
To protect others with gentleness and kindness, moistening them with grace so that no anger or resentment arises—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To ensure that the roots of merit and virtue reach their ultimate essentiality, to promote the transformation of the Way, and to deliver all who have not yet attained it—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To contemplate through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) the principles of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, fully understanding these matters so as not to fall into the four inversions—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one uses the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to ensure that the roots of all goodness are not lost, establishes the present to eliminate all unwholesome states, and through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) brings about extensive transformation and liberation for all beings—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-action?
If one teaches sentient beings through the merit and virtues of the five desires, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If one protects and guards countless people, and by means of this sequence offers the Buddha’s Dharma-precepts to protect their place of birth, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To extinguish the dust and toil of craving through this tranquility, and to instruct sentient beings so that they become extraordinary—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To dwell in the mundane world while sporting in infinite play and mastery, and to transform sentient beings through such a retinue—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To establish oneself in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) with the resolve to protect the factors of awakening, reaching everywhere without obstruction—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one believes in the wisdom of the perfection of learning and, by means of this wisdom, delivers all beings across [to liberation], this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of mental intention?
If one practices without soliciting assistance and does not harbor thoughts of reward, this is called giving;
if one observes the precepts without transgression and encourages others toward the Buddha-way, this is called ethical discipline;
if one cultivates equanimity and acts with gentleness, this is called patience.
To cultivate diligence without slackening, restraining oneself in both advancing and retreating—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
To be able to practice accordingly, relinquishing all negligence and harboring no confusion—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To hear of the sagely and enlightened virtues and thereby encourage and assist the Path—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of diligent cultivation?

To be able to relinquish all that one possesses without any attachment or begrudging, entering the great ocean to procure various treasures in order to rescue sentient beings—this is called generosity.
If one guards the prohibitive precepts, remains free from what is observed by others, and does not become attached to name or form, this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

If someone harbors a poisonous intent and wishes to inflict harm—even to the point of cutting off one's head or dismembering one limb by limb—if one’s mind harbors no resentment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one can transcend all debates, with a mind as vast and expansive as the great ocean, such that even if it were to dry up all at once, one could pass through it at will, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, while amidst the passions of the central palace, one does not lose the four dhyānas, this is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā).

If one is able to observe all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, diligently remaining without attainment, and penetrating deeply into the subtle and wondrous without losing noble clarity, this is called wisdom (prajñā).
These are the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of right truth?
To give gifts while relinquishing all attachments and harboring no expectations is called generosity (*dāna*).

To practice the subtle and wondrous, not to transgress the prohibitions, and not to abandon the noble meaning; having given, to release all negligence, to depart from the evil realms, and to be able to establish one's resolve—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To be able to endure all things without contention, constantly bestowing kindness and benevolence upon wholesome dharmas—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To be universally diligent in study without cowardice—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).

If one can diligently cultivate meditative reflection for oneself, entering into the extraordinary activity of *samādhi* and harmonizing and protecting the mind, such that one’s aspirations are like those of the Great Wheel-Turning Sage King Mahāsudarśana—who, though dwelling within a kingdom, eliminates thoughts of greed, anger, and malice, and regards sentient beings with compassion—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Yet, regarding the sagely clarity, one is universally unattached; fully perceiving great compassion, one possesses a mind free from harm—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of swift progress?
To dwell in non-attainment while performing meritorious giving, with a mind serene and without any point of return—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To uphold the prohibitions and precepts without seeking worldly possessions or harboring any conceptual thoughts—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To accord with all dharmas without falling into inversion, practicing benevolence according to the occasion—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To never turn back from what one delights in, but to practice diligently day after day until its accomplishment—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To maintain wisdom and meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*) without limit—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If there is a bodhisattva who, while practicing the path of the śrāvaka, possesses wisdom that reaches the state of non-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), and whose wisdom regarding the stage of the pratyekabuddha likewise reaches non-remainder; who does not fall into desire or among the ranks of ordinary worldlings, yet remains without deficiency or leakage; and who, wishing to exhort and deliver others, dwells therein with a mind free from attachment—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the profound *pāramitā*?
If one practices giving without thinking, "I am the giver who bestows upon all," this is called the perfection of giving (*dāna*).
To maintain the precepts in accordance with sentient beings without relying on birth and death—this is the teaching of the sagely and wise, and is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To abandon the teachings of false views and first resolve upon the Great Mind, establishing benevolence and harmony through these profound precepts; to employ boundless patience (*kṣānti*) and follow the understanding of non-self; to harbor no deluded thoughts and have no expectations for glory or gain; and to neither have expectations nor lack them—this is called "no expectation," and is named patience.

To establish diligent practice amidst the teachings of false views, yet to be entirely without attachment within the three realms and not even think of extinction (*nirvāṇa*)—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
To practice the path of equality and true correctness amidst the various heterodox views and karmic actions of those outside the Buddhist teachings—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To abide in wisdom, cultivating the correct and true Dharma without confusion, to travel wherever one may go without obstruction, and for the mind to remain tranquil and ever free from negligence—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Miscellaneous Practices?

To provide various kinds of flavors in one's giving, each distinct so as to accord with the inclinations of those who receive them; to plant manifold merits without craving for one's own body; and furthermore, to proclaim various chapters and verses, or to take up a Buddha-field to fulfill one's vows—this is called generosity.
To establish the prohibitions and precepts to purify a Buddha-field without violating one's vow—this is called ethical discipline."

If all sentient beings in that buddha-field have their defilements thinned and diminished, and their minds are free from anger and harm through such encouragement and assistance, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one can walk alone, surpassing the assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, even when various assemblies abound in lust, anger, and delusion, one remains within them with a mind undisturbed, this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).

To employ wisdom to grasp skillful means, so that wherever one enters or dwells, one never acts in falsehood; to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma without relying on anything else—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Purity?
If one purifies the Buddha-field with one's own mind so that it is free from all blemishes and impurities, this is called generosity.
If one is able to be reverent toward all assemblies and is not treated with contempt, this is called ethical discipline."

If one can achieve a Buddha-land with perfect equanimity, level as the palm of a hand, fine, soft, and supple like celestial raiment, its ground interspersed with various kinds of jewels, and remaining free from negligence—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one circulates through incalculable assemblies such that all lands are filled with reverence, as if yearning with thirst—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If one is able to fully accomplish the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), whose radiance shines afar to remove the diseases of mental defilement and eliminate all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*)—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one understands that sentient beings are like illusions and yet preaches the Dharma for them, extending even to birds and beasts without ever abandoning them, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
Chapter Eight: On the Limitless. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"What are the six matters regarding the Perfection of the Limitless?"
If one sees people harboring the mental hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), first bestows gifts upon them and subsequently preaches the Dharma to transform and enlighten them—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If they harbor worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), instructing and admonishing them to eliminate these so that none remain—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).

If foolish people of the world are deluded and give rise to the notion of a self, one does not harbor timidity or weakness and remains fearless, explaining the distinctions for them until they reach the boundless—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one employs skillful means to remove hindrances from wisdom so that it is free from obscuration, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To abide in the patience of non-self, to abandon all erroneous activities, and to remain undisturbed in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).

If one achieves eloquence through wisdom, such that what is entered is equanimous and what is spoken is boundless, and if one remains unhindered in all meditative concentrations, focused minds, doors of liberation, and right attainments (*samāpatti*), this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the degree of believing in the Way?
If one can decisively understand that which is to be given in alms and assist the dharmas of the Way, this is called giving.
If one examines the prohibitions and precepts and finds them free of deficiency or leakage, such that one's conduct is complete, this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To abide in the four dhyānas, practice the matter of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and eliminate all notions of attachment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one dwells in the dharma of emptiness and practices equal skillful means, such that the actions of body, speech, and mind commit no transgression, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one cultivates meditative concentration (dhyāna) without attachment to either the internal or the external, this is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā).
To abide in the twelve links of dependent origination through boundless wisdom, without confusing the various dharmas and in accordance with noble clarity, is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of saving sentient beings from calamity?
If one practices loving-kindness as the foremost priority, maintaining a joyful resolve and purifying the three spheres [of subject, object, and action], this is called giving (*dāna*).
If the mind is single-mindedly focused, pure, and stainless, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one can endure all manner of suffering and restrain the mind even when excluded from the hells, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one embraces the four immeasurables, practices benevolent giving and kindness, benefits others as one benefits oneself, and employs timely skillful means to rescue and protect those in peril, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To manifest as an asura while practicing purity, dwelling in self-mastery to bring peace and protection to sentient beings, and to uphold the Dharma free from anger to rescue and protect others, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one’s mind is pure and its contemplations are complete, abiding in tranquility and truth to transform sentient beings, making subtle distinctions without weariness in preaching the Dharma to dissolve their afflictions—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
"What are the six matters of the Dharma-pāramitā?
If one can attain the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, this is called generosity (dāna).
To delight in the sūtras, establish supreme vows, and achieve the gates of liberation while guarding body, speech, and mind—this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
To give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and abandon minor kindness, and to always maintain a gentle heart for the sake of sentient beings—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To possess the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) such that one can fly with ease, and to always practice skillful means (*upāya*) as the foremost priority—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To abide in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as the foundation, and to thoroughly master and fully realize the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).

To master the characters of prophetic texts and attain dhāraṇī; to cause the Dharma one expounds to enter the minds of all; to encompass the four fearlessnesses and proclaim non-retrogression—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Tranquil Bliss?
If, when practicing giving, one is able to collect the mind; having collected the mind, one aspires to dwell in solitude and receives encouragement and assistance—this is called giving.
To be able to uproot all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and cause them all to become completely clear and pure—this is called morality."
To understand impermanence and suffering in whatever place one is born, and to restrain all attachments while cherishing benevolence and harmony—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To seek emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, reaching the state of quiescent dharma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To extinguish all defilements through meditative contemplation, and to maintain this concentrated mind without abandoning the awareness of awakening—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If, through wisdom, one delights in tranquility, serenity, and luminosity, attains the eight gates of liberation, and explains them for the sake of others without falling into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of joyful contemplation?
If one is without deluded thoughts and does not reckon a self-existent person, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

To examine past and future events, to reflect within the mind upon their constant cycles, and to fully recognize and remember them while attaining non-attainment—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If the mind dwells upon all phenomena such as transgressions, and observes and fully discerns the notions of sentient beings, life-span, and the person, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To abide steadfastly in what is observed, universally giving rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without ever relying on anything, and to gather together the practice of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one does not perceive desire and abandons all defects, committing no offense against the nature of faulty phenomena, not losing the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), remaining untainted and pure, casting aside [attachment] yet being without pity, self-taming the mind while transforming sentient beings, and remaining unmoved within the fundamental stage—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of entering into all things?
All dharmas are without a giver, yet one attains them of one's own accord; by means of this, one encourages and assists others to rescue those who are destitute—this is called giving (*dāna*).

If one uses great compassion to encourage and assist sentient beings, establishing them in stability, always possessing noble wisdom, being fundamentally free from resentment, and responding with joy, this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
If one can embrace the dharma of non-retrogression, maintaining it with firm resolve without laxity, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one has faith in the primary source, maintains wisdom, and devises skillful means (*upāya*), this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If one thoroughly masters and accomplishes meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to heal and treat countless sentient beings without causing them harm, remaining compliant and unmixed [with defilements], this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one dwells in the dharma of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-dharma*) by means of wisdom, being steadfast in faith, diligent, mindful, and concentrated; if one abides without doubt and does not calculate the existence of a life-principle (*jīva*); if one employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to remain capable in the world; and if, through the wisdom of those who have studied and those who have not, as well as that of the *pratyekabuddhas*, one achieves the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the sphere of discourse?
If there is giving without a dualistic mind, always rejoicing in equanimity and being without partiality, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

If one perceives the precepts as mere outward ornamentation, being flatteringly insincere and violating prohibitions, yet understands these to be false imaginings and remains unattached in mind while transforming those who have transgressed, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one remains patient when things are inverted and does not comply with them, yet speaks of this state as having its own retribution, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To seek retribution through diligence, yet abandon all such expedient means regarding that state, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, if one discards all that exists, remaining amidst existence while being without existence, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one contemplates with constancy that the various retributions resulting from flattery and deceitful deeds are of no benefit, and perceives their locus as being without a locus, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-harming?
If one bestows gifts upon the Protectors and ordinary beings with a mind that is without distinction, this is called generosity;
if one observes the prohibitive precepts without attachment, desiring to rescue all sentient beings, this is called ethical discipline."
To harbor no thoughts of harm and to be capable of enduring the eight worldly dharmas as the fundamental limit is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to be able to awaken to what Māra has established, to practice with earnest faith and diligence, and to eliminate all hindrances is called vigor (*vīrya*);
to remain undisturbed in concentration, to enter the gate of unimpeded morality and attain the fruit of equanimity is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one employs wisdom to circulate through and return from all mundane and supramundane dharmas without sustaining any loss, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters concerning the ultimate perfection of non-defeat?

To have a disposition that is focused and harmonious, not dwelling on form while following its underlying principle; to practice the giving of the Dharma as well as the giving of food and clothing—this is called generosity.
Although one upholds the prohibitions and precepts, the mind remains simple and honest without flattery or deceit—this is called ethical discipline."
The mind is like space, formed through the coming together of conditions; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
The diligent effort one cultivates in all that is taught does not employ wealth or worldly affairs, nor does it proclaim false words; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That which is meditated upon is forever free from attachment; this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To honor the sages and follow their teachings, using their words and writings to benefit others—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
What are the six matters of the perfection of poverty (dāna-pāramitā)?
If one sets aside the establishment of merit through physical forms and instead practices the giving of Dharma or the giving of food and clothing, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If one’s nature is not fragmented and what one upholds is free from flattery, remaining compliant with the prohibitive laws, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To practice benevolence and harmony in accordance with the voidness of space, possessing a mind free from increase or decrease, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If, in the midst of poverty and distress, one sets one's will upon food and clothing while maintaining the tranquility of body and mind, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If, having reached the Brahma-heaven, one expounds the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and encourages others toward the Way and its virtue, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one is abundant in wisdom and, despite being amidst the many worldly dusts of wealth and enterprise, perceives defilement wherever there is negligence, yet does not abandon or distance oneself from them nor feel weary or disgusted by them, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of non-retrogression?
If, in whatever one gives, one does not cling to the dharmas of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and one’s path does not regress, this is called generosity.
To not turn back and not violate the prohibitions and precepts until one attains the Buddha-way—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To transcend the stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, without falling midway, and thereby attain *nirvāṇa*—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If, through diligence (*vīrya*), one employs skillful means (*upāya*) without error or loss, reaching all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)—this is called diligence.

If a bodhisattva, while amidst all five worldly pleasures, is able through skillful means to contemplate with single-mindedness, extinguishing all defilements and following wisdom—this is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā).

If they uphold wisdom to transform ordinary people, śramaṇas, and brahmins, extending upward to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, establishing right view for transcending the world and founding great compassion—this is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of transformation?
If one practices giving without aspiring for nirvana and without wearying of worldly customs, this is called generosity.
If one studies the prohibitions and precepts yet what one has heard is meager and unable to be broad and extensive, this is called ethical discipline."
If one practices benevolence and compassion yet is unable to distance oneself from dwelling in a state of defilement and resentment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*);
if one applies diligent cultivation yet remains intent on worldly glory and pleasure, unable to restrain the gates of the senses, this is called vigor (*vīrya*);
if one studies meditative contemplation while practicing patience toward external things and disregarding the notion of self, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That which one aspires to through wisdom transcends worldly affairs yet cannot be extricated from them;
this is called wisdom. These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of purification (vyūha-pāramitā)?
To practice giving without expecting a reward, extending blessings to all beings—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To observe the prohibitive precepts without indolence, constantly upholding and diligently cultivating them—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, with a mind of harmony and gentleness that is free from dependence, applying diligence in accord with the Way—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To abandon both self and others without distinction is called diligence;
if, through meditative concentration, one does not calculate possessions and does not create causal conditions, yet possesses strength and power, this is called single-mindedness;
if one discerns and understands all the aggregates and hindrances without weariness, this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of firmness?

That which is manifested by Māra cannot shake or destroy one’s tranquility; the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving is such that no [discriminative] thought arises in the mind, and they are able to relinquish all possessions—this is called generosity.

If one finds beauty and joy in the prohibitive precepts, yet does not cling to auspicious days or select specific seasons, but solely encourages and assists the Path—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
If that which one harbors is supple and cannot be destroyed, and one eliminates all fetters (*saṃyojana*)—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one arouses diligent effort (*vīrya*) without regarding it as a hardship, and does not grow weary of traveling through various lands to transform and teach others—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).

If one extensively exhorts and transforms others for the sake of all through meditative contemplation, attaining mastery over right concentration and dwelling therein without hindrance, this is called single-mindedness;
if one contemplates the noble and luminous Dharma with patience, such that all actions are never chaotic or disordered, this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of flourishing (ṛddhipāramitā)?
If one practices giving without falling into inversion and abides in the Middle Way of the True Dharma, this is called generosity;
if the precepts one upholds are forever free from conceptual thought and thus blaze with intensity, this is called ethical discipline."
To possess a mind of benevolence and harmony without attachment, and to cast off all karmic causes and conditions that lead to harm—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If, regarding the disputes over the self and household affairs, one severs all suffering and affliction, extinguishes all attachments, and brings the defilements of the body to eternal cessation in accordance with the teaching of emptiness—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If one becomes weary of impermanence, thoroughly understands the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination, and the nature of the mind remains firm and stable—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one abandons both wisdom and ignorance such that they are forever non-dual, this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of fulfillment?
If one gives whatever is to be given, encouraging others toward liberation and having no longing for birth and death, this is called *dāna* (generosity).

To uphold and observe with vigilance, never forgetting others, and furthermore, when the Bodhisattva mind contemplates the precepts, never establishing the timid dharmas of the *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*, this is called *śīla* (ethical discipline).

If one accomplishes countless Buddha-lands through benevolence, harmony, and pure adornment, extinguishing the three [self-centered] matters while aspiring to transform and teach others, this is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To apply diligence constantly without weariness, advancing the mind toward the ultimate meaning—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To repeatedly explain the meaning with a tranquil and undisturbed mind—this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).
To employ noble wisdom to encompass the three gates of liberation without prematurely attaining realization—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the Perfection of Worldly Crossing?
When one practices giving, yet the mind remains preoccupied with worldly affairs and does not encourage [others] toward the Way—this is called generosity.
If one is unable to exercise caution due to negligence, and constantly hesitates in action rather than proceeding directly, this is called *śīla* (precept-keeping);
if one combines the power of exertion with a strong desire for self-restraint, remaining capable and patient, this is called *kṣānti* (patience);
and if one constantly and diligently practices mundane dharmas, this is called *vīrya* (diligence).
That his mind has no dualistic thoughts regarding the place where he is born by virtue of his vows is called single-mindedness;
that he uses worldly wisdom to transform and instruct others without departing from the world is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Deliverance from the World?
If one bestows teachings as well as gifts of food and clothing, proclaims and explains the intent of the Way, and because of this Way sits beneath a tree, declaring to oneself:
'How wonderful!'"
"The retribution of merit is that whatever one wishes shall surely accord with one's intent.
To swiftly reach the ultimate tranquility and thereby return to nirvana is called giving (*dāna*).
To enter the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, to advance further toward great protection, and to eliminate all points of obstruction is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one constantly upholds benevolence and harmony regarding untainted dharmas, this is called patience;
if, having attained the dharma of non-arising, one sits beneath the Bodhi tree to instruct and transform sentient beings, this is called diligence;
if a bodhisattva possesses the samādhi of equanimity, with all faculties complete and noble wisdom perfected, this is called single-mindedness (concentration).

If one practices the True Dharma with single-minded devotion, harboring no thoughts of resentment or harm, and free from the intent of a śrāvaka or the conduct of a pratyekabuddha, taking refuge in all-knowledge—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the unsurpassed *pāramitā*?

If one has faith in the countless, pure Buddha-fields and, out of compassion for sentient beings, does not abandon them, desiring to deliver them throughout incalculable eons—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To abide in the perception of the Dharma, to cast off the three evil destinies, and to take up a pure Buddha-field—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

If, upon attaining the Way of the Buddha, one causes all those in the assembly to become the purple-golden color [of a Buddha’s body] and discerns the chapters and phrases [of the Dharma], this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one practices impartial giving, just as when the Buddha Vimala was a bodhisattva he reverently advanced toward the Ultimate Truth (*tathatā*), this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If, while living at home, one honors the four *dhyānas* without losing the concentrated mind, or if, amidst the palace ladies, one maintains a pure buddha-field with few desires and little affliction, such that the assembly receives its karmic retribution accordingly, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one encompasses Buddha-lands of incalculable lifespan and boundless purity, and possesses immeasurable eloquence while dwelling among the assembly, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-confusion?
To practice giving with the encouragement and assistance that accords with the Dharma, thereby swiftly attaining supernormal powers—this is called generosity (*dāna*).

To uphold the prohibitions and precepts without violation or interruption, perfecting the dharmas of the sages and saints, attaining the ultimate Way, and fulfilling the stages of a bodhisattva—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one can eliminate all that is contrary to the Dharma and uphold the Dharma of meritorious achievement, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one can grow weary of the world and uphold the complete scriptures, believing and contemplating with full conviction the meanings of good and evil as taught by all Buddhas, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If one dwells in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), yet remains amidst sensual desires while observing the path of the sutras—awakened and without abandoning them, yet without attachment—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To thoroughly understand the fundamental source of the Bodhisattva path and its dharmas, and to discern all that is right or wrong and flawed—this is called wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Non-Enmity?
To always be able to protect whatever dwelling place one occupies so that nothing is lost is called generosity (*dāna*);
not to fall back into the stages of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, nor to realize the fruit prematurely, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and to sever the notion of self, no longer reckoning the body as "I" or "mine," thereby eliminating the causes and conditions of fetters and obstructions, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To remain far removed from the world’s foremost delusions and to turn toward wisdom by conforming to skillful means is called diligence;
to sever all views and, regarding all phenomena, attain complete and eternal quiescence is called single-mindedness;

and to dissolve doubt, to maintain equanimity through wisdom, to follow the practice of non-conceptualization, and to abide with one-pointed mind on the Path as a venerable one of omniscience is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the Perfection of Overcoming Enmity?
If one gives to sentient beings with the hope of seeking a reward, yet harbors resentment toward the Dharma Jewel, this is called giving; [the rest follows].
If one severs the three afflictions and the realms of toil and suffering, and aspires toward Tuṣita and even unto final nirvāṇa, this is called upholding the precepts;
if one harbors resentment toward other bodhisattvas and genuine beings, this is called patience;

if one follows benevolence and harmony to transform many, providing timely encouragement and assistance, and through diligent cultivation accumulates immeasurable merit—just as the vows of bodhisattvas of former ages—to liberate those who rely on affection and love, and to discipline oneself so as to perfect the Way, this is called diligence.

If one speaks of the accomplishment of unimpeded samādhi and meditative concentration, such that the bodhisattva’s correct reception brings peace and security to all people, this is called single-mindedness (citta-ekāgratā).

If, for the sake of one’s own person, one seeks the source of wisdom and the roots of virtue, attaining ultimate mastery over the meaning of the Way and perfect enlightenment, yet does not understand the various meanings according to their preferences, this is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of gathering and maintaining?
If one encourages others toward their aspirations and gathers and maintains merit, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If one arouses the precepts and takes hold of sentient beings to heal them and lead them to the ultimate meaning, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one can establish and embrace gentleness and harmony, this is called patience;
if one practices with timely dedication and cultivates diligence without becoming lax or desisting midway, this is called vigor;
if one enters meditative concentration according to the occasion to transform countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, this is called single-mindedness.
If one uses noble wisdom to eliminate all faults and obstructions without attachment, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six [perfections]. What are the six matters of the perfection of non-appropriation?

If, through what has been given, one attains eloquence such that whatever is encountered neither increases nor decreases, and one establishes various categories within oneself—this is called giving (*dāna*).
Not delighting in domestic life and yearning for the Bodhisattva path—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Being able to endure profound and essential teachings without doubt or entanglement—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To be refined and eloquent without depending on others is called diligence (*vīrya*);

to understand and serve the reality of emptiness through meditative contemplation, to contemplate the fundamental nature of persons, and to follow the Dharma while mindful of non-arising is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
and when encountering profound principles or even further nirvana, to enter samādhi through the scriptures one has studied so as to extinguish both sin and merit is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of retribution (vipāka-pāramitā)?
If one can fully complete all acts of giving so that no deficiency remains, thoroughly manifesting blessings and auspiciousness, this is called giving.
If one can diligently cultivate and thoroughly protect the body so that it is fully endowed with what is appropriate, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
if one’s conduct of gentleness and harmony brings the meaning of whatever is taught to ultimate fulfillment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*);
if one diligently cultivates all practiced deeds so that they are entirely auspicious and free from transgression or loss, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To discern the past through meditative concentration and to verify the states of former lives with wisdom is called "single-mindedness";
to achieve noble wisdom and proclaim ultimate sincerity so that nothing remains unpenetrated is called "wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-retribution?

If one establishes diligent effort in whatever is given, and upon seeing various calamities and hardships, is immediately able to awaken to them; if one does not dwell on the attainment [of results] and harbors no expectations, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If, while dwelling therein, one brings forth hundreds of thousands of canopies, establishing *nirvāṇa* within the lineage and not abiding in inversion, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If, in one's practice, there is no grasping at the actions of body, speech, or mental intention, and one maintains harmony and gentleness, this is called patience (*kṣānti*);
if one's conduct is tranquil and free from deluded thoughts, this is called diligence (*vīrya*);
if, through meditative reflection, one abides in the stage of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) without generating conceptualizations, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That which is observed by the eye of wisdom does not, through extinction, return to a state of non-reliance;
this is called wisdom. These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of spontaneity (*svabhāva-pāramitā*)?
If one gives rise to [an intention] yet the mind remains free of conceptualization, this is called giving;
if one’s mind does not hope for the reward of merit, this is called morality;
if a person is selfless and naturally gentle, this is called patience.
To diligently practice all things without engaging in dualistic dharmas and being without causal conditions is called diligence;
to abide in meditative concentration without attachment to the internal, the external, or that which is in between is called single-mindedness;
and to observe all things while never making conceptual distinctions regarding any dharmas is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of non-existence?
When the mind does not dwell upon future matters or the merit established therein, this is called giving;
To understand that all wandering through the three realms is like an illusion or a magical transformation—this is called upholding the precepts.
Whether there are perceptions of various virtues or no perception of virtue, to always maintain a heart of benevolence and harmony without harboring such thoughts—this is called patience.
To practice the Way while having nothing to practice—this is called diligence.
To be within the triple world without any longing, and for the mind to universally take refuge in and protect all sentient beings—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To not conceive of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while performing such practices—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Universal Extensiveness?
To exhort and transform countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to abandon stinginess and delight in giving—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To restrain oneself in accordance with karma so as to be universally identical with all—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To be capable of undertaking all skillful means without failure is called patience;
to be able to establish oneself in the four foundations of mindfulness without indolence is called diligence;

to be free from stinginess while guarding the six matters, to abide in the teachings of the Way without turning back, and to be able to embrace and bring forth the eighty-four thousand practices of samādhi is called single-mindedness.
If one can awaken to and fully comprehend all karmic activities of worldly afflictions and entanglements, and vows toward holy wisdom, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the Infinite Flower-like Deliverance?
If, when practicing giving, one carefully guards the six sense-faculties and does not turn away from the Way and its Dharma, this is called generosity;
if one constantly practices reverence and humility, bestowing gifts with a lowly spirit and without arrogance, this is called ethical discipline;
if one is able to endure and resolve all fetters and tear asunder the various nets, this is called patience.
To diligently cultivate practice by administering medicine according to the ailment so as not to fall into the coverings of transgression—this is called diligence.
To cast aside arrogance and offer unconditioned compassion—this is called single-mindedness.
If, through noble wisdom, one proclaims the teachings such that none can withstand them—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the immeasurable *pāramitā*?
If whatever one bestows is always in accord with wisdom, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To constantly practice vigilance with immeasurable precepts, never committing any transgression or failing, is called the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To act with benevolence and harmony so as to attain the three gates of liberation, and to encourage others therein while not falling into perceptions of form, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one attains the four right efforts through diligent cultivation, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, through meditative contemplation, one practices loving-kindness and compassion to bring forth the seven factors of awakening, this is called single-mindedness;
if, through noble wisdom, one cultivates and establishes great compassion to bring forth the eightfold path, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Seeking with Yearning?
If one is able to leave the household life and seek a bowl and robes, obtaining them immediately, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If one’s conduct is characterized by contentment and one is fully endowed with the merit of the precepts (*śīla*), this is called keeping the precepts."

To bring forth a treasury of merit that severs all afflictions and the calamities of birth and death; if one becomes a king, and when his consort or attendants give gifts, to hear of it with silence and harbor no resentment—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To seek various benefits and righteousness, accumulating merit and virtue through skillful means and diligent toil; from the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until the present, to practice giving without ever becoming weary or indolent—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To exhort and praise others in accordance with their inclinations, thereby awakening them from the dust and toil of worldly existence—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one encourages unsurpassed wisdom in accordance with the times, attains supreme perfect enlightenment through this samādhi, and seeks to deliver sentient beings by acting in accord with them—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of disenchantment?
If one gives whatever one possesses until reaching the state of a wealthy householder’s treasure, this is called generosity.
If one maintains the precepts and cultivates the ten wholesome paths, yet does not become weary of them and instead exhorts and transforms others, this is called ethical discipline."
If one gradually guards the prohibitions and, having received the power of the Way, remains solitary and tranquil, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one does not distance oneself from or abandon thoughts of gratitude and virtue, yet abandons deluded imaginings to diligently practice, this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
If, through meditative reflection, one reaches the point of casting off all that is unrighteous, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one experiences suffering and affliction within the triple world yet speaks of the wisdom of one's own body, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of sublime joy?
To give such merit and reward that one is reborn among humans, where all desires are abundantly fulfilled yet one remains free from arrogance—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To observe the precepts so as to be born in the heavens, or to have a constantly long lifespan if born among humans—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) upon being born as a human—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To advance in diligent cultivation with unfailing skillful means, ensuring that practice accords with ultimate realization—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To speak of meditative reflection (*dhyāna*) as discarding the retributions of internal and external causes and conditions, such that wherever one is born, one immediately acts in accordance with the True Reality (*tattva*) as desired—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*) is free from false conceptualizations—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of non-attachment (*aratipāramitā*)?
To practice giving for the sake of saving others without expectation of reward, yet not abandoning various views—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
Though one observes the prohibitions at home, to renounce the household life and not crave worldly glory is called upholding the precepts;
to act with gentleness and harbor no resentment is called patience;
to practice what one has undertaken with diligent effort, disregarding hardship and seeking no pleasure, is called vigor.

To abandon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) that are associated with the [five] hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), thereby bringing about the end of suffering and affliction, and to perceive the various fetters and attachments as difficult to encounter—this is called "single-mindedness" (*ekāgratā*).

If one harbors inverted perceptions regarding noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*), such that despite undergoing various sufferings one does not act in accordance with the Dharma—this is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.

Chapter Nine: On Hearing and Retaining.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of hearing and retaining?"

Seeing the masses in dire straits and unable to save themselves, if one proclaims the gift of Dharma, subdues them, bestows treasures, and causes all people to hear it, this is called giving (*dāna*).

Constantly taking the roots of virtue and various wholesome practices as one's foundation, both practicing them oneself and exhorting others to do so—such that even if they hear [the teaching] but do not uphold it, they still attain great wealth—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).

If, upon hearing well-spoken words, one can endure all sufferings without being troubled; or if a Bodhisattva, even when acting as a brahmin, hears something from a fool and practices for twelve years to initiate and establish the Unsurpassed Great Way, thereby awakening to what has arisen—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one can diligently renounce family affairs without regarding it as difficult, this is called diligence;
if one understands impermanence and hears the principle of dependent origination without falling into indolence, this is called single-mindedness;
if one studies without a teacher and applies skillful means with equanimity toward all hatred and love, this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters regarding the immeasurable length of birth and death?
If a donor of generosity attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this is called giving.
To be able to rely upon infinite great compassion is called upholding the precepts;
to exhort and aspire toward the great vows with gentleness and flexibility is called patience;
to bestow extensive learning upon all beings is called diligence.
If one remains tranquil while applying the principle of non-self, this is called single-mindedness;
if one employs subordinates and servants, instructing them in patience, harmony, meditative reflection, and the propagation of the noble path, this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-interruption?
If one establishes the four ways of benevolence through what is given to rescue those in peril and distress, this is called generosity;
if one guards body, speech, and mind, always being cautious in these three, this is called ethical discipline."

When one’s person, body, and mind are in harmony, and when one’s will attains the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) so that these four matters harmonize their activities, this is called patience (kṣānti).
If one diligently cultivates the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), remaining uninjured by anything, and establishes the ultimate truth through such training, this is called diligence (vīrya).
When one employs tranquility to attain the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), this is called single-mindedness (ekacitta).
If one cultivates the matters of the Four Noble Truths with sagely clarity such that there is no further falsehood, this is wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the ripening of desire and joy?
To give all that one possesses without stinginess is called *dāna* (generosity);
to transform and enlighten through meritorious deeds while perceiving the gate of liberation through emptiness is called *śīla* (ethical discipline);
