if one employs supreme virtue in instruction to transform others through precepts, such that the mind abides in these practices and one manifests this discipline to deliver sentient beings, possessing patience and a compliant mind that is exceptionally harmonious and capable of endurance, this is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To employ the application of the Dharma according to the times to transform and instruct through various teachings is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To understand what is appropriate for the occasion and practice a compassionate heart, exercising the four immeasurable states of mind (*catur-apramāṇa*) to sever the suffering and pleasure of others, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To desire to instruct and admonish all sentient beings with universal pity and protection in accordance with the Dharma, ensuring that one’s conduct is always timely and never misses the mark, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā)?
If one establishes what is to be given such that whatever is desired cannot be thwarted, this is called generosity (dāna).
To maintain a mind of vigilance and not abandon the multitude is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*);
to be benevolent, harmonious, and patient, such that one naturally enters into harmony and patience regarding all phenomena, is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to single-mindedly and diligently cultivate contemplation and establish [the path], so that all places of non-virtue are entirely dispersed and destroyed, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one abandons what is heard through meditative reflection, and the body, speech, and mind peacefully receive all the light of wisdom, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
if one eliminates desire and removes all defiled conduct through the sublime and bright virtue of the sages, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of supernatural powers?
If one gives lamps as an offering and, by reason of that, obtains the retribution of the divine eye with its penetrating vision, this is called giving.

If one upholds the prohibitions and precepts, listens to the sutras with single-minded devotion, and without committing any transgression attains the hearing of the divine ear, this is called maintaining the precepts."
To employ benevolence and harmony without duality to encourage and assist others toward the arousal of the aspiration for the Way is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To achieve and attain the recollection of past lives and the events of former existences, to manifest supernatural powers spontaneously for the sake of sentient beings, and to accumulate merit and virtue while self-disciplining in every birth is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To possess the attainment of supernatural powers and the transformations of the divine feet that are difficult to fathom and infinite, and to relinquish all attachments to consciousness to enter the meditative absorption of equality (*samādhi*) is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To attain the retribution for these causes and conditions of grace, to eliminate all defilements through wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and to thoroughly fathom and manifest holy clarity by means of samādhi—this is called wisdom that exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*);
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the worldly skillful means pāramitā?

Not being able to encourage the study of the various pāramitās, but instead admiring only the propriety of worldly arts and crafts, and applying such skills to other practices so that they cause others to cultivate virtue—this is called *dāna* (giving).
Furthermore, by ensuring that one will receive a future reward and causing countless people to love and delight in the diligent pursuit of the Way—this is called *śīla* (precept-keeping)."
To be able to master all arts and skillful means so that they are fully realized without exception and nothing remains unpenetrated—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To swiftly practice the Dharma of a bodhisattva and bring it to fulfillment—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If the mind is thus well-disposed, this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To consult and receive the teachings of the Way is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of compassionate protection and nurturing of all beings?
If one protects all sentient beings with the mind and practices giving with a heart of loving-kindness, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

Because of [the welfare of] sentient beings, one does not covet one's own body; by means of this, one maintains the precepts and makes timely vows, thereby attaining mastery over the places where one is born, training and transforming sentient beings, and establishing the Path through the performance of virtuous deeds—this is called maintaining the precepts (*śīla*).

Just as in the past there was a king named Māndhātṛ, who gave rise to diligence, cultivated his thoughts with earnest concern, and followed the teachings according to the occasion—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one acts as a king and people seek to cut off one’s head, yet the mind does not give rise to anger, and immeasurable numbers of people thereby attain birth in the heavens—if one can endure such diligence and further provide wealth and resources to guide them, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That which is not lax in meditation, having no place for concealment, and extinguishing the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one employs noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) to instruct countless multitudes, so that all receive the great fruit of retribution, and regarding the various defilements of the six matters of virtue, the rewards of valorous effort remain unassailed—neither increasing nor diminishing because of the past—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of compassion?
To be able to give with a mind that spontaneously gives rise to the thought of wishing for all sentient beings to be universally at peace—this is called giving.
If one abandons others while not disparaging oneself, and completely disperses all fetters, this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
If one can endure being reviled or struck with staves, enduring it all and likewise transforming others to practice endurance, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one employs diligence to fulfill the roots of all virtues, crossing over the immeasurable multitudes without weariness or aversion, and further, through single-minded application, exhorts the multitude of people to leave the household life and study, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one loathes the evil realms and delights in the merit of meditative concentration until its fulfillment, this is called single-mindedness;
if one compassionately purifies all impurities without negligence or cessation, and bestows the gift of Dharma to instruct and transform sentient beings, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of joy?
If one can practice benevolence with a heart full of gladness and harbor no resentment, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To maintain the precepts with firm faith and thereby achieve virtuous merit, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one achieves gentleness and a sense of shame such that one does not retaliate with coarseness, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one diligently cultivates a mind free from anger and resentment, protecting oneself and bringing peace to others while maintaining wholesome reflection without harboring thoughts of boiling water or fire, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one delights in tranquility, purifies the mind, establishes and accomplishes the severing of all greed and desire, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To practice giving with a mind free from attachment; to uphold the path of the Dharma while resting all expectations for reward; to contemplate wisdom and receive the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); having selected these factors of enlightenment, to cultivate them according to the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and establish the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); and to abide neither in inversion nor in harm—this is called wisdom. These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of encouraging and protecting?
If one gives while the mind is free from attachment, upholding the Dharma of equality without harboring delusive thoughts, this is called giving.
If one approaches the factors of awakening with vigilance, and the mind receives the power of diligence without harboring affliction or feverish distress, this is called ethical discipline."

To practice with a mind free from conceptualization and a will that is clearly manifest, remaining inwardly and outwardly at peace while abandoning all greed and envy—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To understand conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and contemplate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) such that the mind does not dwell in duality—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, through the power of meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), one attains tranquil diligence and becomes the foremost among all wherever one travels—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one believes in the holy clarity and follows the path of the Way’s principles, opening and transforming others out of boundless compassion, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of encouraging those with wrong views?

If one encounters various minor heterodox teachers and enters their sacrificial rites to comply with their intentions in order to transform them—just as the brahmin Sūlana performed meritorious deeds through such means—this is called giving (*dāna*).

If one is drawn into a gathering of thieves who have perverted the precepts and is led away by them, yet manifests one's conduct so as to bring about their transformation and deliverance—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one encounters various afflictive behaviors among the masses and is provoked by them, yet does not feel resentment or weariness—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice giving while entering the mundane world without being defiled by its dust, and to proclaim the meaning of profound stillness for others—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To arouse meditative reflection and dwell within the depths of the dark mystery, finding joy therein, yet finding no joy in joy itself but delighting in the joy of the Dharma—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one assumes the form of a *brahmacārin* desiring to transform sentient beings, instructing and admonishing them according to their inclinations and conduct—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of encouraging right view?

If one enters among worldly customs to establish the teaching of the Dharma—teaching that through giving one gains merit, through observing the precepts one is reborn in heaven, and that all actions, whether good or evil, have their respective retributions—and thereby delivers them, this is called giving.
If there is no Buddha in the world, that a bodhisattva has never followed the teachings of evil friends is called upholding the precepts;
that a bodhisattva is pure, bright white, and flawless—like a fine tree growing upon the Snowy Mountains where devas, spirits, and nāgas once came to sport and delight—is called patience;
and that one diligently practices what is received, eliminating the notions of self and other, like a merchant who travels afar to accomplish his purpose, is called diligence.
If one cultivates and refines the four dhyānas with wisdom such that there is nothing to protect, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If, through noble clarity, one feels great compassion and establishes all sentient beings who have not yet attained [realization], just as was taught in the original instructions of former studies—such as instructing eighty-four thousand cities and towns with a single verse of gāthā—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of encouraging abiding in the vision of deliverance?

Suppose a bodhisattva, even while dreaming, has no mind of stinginess or envy; though a Buddha has not appeared in the world, he harbors no divergent thoughts—how much less so when one is actually present?"
This is called giving;
if, when encountering evil offenses or even the loss of one's body and life, one never transgresses the prohibitions, this is called upholding the precepts;
being born wherever one may be together with radiance, and upon birth immediately hearing of fundamental pure patience and thereby attaining the Buddha-way, this is called patience.
To always see beings being proclaimed and transformed in every place where one is born, and to instruct others with these teachings of the Way—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To maintain wholesome mindfulness of the Way in every place of birth, to joyfully establish karmic actions, and to have insights that arise naturally from one's own fundamental nature—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If, whether transcending the world or observing worldly affairs, one is without a teacher or master, standing alone in body and not receiving [instruction] from another, such that one’s wisdom thus constantly proclaims ultimate sincerity, and one’s body, speech, and mind have never been deceitful—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of non-abiding through exhortation?
If one uses skillful means and compassion to rescue those in distress and misfortune, this is called giving.
To be cautious in body and mind, with no transgressions and no negligence, is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and never regress, is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*).

To contemplate all things as ungraspable, diligently practicing skillful means without abiding anywhere, and to encourage the six perfections through this non-abiding, is called the perfection of diligence (*vīrya*).

If one is entirely without attachment to either the internal or the external, yet sentient beings are deluded, their minds obstructed and lacking understanding, calculating a self where there is no self and failing to realize non-self; for them, one explains that all things are empty through analytical discourse—this is called single-mindedness.
If one does not abandon the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, but relies upon the noble and luminous Dharma through omniscience—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of encouraging non-attachment?
If one gathers and bestows grace upon all within the three realms so that they all attain joy, just as the inspiration possessed by Dīpaṃkara, this is called giving.
If one practices the prohibitions and conducts without dependence and without seeking anything, this is called ethical discipline."
If their mind is benevolent, harmonious, and supple, and they have never harbored delusive thoughts regarding any phenomena, this is called patience;
to diligently cultivate all practices without attachment is called diligence;
and that which is seen through meditative concentration—entering the stages of a bodhisattva without falling into inversion—is called single-mindedness.
If one uses noble wisdom to eliminate all afflictions and returns them to the Great Way, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Encouraging the Mind?
To think within oneself that the salvation brought about by a bodhisattva desires to bring the Buddha-land to ultimate perfection—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To maintain one’s own conduct, severing the three evil destinies and refraining from sinful karma—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To manifest the marks and signs of merit through compassionate benevolence and harmony, being upright and exquisitely sublime such that all who see one rejoice—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To diligently practice and enter the great ocean to obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel, thereby exhausting all hardships and attaining the dharma of mastery—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To use meditative contemplation to eliminate worldly afflictions and attain them according to one's vows—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To use holy wisdom to destroy all demons, such that those established in training and transformation do not fail to follow the teachings—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the encouragement of patience?
To give whatever is produced with the mind fixed on the Buddha-way, never forgetting it for a moment—this is called giving.
To rescue and protect those in the hells with a mind of tranquility, such that Māras cannot assail them and the Dharma does not turn back—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To follow what is right in all directions, practicing the True Dharma without harboring jealousy—just as the Prince named Guṇaprabha, who possessed mastery over giving, on a single day relinquished everything he owned to the disciples of the Buddha; desiring to provide carriages, elephants, horses, forty *li* of banners and canopies, lush ornaments, garments, jewels, and countless flowers and incenses; giving away eighty-four thousand ladies-in-waiting; abandoning his kingdom and renouncing his kingship; and giving away his hands, feet, ears, nose, head, eyes, flesh, muscles, limbs, wife, and children, never opposing the wishes of others, leaving the household life to become a *śramaṇa* and revering this True Dharma—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To uphold the various precepts while abiding in diligent cultivation without attachment is called diligence;
if, even in a dream, one sees many jade maidens and does not regard them with greed, possessing bodily marks of excellence and a pure countenance, this is called single-mindedness;
if, upon entering a city, one maintains a mind of clear wisdom, and should see a bhikṣu, reveres him with sincere heart without any discursive thoughts, this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of creating karma?

If one personally establishes oneself in the pure cultivation of the Brahma-faring life, and through such encouragement and assistance gains much in offerings and sustenance; yet when the Dharma is on the verge of extinction and robes barely cover the body, one acts like a student of the will who practices as if amidst withered flowers—manifesting what appears to be the destruction of the Buddha’s body without losing anything at all. Offering five branches of fresh flowers and five branches of old flowers alike to the Buddha, by this retribution the Way and Dharma flourish, and the True Dharma is established for five hundred years, and the Semblance Dharma is likewise so. This is called giving (*dāna*).
If one uses the various precepts to eliminate the evil karmic actions of others and provides relief according to their deficiencies, this is called *śīla* (morality).

To follow benevolence and harmony such that, even when encountering obstacles and lacking prosperity, one inevitably overcomes distress—just as merchants entering the great ocean encounter a *makara* fish, yet suddenly find twenty-five bathing pools, each with a white elephant upon which they may ride to escape the great danger—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).

Even if one encounters the joys and tranquility of the heavens and the world, just as in the past there was no guide to inspire diligence, yet the Great Brahmā named Yingmiao exhorted the Lord of Devas and instructed sentient beings so that they might be born in heaven—this is called *vīrya* (diligence).

Dhyāna is that which is unborn, as expounded by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; if a Bodhisattva exhorts sentient beings to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, from the Ābhāsvara Palace up to the Heaven of No-Thought, this is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā).

The activity of holy clarity is to speak of worldly matters for the sake of the mundane, and to lecture on supramundane activities, cultivating the ten virtuous deeds to benefit the masses—just as in the past there was a sovereign named Deśana, whose king possessed "Good Eyes" and delighted in the Dharma, having understood this meaning throughout countless lifetimes; guided by the compassionate conduct of various kings and by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he proclaimed these teachings to all. This is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-action (*akṛta-karma-pāramitā*)?

To take delight in and rejoice in meritorious achievements within the mind; to encourage and assist all from their very source with the heart; for that which is encouraged and assisted constitutes attachment; as in the past, when the Bodhisattva saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he scattered five stalks of flowers as an offering to the Buddha; the roots of virtue thus planted caused him to obtain this merit and fortune, such that his Way and Virtue were forever free from delusive thoughts, and until the Dharma was extinguished, all relied upon them—this is called giving (*dāna*).
As for the diligence (*vīrya*) in what one studies..."
To regard body, speech, and mind as devoid of expedient means, calculating that there are lands and places of birth and death, is called maintaining precepts;
to cultivate benevolence and harmony while yearning for and seeking the root of suffering is called patience;
to apply diligence in establishing worldly affairs so as to transform others and lead them into the Way is called vigor.
If one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to contemplate the length of the lifespan in the Brahma heavens, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To follow the holy brilliance without ever uttering idle words—just as the Bodhisattva named Tathāgata-sūrya (Sun-like Tathāgata) proclaims a single grade of Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, while those with other bodies proclaim various grades—and to establish them in tranquility so that they attain parinirvāṇa; thereafter, for the duration of years that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) remains before it finally vanishes, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of having a remainder?
When the Bodhisattva of old, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, made offerings and presented gifts while vowing his path and aspiration—this is called giving.
To have a remainder of body and speech, relying upon and abiding in the prohibitions, yet having little faith and delighting in one's own person—this is called ethical discipline."
To have a nature that is harmonious and gentle, devoid of coarseness or wildness, and to take refuge in the power of seated meditation—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To diligently cultivate practice in the interim, yet remain attached to what is pleasurable without reaching the ultimate truth—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To contemplate in meditation with longing for the practice of attending to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and to find joy therein—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If, upon hearing the noble and enlightened teachings, the mind either has attachments or is without attachments, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What is meant by abiding in the perfection of giving with remainder?

Unable to accord with the truth and instead turning toward divergent paths, their resolve is fixed upon the sphere of emptiness as the retribution for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they do not cultivate the Buddha-way and, having entered the karma of the ten stages, they subsequently regress. One should know that such is the meaning of what is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of conduct with remainder.
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) without remainder?

To encourage and assist sentient beings in the cycle of birth and death regarding their retributions, to be as patient as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and to remain tranquil and settled without regressing—this is called giving.
To observe the prohibitions of the Dharma with such detachment from wisdom that one can penetrate deeply into it—this is called morality (śīla)."
To be benevolent and harmonious, fearing the arrival of the evil realms and the places of diligent suffering, such that the mind commits no transgression—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To diligently cultivate practice in order to seek out the works of Māra, desiring to eliminate his realm so that no source of depravity remains—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To govern one's conduct through meditative reflection, knowing the limits of one’s lifespan and reaching the ultimate root-source—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If, through wisdom, one perceives and knows their past lives, severs all suffering and affliction, and possesses noble aspirations—this is called the perfection of wisdom without remainder.
Why is it named a "perfection" (pāramitā)? Because it has reached the further shore.

This means that when a bodhisattva attains the ability to transform others in accordance with their inclinations and follow what the world desires, they are then said to have perfected the six pāramitās without remainder.
What are the six matters of the prajñāpāramitā?

When a bodhisattva practices giving by honoring elders and superiors without expecting any recompense, and though consuming worldly food and drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, does not harbor anxiety in his mind for the sake of his own body—this is called generosity (*dāna*).

When he cultivates the principles of the Dharma and approaches the foot of the Bodhi tree, harboring no doubt regarding any phenomenon, and through this reaches all-encompassing compassionate wisdom—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
When he employs meditative contemplation upon phenomena that are without attachment, such that all-encompassing wisdom arises from it—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one reverently and diligently cultivates dwelling in the wisdom of the Path to transform the five aggregates and the hindrances, this is called diligence;
if, through meditative concentration, one achieves supreme perfect enlightenment, attains the divine eye to know past lives and behold all that has been experienced, this is called single-mindedness;
if, by means of noble clarity, all outflows are completely exhausted, one attains the Buddha-eye, universally penetrates all dharmas, and the mind is free from hesitation, this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of maintaining the light of abiding?
Abiding in the true Dharma, making offerings to the Buddha's teachings, and preserving the sūtras—this is called giving.
To enter the state of the Tathāgata wherever one dwells, with body luminous, speech pure, and free from all discursive thoughts—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To practice with gentleness and compliance, not approaching worldly dharmas and remaining unmoved by them—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To clearly understand the activities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, to eliminate all afflictions (*kleśa*) and even reach nirvāṇa—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Therefore, to seek among sentient beings through meditative contemplation, exhausting all mental activities with the voice of wisdom—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To know how to attain liberation without missing the proper timing, practicing noble, luminous compassion—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the arising and accomplishment?
When a Buddha appears in the world, he achieves the enterprise of great wealth; immeasurable worthies and sages receive the teachings of the Buddhas of the past—this is called giving.
By means of practice and encouragement, one attains liberation; when a Buddha appears in the present world, he eliminates all worldly afflictions—this is called ethical discipline."

To be harmonious and benevolent while receiving the World-Honored One’s teachings, and further to know contentment without harboring weariness even toward great deeds—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one diligently cultivates the establishment of great vows, such that even when in a royal position one’s merit does not violate the Dharma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, through meditative reflection, the mind constantly recollects the Buddha without losing the Ultimate Truth—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one uses holy wisdom to encourage and assist others toward extinction (nirvāṇa), just as the Buddha transformed the bodies and minds of the five disciples, this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Non-affliction of Mind?
To practice benevolence according to one's vows and dedicate oneself to the Way in order to transform others is called *dāna* (giving).
To follow supreme conduct in order to protect others by governing one’s body, speech, and mind is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).
That which is cultivated as kindness and harmony is profound and subtle patience; when the True Dharma is about to perish, to remain firm in one’s resolve is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To establish diligent cultivation and bring forth the wisdom of the Path with a mind free from delusion is called diligence;
if, in meditative contemplation, one maintains emptiness and non-existence, being without conceptual wishes or aspirations for anything, this is called single-mindedness;
because of that noble clarity, one reflects upon the sorrows of the world with compassion, desiring to rescue and deliver all beings—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters concerning the Buddha’s manifestation and establishment of the householder’s *pāramitā* of deliverance?
If one brings forth five matters through what is given as a gift, what are these five?

First is the accomplishment of the seat; second is the place of exposition; third is the accomplishment of the retinue; fourth is the accomplishment of the joy of the Dharma; fifth is the accomplishment of its commentaries—these are called generosity (*dāna*).
To establish practice through what is bestowed, fulfilling the prohibitions without transgression, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To abandon the notion of a person through benevolence and harmony, and not to calculate for the sake of a life-span, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one manifests the meaning of the Path by diligently cultivating and honoring impartial action, this is called diligence;
if one universally cultivates equanimity through meditative reflection of the mind, practicing supreme virtue with a mind free from aspiration, this is called single-mindedness;
if one returns to the Noble Truths through the light of wisdom, penetrating all things without obstruction, this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of renunciation (*naiṣkramya*)?
If there is giving that accords with the mind and leads to untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*), this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To guard one's body and speech through vigilance so as to accord with nirvana is called the precept of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To be gentle and harmonious, weary of the triple world, and remain unattached is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Diligently cultivating upright conduct, returning to the four foundations of mindfulness, and giving rise to the aspiration for the Way is called diligence (*vīrya*).

Therefore, to cultivate meditative contemplation and abide in the four immeasurable minds, while feeling weary of and detesting the hardships of wandering through birth and death—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To employ sacred clarity to transcend the mundane, abandoning thoughts of sorrow and grief to cultivate the ultimate truth—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six practices of the Perfection of Compassionate and Extensive Learning that brings about deliverance?
To proclaim and teach with diligence, providing for those who are destitute and impoverished, is called giving (*dāna*).
To receive and uphold the Dharma, even at the cost of one's own body and life, without any craving or attachment, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

Precisely because the True Dharma is about to perish, the Bodhisattva resolves his mind to act in accordance with the exigencies of the time, sacrificing his own person to protect the True Dharma; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If, through diligent cultivation, he attains *dhāraṇī* and maintains constant awareness without forgetting, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, through meditative reflection, his mind realizes the nature of the twelve links of dependent origination such that nothing arises, this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
If one employs wisdom to experience all things while practicing tranquility, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Precepts through which renunciation remains uninterrupted?
To fulfill the wishes of others and carry out the instructions of the Dharma Master is called giving (*dāna*);
to observe the precepts while adhering to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) without the slightest resentment is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
to be intent on benevolence and harmony, harboring no thoughts of harm, being humble, respectful, and compliant without self-aggrandizement is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice with diligent devotion, possessing strength and vigor rather than cowardice or weakness—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To apply the mind in meditation and cultivate the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), penetrating far and near so that there is nowhere one does not reach—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To be intent upon wisdom and thereby fully realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*)—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
This constitutes the sixth heading at the beginning of the twelfth scroll. Below "The Six Pāramitās," the Cinnabar Edition contains a note stating:
"According to the original heading, 'The Buddha’s Flourishing Pāramitā' has been omitted."
Chapter Ten: Supernatural Powers. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of abiding in supernatural powers?
To practice giving even of one's most precious wealth without greed or stinginess, honoring the Way and Dharma while receiving the true teaching—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To act without attachment, not relying on either the heterodox or the orthodox, but setting one's will upon the Great Way—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To be benevolent and harmonious, harboring no doubt and remaining forever free from hesitation—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To set one's will upon diligent cultivation and establish great vows without deviating from original aspirations—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That the radiance of meditative contemplation illuminates both the distant and the near—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To follow the sacred clarity in accordance with the stages of the Way, maintaining a firm and steadfast grasp upon every matter through its underlying conditions—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of the Uninterrupted Power of Supernormal Knowledges?
If one establishes the temples and viharas of the Tathāgata as the foremost priority for the sake of those to be saved, this is called giving.
To seek the path of practice so as to bring forth the faculty of wisdom and uproot the source of ignorance is called precept-keeping;
to be intent on gentleness, to reach the ultimate limit, and to give rise to the true and correct is called patience;
to practice with diligent cultivation, to penetrate the perception of form while remaining without conceptualization, is called vigor.
To thus contemplate with serene stillness, concentrating the mind until one reaches the gates of liberation—this is called "single-mindedness" (ekāgratā).
To follow and uphold the sagely brilliance, practicing and maintaining the dhāraṇīs, observing correct conduct, and abiding in the state of detachment—this is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of entering the desire [realm] for the sake of crossing over?
If one gathers and combines powers and resources to provide for enemies, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If one’s practice is weak and inferior, yet one gradually accords with power to establish great influence, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To use gentleness and flexibility to eliminate the various hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and to practice the meaning of the Path—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To sever the heart of enmity, like a prince who delights in purity and integrity—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To constantly engage in meditative reflection, with a mind that is not negligent and focused solely on concentration—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Therefore, the sagely and enlightened ones diligently cultivate vigor in order to deliver others from the hardships of the evil realms, hells, and the cycle of birth and death;
this is like the practice undertaken by those of antiquity—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of establishing the means of deliverance (*prajñāpāramitā*)?

If there are practitioners who rescue others from the evil realms and guide those within the cycle of birth and death so that they may transcend it—resembling the reward of the *uṣṇīṣa* mark on the crown of the head—this is called giving (*dāna*).

As for those who uphold the practice, if there is no Buddha in the world, they transform and enlighten the multitude, each causing them to find their proper place, just as in the past when the noble King Māndhātṛ transformed the world through compassion; this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

To be harmonious and benevolent such that anger does not arise—just as Kṣāntivādin did not give rise to a heart of resentment even when his hands, feet, ears, and nose were severed—is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To be diligent and tireless in practice, remaining steadfast and never faltering, like a wish-fulfilling gem from the ocean that immediately grants whatever one seeks—is called diligence (*vīrya*).

As for the meditative cultivation of *dhyāna*, it is like being within the royal palace, transforming and enlightening the nobility so they resolve to seek the Way, surpassing all others; like a lion cub who commands with sovereign authority, causing all to bow like grass before the wind—is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If, upon entering the realm of the sagely and luminous multitude of wisdoms, one relinquishes everything entirely and is able to bestow gifts upon others without ceasing their aspirations—just as the ancient kings gave away even their heads and crowns—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the progress of effort?
To give away one's clothing and belongings to sentient beings, just as the King of Turtles rescued those in distress at sea—this is called giving.
To uphold the Dharma one has received, surrounded by a retinue like that of a lion, rescuing merchants in the same manner—this is called ethical discipline."
To hear what is gentle and mild—such as when a brahmin intended to harm the king and take his head, yet the king immediately bestowed it upon him—is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice diligence (*vīrya*) such as the son of a brahmin named Siyi, who abandoned the five desires to rescue and protect others and exhorted them toward liberation—is called diligence.

His meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) was like that of Aristanemi, who, while among the heterodox teachers, rescued his own disciples as well as others; this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To transform and enlighten countless hundreds of thousands of people through sagely and brilliant deeds—just as the king of birds rescues those who are ungrateful—is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Responding to the Multitude?
If one takes pity on the people of the world and provides them with relief, purifying their conduct through transformation just as one who is free from defilement does, this is called giving.
To practice the supreme conduct and abide in the Brahma-heaven, establishing the roots of virtue for those in Jambudvīpa so that they may enter the Dharma, this is called ethical discipline."

To practice benevolence and harmony toward sentient beings, not sparing even one's own body or life—just as one who, seeing his ship wrecked at sea, sacrifices his own life to save the multitude—is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To practice diligence (*vīrya*) in transforming countless beings and achieving much success—just as a guide named Puṇyakārin gathered various treasures from the sea to relieve the destitute—is called diligence.

To practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) out of compassion for others and to provide them with assistance—just as a youth named Arthasiddhi practiced loving-kindness for eighty thousand years to bring peace to sentient beings—is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one employs noble clarity to understand the wisdom that transcends the present world, and through this wisdom realizes emptiness and non-existence—just as Subhūti understands emptiness and discerns metaphors, being able to distinguish all motes of dust and leaves of trees—and if the reward for such encouragement and assistance exceeds even this, it is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-retribution?

That which provides salvation without receiving karmic retribution, even unto *nirvāṇa*, like a great canopy that provides shelter—such is the boundless cultivation of the Bodhisattva; when sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attain deliverance through this, it is called giving (*dāna*).
To practice the Dharma with all outflows (*āsrava*) exhausted, reaching the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and embracing universal protection, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To aspire to benevolence and harmony without ever harboring resentment until one attains the Buddha-way is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to diligently practice by relinquishing body and life, offering all things to the Triple Gem, is called diligence (*vīrya*);

to cultivate meditative concentration beneath the Bodhi tree, proclaiming and praising verses while upholding the contemplation of the Dharma through such conduct, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

That which one follows with sagely clarity does not depend on mere intellectual wisdom; it is like the *śāla* tree leaves in the ocean, whose fragrant beauty cures disease. In this way, the bodhisattva uses the fragrance of the Way and its virtue to transform all beings, causing them to give rise to the mind of the Great Way; this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the absence of pleasure?

To deliver sentient beings as if they were already in *nirvāṇa*, just as the worthy one named Hanlin delivered the deluded masses—therefore, one should clearly understand that the original conduct of a bodhisattva is illustrated by this former analogy; this is called giving (*dāna*).

His prohibitions are immeasurable; weary of all hardships, he aspires to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), just as the bodhisattvas of antiquity practiced with diligence to enter the sea and obtain immeasurable treasures; thus, this is cited as an analogy, and it is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To practice benevolence and harmony such that, like King Kāśī, one does not harbor anger even when having one’s head, nose, hands, or feet severed—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To diligently practice cultivation so that none could see one as one departs from Kapilavastu, thereby entering the Way with equanimity and attaining Buddhahood—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To possess the four dhyānas in their entirety through meditative reflection, and to purely cultivate the Brahma-conduct of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

Furthermore, to perfect the *pāramitā* of wisdom is likewise difficult to achieve; to remain in the world while maintaining right reception and a mind always in equanimous concentration—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of timely progress?
To obtain a place of rest and sequentially bestow relief upon all calamities and hardships is called giving (*dāna*).
To act with such caution as if born among turtles—when serving as a turtle king, protecting one's own body while also rescuing others—is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

To be intent upon benevolence and harmony, to draw near to various practices, and to protect one’s body and speech; to act with compassion and patience like a noble person, severing all bonds of attachment without harboring malice—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To practice with diligent effort, such that whenever a Buddha appears in the world, one beholds him; to apply the seal of the Tathāgata’s equanimity to all practices for three thousand years without ever ceasing or becoming lax—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

As for what is called meditative reflection (*dhyāna*), it is to remain amidst the palace and among the female attendants, constantly cultivating purity and never being indolent—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To abide within birth and death while following wisdom, and wherever one goes to protect all notions of self so that they realize there is no self—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Radiance?
If one offers flowers and incense to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas without seeking personal adornment, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To practice with careful vigilance and compassion for others, like a bird flying through the sky empty of possessions and free from attachment or delight, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To aspire toward benevolence and harmony, to reconcile all things through emptiness, and to attain the treasury of the Dharma—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To exert diligent effort as a bridge to rescue those in peril and distress—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
To contemplate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as it was practiced by the original bodhisattvas in past kalpas, deeply entering the path of practice—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To cultivate and give rise to noble, clear *dharmakṣānti*, maintaining a mind like that of two children or as firm as the earth—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of immeasurable light?

To provide salvation through skillful means and expedients, thereby bringing about the retribution of the Buddha’s great radiance that pervades countless Buddha-lands—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To diligently cultivate what one upholds, encouraging others toward the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
For those who are harmonious and gentle, to encourage them toward the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) without attachment—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To diligently cultivate and practice the dharma of emptiness, and to encourage others toward the Great Way so that they return to this empty non-existence—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To employ meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to assist in transforming sentient beings, remaining ever-untiring and unfailing so that they do not regress—this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).
To cultivate holy clarity and abide in the eighth stage, such that all whom one transforms and guides receive its benefit—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. "What are the six aspects of the perfection of the light of the reward of peace?

If, when one reaches the path of Māra at the time of death, the response of one's merit is like that of a being from the Tuṣita Heaven suddenly descending to convert hungry ghosts and eliminate their suffering of hunger—this is called generosity; [the remaining five follow in the same manner]."

To subdue the paths of Māra and offer compassionate pity, relinquishing bodily bonds and being liberated from the calamities of sin—just as in ancient times the crown prince named Surata was freed from suffering and affliction—is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To practice benevolence and harmony among fish, providing peace to turtles and crocodiles so they may dwell in seclusion and find food, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To diligently cultivate practice and, amidst fear, peril, distress, and hardship, compassionately rescue those such as the daughters of kings, is called diligence (*vīrya*).

The meditative cultivation he practices consists of healing those afflicted by the calamities of the pestilence eon with medicine, just as the youth of old performed acts of long-term benefit; by means of his five leaders, he brings peace to all the non-evil beings of Jambudvīpa—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

By means of this holy wisdom he rescues and protects all, just as in the ancient parable of the five hundred merchants who, together with five hundred jade maidens and various other women, followed a guide to protect five hundred million people through single-minded vigilance—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Non-retrogression?

To have already accomplished the rescue of others yet take no pleasure in the practices of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but instead vow to seek the unsurpassed, truly correct Way—this is called giving.
To be reverently cautious in what one upholds, contemplating the ultimate meaning without negligence or abandonment—this is called ethical discipline."
To abide in benevolence and harmony, being able to manifest ultimate understanding without harboring resentment within, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice in accordance with the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to provide rescue and deliverance so that one does not become lax, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) such that the words and phrases are clearly elucidated without confusion or delusion, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That which is called the noble and enlightened attainment of the seventh stage, the ground of non-retrogression, is termed wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of joyful play?
To bestow gifts in order to open the way for those who are difficult to transform and cause them to resolve upon the path is called *dāna* (giving).

To provide sustenance through practice when a Buddha appears in the world, explaining the retribution of deeds to deliver and liberate others—just as in the past Prince Śeṣa rescued the multitudes from peril—is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).

To cultivate benevolence and harmony, like a meritorious king who brings peace and tranquility to the myriad people, such that one’s own person is at peace and others are at peace, and all being thus at peace, one’s own self is also at peace—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To advance with diligent cultivation and attain dhāraṇī and immeasurable eloquence is called diligence;
to practice meditative concentration and employ it as an aid so that the retribution of this merit brings peace to sentient beings is called single-mindedness;

and to abide in the six stages of dwelling through holy clarity, attaining the patient acceptance of the compliance with phenomena (*anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti*) and reaching the stage of non-retrogression is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of purity?
If one gives rise to [generosity] without relying on anything, and does not seek any recompense from sentient beings, this is called giving;
To practice with vigilance and always maintain sincere faith, cherishing the seven factors of awakening to awaken those who have not yet awakened—this is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).
To practice benevolence and harmony, maintaining compassionate thoughts for all sentient beings, neither craving one’s own body nor begrudging one’s life—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To apply oneself diligently to the chosen practice of discerning all dharmas, uniting with supreme conduct to bring forth the various states of awakening—this is called *vīrya* (diligence).
If one practices meditative contemplation without any conceptualization and remains free from negligence, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
that by which noble wisdom attains the Way of the Buddha and delivers all beings, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
these constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of establishing worldly laws?
To repay those one has saved with immeasurable merit, leading them to eternal peace free from further hardships—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To be cautious and earnestly seek the Dharma, practicing the eightfold path until reaching the wisdom of equality—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To maintain thoughts of benevolence and harmony, to resolve upon the Way and its righteousness without doubt, and to tear asunder the net of afflictions—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice diligently in the present Dharma so as to attain long-lasting peace and security—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
That which is termed meditative reflection, the fundamental practice of vigor, the cessation of stillness, and right concentration—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To follow the sagely clarity, having completed what was to be done, and receiving the four foundations of mindfulness—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Purifying the World?
To save the trichiliocosm through one's practice, maintaining an undivided mind from beginning to end—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To bring universal peace to all since birth, circulating among the sentient beings of the three realms—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
From the moment of first resolving the mind, to teach and transform the multitudes until they reach the state of no-attainment and no-abiding place—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To cause all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to attain parinirvāṇa through diligence—because their minds are difficult to withstand, being like those who have first resolved to leave home and study—is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To practice meditative contemplation so that all sentient beings may gather their thoughts, focusing exclusively on the sutras and the Dharma without negligence, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To reach even the hells with holy wisdom to rescue them from peril and distress, such that as soon as they are born and fall to the ground, there is something proclaimed by their mouths—the preaching and expounding of the Way of the Sutras until they attain the scriptural canons—is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the seed of accomplishment?
That which is saved attains harmonious retinues and infinite great wealth; this is called giving.
To practice with such careful vigilance that one’s retinue becomes harmonious and free from transgressions is called the precept of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To cultivate benevolence and harmony such that each member of the retinue finds peace within themselves and cannot be corrupted by others is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*).

If one diligently cultivates all members of the retinue so that they do not indulge in self-indulgence or heedless conduct, but each performs their duties with focused intent without negligence, this is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya*).
To practice meditative concentration such that all those who are angry or disputing are brought into harmony and the retinue is made luminous—this is called single-mindedness.
To cultivate holy wisdom such that all members of the retinue possess intelligent illumination and are free from obscuration—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of bringing about the formation of a retinue?
To transform and exhort the great assemblies over five hundred years, causing them to resolve upon the Way—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To practice caution and reverence, encouraging harmony and unity so that countless people do not engage in strife, remaining like the retinue of a Buddha—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

That his benevolence and kindness serve as a treasury for immeasurable sentient beings—just as in the past there was a great fish in Makara that could receive the waters of the sea—and that throughout the beginning and the end, he acts as a companion to others like a fish in a well, is called patience (*kṣānti*).

That he diligently practices much protection for the multitude, removing lust, anger, and ignorance—just as the moon-pearl treasury in the ocean causes the waters to recede according to the seasons—is called diligence (*vīrya*).

That his practice of meditative contemplation is like that of Ārāḍa Kālāma, who studied extensively the subtle arts of external heterodoxy, yet out of great compassion for sentient beings exhorted and transformed them so they were reborn in the Brahma Heaven, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To practice in accordance with holy wisdom and feel great compassion for others—just as Subhūti saw a strange man capture a deer king and confine his five hundred followers in dire distress, yet liberated them all, and subsequently transformed all sentient beings throughout the world, establishing them in the ten wholesome paths of action—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of not breaking up one's retinue?
If one abandons double-tongued speech and always speaks with sincerity, never causing strife or discord among those seeking merit, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

If one constantly harbors a mind of loving-kindness and does not harbor malice, such that one’s reputation spreads far and wide and all respect and love one, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
That which is called benevolence and harmony, maintaining an impartial mind, and showing compassion to all sentient beings without partiality—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That one cultivates diligently not for the sake of food or clothing, but transforms and enlightens sentient beings solely through the Dharma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That one’s resolve is fixed in meditative reflection, attaining *dhāraṇī* and immeasurable eloquence—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Therefore, the sagely and enlightened one maintains liberation, unraveling all fetters and bonds so that there is no obstruction; this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
What are the six matters of the *paramitā* of purifying the arrival from the removal of dust?
If one can eliminate depletion and increase merit, healing all epidemics and causing universal peace and security, this is called generosity (*dāna*);
if one provides protection for those who are obstructed and unable to save themselves, causing their minds to open and be liberated, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
if one encounters masters, teachers, or elders who revile them, yet remains reverent and takes refuge in them without harboring anger or resentment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To diligently cultivate such that the mind remains upright while in the womb, to treat various illnesses and provide protection and guidance for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To care for and serve a mother who is ill, providing her with whatever she lacks, such as medicine and food and drink—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To use sacred wisdom to resolve the doubts of countless beings, so that each attains enlightenment and reveres the unsurpassed truth—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Contemplating the Buddha-lands?
Constantly harboring benevolence and compassion, not casting harmful glances upon others—this is called giving.
To have a mind free from obstruction and hindrance, and a mind of careful mindfulness, is called upholding the precepts;
to be benevolent and harmonious in nature such that upon seeing enemies one regards them as an only child and harbors no malice, is called patience;

to be fully endowed with supernormal powers so that there is no flaw within or without, and to observe the transformations of the ten directions without becoming lax or negligent, is called diligence.
If one purifies their practice and refines the divine eye to see all births and deaths within the five destinies, this is called single-mindedness;
if for countless lifetimes one has softened the mind, with speech that is harmonious and elegant, and discerns noble wisdom, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Vow?
To encourage and assist sentient beings so that they may receive merit by means of the virtue of retribution is called giving;
to practice with such care that all hindrances are eliminated and no obstructions remain is called ethical discipline."
To be without attachment and not to consider oneself a hearer, yet to fully realize that sounds are entirely empty and to give rise to benevolence and harmony—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To apply oneself with diligence to what one aspires to, advancing day by day until reaching the unprecedented and entering the Unsurpassed Way—this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
To protect all deluded multitudes through the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To be sagely and wise, to find the afflictions of sentient beings unbearable, and to reverently practice the Dharma of gentleness and compliance up to the level of noble harmony—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of non-negligence?
To give gifts while encouraging and assisting in the Way and its Virtue, rather than engaging in worldly occupations, is called giving (*dāna*).

If one’s kin are weak, yet one protects and upholds their practice of the Way, such that even if someone comes and dismembers them limb by limb, one does not give rise to a poisonous mind but instead compassionately encourages them toward the Dharma—just as a hunter who harbors resentment might feel joy in his heart if someone were to come and dismember him limb by limb, and the hunter would not harbor malice—this is called keeping the precepts (*śīla*).
If, through benevolence and harmony, one proclaims virtuous principles and, even when cast into fire to endanger one's life, does not harbor resentment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To diligently cultivate practice until reaching extinction (nirvāṇa), observing that conditioned phenomena are like a blazing fire and extinguishing them through the Dharma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To contemplate in meditation, removing all defilements and delighting alone in a solitary place, and using the laws of precepts to rescue the ignorance of the multitude—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

Wisdom has no partial attachment and equalizes the mind; it is like a prince who, having been granted land, ensures it is free from transgression while possessing power—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of circumspection (pariṇāmanā-pāramitā)?
To possess abundant wealth and resources and to apply them with compassion, harboring no intent to harm—this is called giving (dāna).
To be cautious and prudent, refraining from flattery or self-display, is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To be gentle and harmonious by nature, never wearying of the merits one performs, relinquishing palaces without any craving or attachment, and practicing timely charity, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To apply oneself with diligence, honoring the Dharma of equality without negligence, is called vigor (*vīrya*).
If one employs meditative contemplation without turning back, falling into the silence and detachment of the unconditioned dharma, this is called single-mindedness;
if one establishes all dharmas through noble clarity, remaining firm and immovable without falling into the dharmas of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Nirvāṇa?
If one does not practice stinginess or greed even when among hungry ghosts, and feels compassion for sentient beings who suffer, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If one perceives the obstructive karma of sentient beings and, out of loving-kindness and pity, shows them the state beyond affliction, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

To practice benevolence and harmony, and upon hearing of the suffering in the hells or seeing those of evil appearance, to increase one’s application of the four immeasurables to compassionately pity them—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To diligently cultivate what one upholds, severing all false views while harboring much kindness and pity—just as the Prince Ajātaśatru, named Kunāla, abandoned his court ladies and endured humiliation without resentment—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

If one finds joy in the liberation of dhyāna and this tranquility—just as in the past when the Bodhisattva sat beneath the Jambu tree, his sublime virtue so magnificent that its shadow covered his body—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one uses noble wisdom to extinguish lust, anger, and delusion—just as a king abandons his kingdom to leave the home life for the Way, with the hair on his body standing on end while the multitude weeps in silence without looking back with attachment—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Noble Dignity?
To be able to sever worldly attachments regarding what one has heard, and to bestow cherished treasures as offerings to create merit—this is called giving (*dāna*).

To practice with caution and refrain from arrogance, remaining humble, compliant, and reverent toward the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
Not seeking fame and not envying worldly glory, but holding only the Dharma as supreme—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Diligently practicing what one follows and serving elders, parents, teachers, and friends—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

Using meditative contemplation to transform and enlighten sentient beings—just as in antiquity King Kuśuma had a crown prince who provided extensive relief, moving about to everywhere to practice the ultimate Dharma, whose original nature was pure and who never harbored malice—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To seek the perfection of wisdom through the noble clarity of diligence while living as a renunciant is called wisdom;
these are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of relatives and kin?
If, by means of the Dharma used to save and transform others, one delights in leaving the household life and sets one's will upon renunciation, this is called generosity (*dāna*);
if, through vigilance, obedience, and compassion, one instructs one’s descendants in the principles of meaning and proclaims the ultimate teaching, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
if, practicing benevolence and harmony, one teaches and guides countless beings against all suffering and distress without ever becoming weary, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To diligently practice with the resolve to listen to the Dharma, and upon seeing those who do not understand, to expound it for them so that each may achieve mental comprehension—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To employ meditative reflection to assist and harmonize sentient beings, demonstrating to them their transgressions and blessings so as to transform them and prevent disorder—just like the ancient Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) Sunetra—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To protect the sagely brilliance so that both [self and others] are of one accord; if one can exercise self-restraint and not violate desire, thereby rescuing and protecting others by proclaiming the teaching and establishing all people—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of mental non-forgetfulness?
To be able to subdue one’s own mind and not follow false views; to emerge from the moat of difficulties and not follow the calamities of greed—this is called the retribution of giving.

To fully observe all the prohibitions one may follow, never severing the Three Jewels, causing the Way to flourish, and transforming those who have not yet reached it—this is called the retribution of the precepts (*śīla*).

To possess a mind and conduct that are benevolent, harmonious, peaceful, and gentle, such that even when the body encounters suffering, one is able to endure all afflictions because of extensive learning—just as when Sūrata was subjected to poison by others, his heart felt no resentment—this is called the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).

If, through diligent practice, one subdues one’s own mind, transcends indolence, and protects others so they do not fall into peril or distress, leading them to long-lasting peace and security—this is called the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).
To abandon indulgence through meditative reflection, and to uphold non-greed, non-resentment, and tranquil concentration—this is called the retribution of single-mindedness.

To abide in the laws of noble wisdom, proper conduct, and ritual etiquette; to rely upon the mind to provide for all benefits; and furthermore, to bestow the gift of Dharma to deliver the masses from blindness and darkness—this is called the retribution of wisdom.
These constitute the six.
Chapter Eleven: The Thirty-two Marks. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of dwelling truthfully in peace and tranquility?
To lift one’s feet from level ground and proceed forward in pursuit of samādhi is called the retribution of giving;
to establish and encourage others so that they are no longer afflicted or harmed, remaining free from suffering from beginning to end, is called the retribution of ethical discipline;
for all people to be unable to shake one’s resolve, such that the mind gives rise to no resentment and the countenance remains serene and pleasant, is called the retribution of patience.
To establish one's intent so as to uphold the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, proceeding directly forward without weariness and never retreating—this is called the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).

To manifest a longing for and delight in unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, causing sentient beings to dwell in peace and to expound upon meditative contemplation—this is called the retribution of single-mindedness (*samādhi*).

To explain the retributions and the places where one is born, such that one always encounters the Buddhas to inquire about and receive the Great Way—this is called the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the *āgatya-sahasrāra-pāramitā*?

If one brings forth all manner of material goods and, by means of various kinds of wheels, practices giving so as to achieve the retribution of the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, this is called the retribution of giving.
If, by means of various extraordinary, exceptional, and wondrous colors, the body remains therein without being destroyed, this is called the retribution of observing the precepts (*śīla*).

If various kinds of rare and diverse fragrances arise, yet the mind does not become attached and remains free from thoughts of increase or decrease, this is called the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).

As for those who practice with diligence and firmly maintain their resolve—just as a master artisan holds a great screen, or like one crossing a river directly on a raft to bring his family to safety—this is called the retribution of vigor (*vīrya*).
If one emanates light that shines universally far and near, penetrating the ten directions through the attainment of mastery, this is called the retribution of single-mindedness;
if one vibrates a great light such that all receive its benefit, and everyone attains holy clarity while all darkness is dispelled, this is called the retribution of wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters concerning the infinite quality of the skin's softness and fineness?

If one writes out characters and texts—not for the sake of mere tranquility, but to transform all sentient beings by demonstrating their transgressions and blessings—this is called the retribution of giving (*dāna*).
To rely upon the verbal teachings and revere what is authentic, not acting with hypocrisy but harboring the true meaning within, this is called the retribution of ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To possess the foundation of all perfected virtues, such that the wondrous spiritual mind neither arises nor ceases—this is called the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).

To truly transcend the flaws of all evils, thereby enabling the arrival of various bodhisattvas (*bodhisattva*) to come and provide transformative guidance—this is called the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).

To be free from resentment and achieve meritorious achievement, maintaining a harmonious and joyful countenance, leaping for joy while dwelling in the Dharma with a mind free of attachment—this is called the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To abide within the cycle of birth and death while remaining peaceful and harmonious, thereby transforming the ignorant and the dark-minded—this is called the retribution of wisdom.
These constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the Infinite Perfection of Level Soles?
If wherever your feet reach there is no difficulty, and wherever your feet tread upon, insects and moths find eternal peace, this is called the retribution of giving (*dāna*);

when you lift your feet, your mind is free from affliction, and in your conduct you do not violate the law, your mind being harmonious and benevolent, this is called the retribution of ethical discipline (*śīla*);
if when you lift your feet you are composed and at ease, your nature being neither abrupt nor agitated, nor fearful or terrified, this is called the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).
When he lifts his foot, the resulting merit is vast and expansive, like space used to rescue sentient beings; this is called the retribution of single-mindedness.
When the soles of his feet are full and his meritorious power is blazing and boundless, this is called the retribution of wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters that constitute the retribution for the perfection of long fingers?

That the fingers are long and beautiful, resulting from past virtue and being free from crookedness or impurity—these are all the meritorious qualities of the retribution for what was bestowed; this is called the retribution for giving (*dāna*).

That the fingers are slender and beautiful, gradually corresponding to one another without being distorted or disordered, resulting from peaceful conduct in past lives; this is called the retribution for maintaining the precepts (*śīla*)."
That his fingers are long, supple, well-proportioned, radiant, wondrous, and soft is called the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
That his fingers are long, subtle, and harmonious with his virtuous conduct, gradually tapering, smooth, and free from coarse veins or patterns—all these are the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).
That his fingers are auspicious, such that all who see them are delighted and find nothing inauspicious—these are all the retribution for single-minded concentration (*ekāgratā*).
The fingers are lustrous, arranged in proper sequence, harmonious, straight, and not disordered; this is the retribution for wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters regarding the perfection of the webbed hands and feet?
That the hands and feet are full, even, and marked with webbing between the fingers is the retribution for giving: it arises from having fully satisfied those to whom one gave in previous lives.
That the fingers are level, upright, stable, and secure, such that there is no crookedness and the mind is joyful upon seeing them, is the retribution for observing the precepts.
That the hands and feet are without blemish, pure, and exceedingly beautiful is the retribution for practicing benevolence and harmony in former conduct.
That the Buddha’s hands and feet are purple-gold in color and do not collect dust is the retribution for his diligent cultivation in the past without indolence;
that his hands and feet are soft, free from coarseness, and possess a most excellent luster is the retribution for his single-minded concentration (*ekāgratā*);
that his hands and feet are fresh, brilliant, and radiant, surpassing all others so that all who see them are filled with joy, is the retribution for his wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six aspects of the perfection of the level knees? Their knees arise upright;

as they gradually turn upward, they are universally endowed with extraordinary qualities. Their virtuous conduct is so preeminent that all who see them do not fail to revere them; this is the retribution for generosity.
That his knees are peaceful and harmonious, without rubbing against one another, is the retribution for observing the precepts;
that his hands and feet are well-proportioned and graceful, moving forward and backward with constant propriety, is the retribution for patience;
