and that he is benevolent and compassionate, walking with feet raised in peace, harmony, and decorum without any abruptness or violence, is the retribution for diligence.
To cultivate equanimity and rectitude without partiality or deviation, and to always practice tranquility—this is called the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To be such that all who behold one rejoice and perceive their radiant image with clarity—this is the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of the Tranquil Treasury?
That its tranquil treasury is peaceful and harmonious, its radiance brilliant and resplendent, yet its substance remains unmanifest—this is the retribution of giving.
That its tranquility is pure and moistening, benefiting and sustaining all beings—this is the retribution of ethical discipline."
His body hairs curl to the right, each being perfectly aligned and not wandering askew; this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
His virtue is lofty and majestic, reaching everywhere to transform and deliver sentient beings; this is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).
He emanates radiance that illuminates all things and brings peace and security to many; this is the retribution for single-minded concentration (*ekacitta*).
Causing others to see auspicious omens and thereby inspire them with the unsurpassed, holy wisdom is the retribution for wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters concerning the depth of the navel being infinite?
That his practice advances daily until it reaches the profound mystery and he resolves upon the Great Way is the retribution for giving;
that his majestic spiritual power and virtue are serene and free from fear, and his mind harbors no difficulties, is the retribution for maintaining the precepts;
that his service is gentle and moistening, reaching deeply into harmony and peace, is the retribution for patience.
That his conduct is complete and free from fear is the retribution of diligence;
that he is as soft, supple, and peaceful as a beautiful flower, being single-minded and undeluded, is the retribution of concentration;
that his navel is unimpaired and that he constantly increases all practices without diminution is the retribution of wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Hair (Lomakūpa-pariśuddhi)?
His hair points upward, curls to the right, is pure and upright, follows the natural order, and stands independently; this is the retribution for generosity (dāna).
His hair is deep blue-black, radiant and beautiful to behold, such that all who see it are filled with joy; this is the retribution for upholding the precepts.
His body hairs are soft, fine, smooth, lustrous, and brilliant; this is the retribution for patience.
His complexion is moist and glossy, never receiving dust or grime; this is the retribution for diligence.
The color of the hair is soft and beautiful, each curling to the right; this is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Each stands waiting without sudden violence, they do not rub against one another, and each is perfectly aligned; this is the retribution for wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Violet-Golden Color?
Its color being like that of gold within fire is the retribution for giving;
its supple and moist color, not being coarse or harsh, is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."
Its pure and flawless color surpasses that of the sun and moon; this is the retribution for patience.
Its radiance shines brilliantly, illuminating both the distant and the near; this is the retribution for diligence.
It is free from defilement and dust, remaining clear and serene; this is the retribution for single-minded concentration.
That light is soft, wondrous, harmonious in color, and brilliantly radiant; this is the retribution for wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the "Lion’s Chest" (Siṃhavakṣas) Perfection?
That his body gradually becomes full and free from deficiency is the retribution for generosity;
that his body is magnificent, exquisite, and possesses towering virtue is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
that his body is firm and strong such that none can violate it is called the retribution for patience.
That all gaze upon him with reverence and never tire of looking is the retribution for diligence;
that his body is vast and expansive as if difficult to reach is called the retribution for single-minded concentration;
that his body cannot be destroyed and is as firm as a diamond is called the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Constant Goodness and Succession?
That the conduct of one's body is fully perfected and complete is called the retribution of giving.
That the Venerable One is unassailable and replete with auspiciousness is called the retribution of observing the precepts;
that one is upright, of exquisite beauty, and brings joy and delight to all who see them is called the retribution of patience;
that one’s conduct and virtuous deeds are impartial and complete is called the retribution of diligence.
To calculate that his marks and signs and complexion are like a masterpiece crafted by a master artisan or a fine painting—this is called the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That they are supple, radiant, pure, and without flaw—this is called the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the reward for long arms?
That the fragrance of one's body is pervasive and uninterrupted, being universally smelled by all—this is called the reward of giving.
To abide uprightly and in perfect composure, such that one cannot be shaken—this is the reward of ethical discipline."
Being harmonious, orderly, firm, and unshakable in mind, with a heart that is well-balanced, is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*);
if one’s own arms reach down to the knees and are exceptionally beautiful, surpassing all others, this is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*);
walking with measured steps and arms reaching below the knees, revered by devas and humans, is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
The manifested body is supple and moist, its brilliant radiance shining upon all; this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the *pīnabāhu* (well-rounded thighs) *pāramitā*?
If one’s limbs and thighs are supple, upright, and elegant, with a kind heart and a harmonious will, this is the retribution for giving (*dāna*);
if one stands alone with composure, free from any constraints and always possessing self-mastery, this is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*);
if one is well able to distinguish locations and reaches peace without calamity or hardship, this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
That the body is upright and the limbs gradually become well-proportioned is the retribution for diligence;
that the majestic radiance is towering and the mark of the invisible crown of the head is the retribution for single-mindedness;
and that all sentient beings, wherever their eyes gaze upon them, cannot help but feel love and respect, is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six aspects of the perfection of the fullness of the brain-combination?
To gradually awaken to the fulfillment of accomplished merit is the retribution for giving;
To have a mind that is steadfast and firm, always harboring harmony and peace, is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
to be as pure as a bright pearl and to radiate light of one's own accord is the retribution for patience;
to cultivate conduct with equanimity, without indolence or negligence, is the retribution for diligence.
Having a body and speech that are gentle and a mind that is peaceful is the retribution for single-mindedness;
being harmonious and moistening such that countless slanders cannot destroy one is the retribution for wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of the Hook-and-Chain (Śṛṅkhalā-pāramitā)?
To see those who come seeking and always remain harmonious and joyful is the retribution for generosity (dāna).
To gradually use awakening and joy to dispel the ignorance of the masses is the retribution for ethical discipline (śīla)."

That their virtues are each manifold yet universally equal, and that they skillfully rely upon one another to accomplish practice through the Way and Dharma, is the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).

That when there is anything to be said, they all remain silent together, harmoniously and equally receiving [the teaching] and seeing it fit to be practiced accordingly, is the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).
That their light is deep blue, brilliant and shining afar, is the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
If one causes all sentient beings in the world who are bound by various calamities to attain liberation for themselves, yet remains unsatiated in seeing this, this is the retribution of wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of the whiteness and purity of the teeth?
That the teeth are exceedingly white and pure, closely set and not sparse, is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*).
That they are supple, moist, white, and beautiful, without spots or stains, is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To be orderly and successive, like a white lotus flower, peaceful and stable—this is the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).
To have teeth that are firm, white, prominent, and free from any black spots—this is the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).
To establish what is bestowed with vast peace and freedom from peril—this is the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
The body is moist, supple, and radiant; beholding its brilliant luster, one never tires of it—this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters regarding the perfection of having even teeth?
The lower teeth are even and level, not slanted or crooked; this is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*).
The upper and lower [teeth] are supple and lustrous, entirely free from coarseness; this is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*).
They are joined in successive, close alignment with no gaps between them; this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
His teeth are even and level, without any variation in height;
this is the retribution for diligence. His teeth are undamaged, firm, strong, and beautiful; this is the retribution for single-minded concentration.

His lower teeth align perfectly with the upper, and his upper teeth align perfectly with the lower; they are stable, secure, and such that all who see them are filled with joy; this is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters that constitute the retribution for the perfection of having forty teeth?
That his forty teeth are complete, all even and regular, and not deficient, is the retribution for generosity;
The teeth are not crooked or tilted, but are perfectly even like water; this is the retribution for upholding the precepts.
The teeth are exquisite and extraordinary, differing from those of others; this is the retribution for patience.
The teeth are penetrating and sharp, with no gaps between them, being neither too tight nor too sparse; this is the retribution for diligence.
The auspicious appearance of the teeth such that nothing seen is not beneficial is the retribution for single-mindedness;
the extreme firmness and immovability of the teeth such that they please the minds of others is the retribution for wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the reward for the broad and long tongue?
When he was a bodhisattva, he listened to the sūtras with his ears and selected the ultimate words to speak; this is the reward for generosity.
He removed the impurities from his tongue and transmitted the Buddha’s words, purifying his mouth to proclaim the meaning; this is the reward for ethical discipline."
Speaking with impartiality and without favoritism is the retribution for patience;
having an extremely broad and long tongue, its color like a lotus flower and its radiance brilliant and majestic, is the retribution for diligence;
and the characteristics of one’s features being marvelous and each distinct from the others is the retribution for single-minded concentration.
The tongue is like a hundred petals, its radiance and color are extraordinary and beautiful, shining brilliantly and casting light afar; this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the retribution of the Brahma-voice?
Practicing the bodhisattva path and proclaiming the sūtras, raising one's voice so that all people hear it clearly and without doubt, is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*);
having a lovely resonance such that all who hear it rejoice, is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*);
the various distinct qualities of the sounds proclaimed are the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
That his voice is never unharmonious and cannot be surpassed is the retribution for diligence;
that his voice is always harmonious and well-regulated, his speech is peaceful and uninterrupted, is the retribution for single-minded concentration;
that all his tones are excellent, mournful yet harmonious and elegant, moving the hearts of the masses, is the retribution for wisdom.
"These are the six.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, King Nanda!"
To cause the body and mind to always remain harmonious and at ease is the retribution for giving;
that the bodily actions, as well as the body, speech, and mind, are concentrated, tranquil, and peaceful is the retribution for ethical discipline;
and that one gives rise to the ten wholesome paths of action, setting one's will upon the realms of devas and humans to cultivate the work of the Path, is the retribution for patience.
To instruct and transform all assemblies without transgression or failure is the retribution for diligence;
to address sentient beings with a compassionate, harmonious, gentle, and moist voice is the retribution for single-mindedness;
and to proclaim the transformation of the Dharma through one’s voice, resolving the doubts of the multitude so that none remain unliberated or unsatisfied, is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Taste among Tastes?
If one provides all manner of food and delicacies such that their flavor is extraordinary and pleases the minds of the multitude, this is called the retribution of giving.
That the recipients of one’s gifts obtain peace and well-being without affliction is called the retribution for upholding the precepts (*śīla*);
that the recipients are harmonious and harbor no contentious thoughts toward the donor is called the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*);
and that the various requisites provided are distributed equitably so as to leave the body free from illness is called the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).
That the food is of supreme excellence, sweet to the palate and free from any foul odor, is called the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
that it is neither hot nor cold, its flavor being harmonious and agreeable, and its texture light and soft, is called the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of the Lion’s Jaws?
His back is broad and level, and like the form of a lion, he strides alone through the three realms; this is the retribution for giving.
Like a lotus flower, his luster and color are wondrous, and his conduct is like that of a lion; this is the retribution for upholding the precepts."
If one advances forward like a lion, free from fear or difficulty, this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*);
that one manifests a great, majestic, sublime, and extraordinary spiritual power is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*);
and that all other teachings proclaim joy and are honored by all sentient beings is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).

Those who see them with their own eyes all take refuge in them; their countenances are joyful as they behold their virtue and offer reverence without ever feeling satiated—this is the retribution for wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of retribution for the eye being like a cow, like the moon, and bringing [light] to cross over to the Infinite?
That the eyes are subtle and wondrous, long and beautiful like the newly risen moon, is the retribution for giving.
That the eyes are clear and distinct, upright and magnificent, lacking not a single deficiency, is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."
His eyes are radiant, soft, fresh, and exquisite, beyond compare; this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
His face is free from timidity, luminous, and glossy; this is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).
His countenance is wondrously beautiful and his physical form is perfectly upright like the newly risen sun; this is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
Light like that of the sun and moon illuminates the eight directions, above and below, such that no darkness can approach its brilliance; this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters concerning the *pāramitā* of the deep blue color of the eyes?
If one feels joy in the heart upon seeing the Buddha, taking refuge with single-minded devotion and regarding him with reverence, this is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*);
that what the eyes behold is tranquil and focused, without a single thing being improper, is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*);
that the eyes are subtle and exquisite such that no one can find fault with them, and that both those near and far are subdued, is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
That what the eyes behold causes no harm and brings much benefit is the retribution of diligence;
that one sees afar into the profound and remote and resolves all fetters is the retribution of single-mindedness;
that what is seen is never wearying, its bottom cannot be reached, and what is perceived is impartial is the retribution of wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six aspects of the perfection of the nose being like that of a parrot?
The nose is like that of a parrot—elevated, level, upright, and exquisite; this is the retribution for generosity.
Constantly abiding in tranquil concentration without any deviation or error is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
having a nose that is beautifully moist and radiant like a bright pearl is the retribution for patience;
being supple, truly patient, harmonious, and gentle, such that all who observe one’s dignified deportment look up to you with reverence, is the retribution for diligence.
That all people behold them with constant respect and affection, never wearying of them, is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
that the mind relinquishes its thoughts and experiences that which cannot be clung to, not dwelling on various fragrances but taking the Way as fragrance, is the retribution for wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *uṣṇīṣa-lakṣaṇa* (the crown-protrusion perfection) that are infinite?
That his crown is perfectly round and naturally gives rise to a brilliant, radiant light is the retribution for generosity;
that the hair of his crown is deep blue, magnificent beyond measure, and each strand curls to the right is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."
The brilliance of the usnīsa is so majestic that the limits of its radiance cannot be grasped; this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
The fleshly usnīsa is full and complete, free from any irregularity or deviation, standing firm and at ease; this is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).
It is smooth and lustrous, turning gracefully with a serene and certain mark of distinction, without being confused or intermingled; this is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
The radiance of his brilliant light shines infinitely; this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters regarding the Tathāgata’s *uṣṇīṣa* (crown-protrusion) as the perfection of the infinite?
The hair is blue-black like the unsurpassed deep indigo, smooth, lustrous, and more radiant than the light of lapis lazuli; this is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*).
The hairs of the head curl to the right, each following its own root without touching one another; this is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*).
His body is pure and free from dust and grime, just as a lotus flower is not defiled by dust or water; this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
That none of the gods above or below can behold his crown is the retribution for diligence;
that all sentient beings in the three realms delight in seeing him and his majestic virtue is far-reaching is the retribution for single-mindedness;
that his speech cannot be defiled even by celestial rain, being as pure as space and resonant like thunder, is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the stride of the wandering forth?
That one strides forth alone without hindrance is the retribution for giving.

If one abandons what is improper and is able to maintain single-mindedness, such that their aspirations and conduct are vast and peaceful, this is called being a child of the Buddha; this is the retribution for upholding the precepts.
That countless devas come to see them, pay homage, prostrate themselves on the ground, and take refuge, is the retribution for patience.
That they are able to protect themselves and have no attachments in their vision is the retribution for diligence.
Valiantly soaring and leaping with infinite supernormal powers is the retribution of single-minded concentration;
being able to bestow all that one possesses without stinginess and proclaiming the teachings of the Way is the retribution of wisdom. These constitute the six [perfections].
(The *Dān-běn* has a note stating: "There is a commentary."
"Among the thirty-two marks, two types of textual passages are missing from the old [translation].

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: On Following the Seasons.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Adapting to the Seasons?
To heal the wounds of the multitude while the mind remains unattached, acting like a lotus flower, is the retribution for giving.
To follow and cultivate the growth of the hundred grasses and trees during spring and summer, removing the cold according to the seasons, is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."
His body is wondrously beautiful, towering and sublime like the brilliance of the many stars; this is the retribution for patience.
He is impartial and compliant, never failing or erring; this is the retribution for diligence.
He completely blocks off all evil destinies and demonstrates harmony and peace; this is the retribution for single-minded concentration.
If sentient beings are on evil paths, one uses various radiances to illuminate them so that they attain liberation; this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of knowing the proper time?
If, during the late night or the break of dawn while lying in sleep, one suddenly awakens to contemplate the True Dharma, this is the retribution for giving.
If one is able to renounce the household life, abandon wealth and enterprise, and become a śramaṇa, this is the retribution for observing the precepts."

Informing Chandaka to return and persuade his father the king and his wife, promising that once he has attained Buddhahood and returned to the kingdom he shall deliver them across [to liberation], is the retribution for patience;
his physical cultivation of practice, his resolve to leave the household life, and his donning of the *kāṣāya* robe is the retribution for diligence;
and his yearning for liberation and seeking the unsurpassed path is the retribution for single-minded concentration.
Entering into the state of profound stillness while discerning the sounds of verses, yet returning to the household life to deliver and liberate sentient beings—this is the retribution of wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of discernment (prajñāpāramitā)?
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he entered Rājagṛha to beg for alms and bring blessings to people; this is the retribution for giving.
Abiding above in the heavens, he proclaimed the transformative teachings of the Way to all devas and humans; this is the retribution for maintaining the precepts.
Having finished his wandering through Rājagṛha, he returned to the summit of the heavens to transform the multitudes through tranquility; this is the retribution for patience.
Standing with the body straight, without relying on or clinging to anything, is the retribution for diligence;
if one contemplates through meditative concentration and understands that within the three realms there is not a single true reality, this is the retribution for single-mindedness;
contemplating and examining the twelve links of dependent origination to see that their origins all arise from the correspondence of causes and conditions is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the *lokavid* pāramitā?
When one goes on almsround and each person receives a benefit so that the recipient is at peace, this is the retribution for giving.

To comply with the world’s intentions during times of famine and alleviate its deprivation—just as Rāmaputra traveled everywhere to rescue many from distress—is the retribution for upholding the precepts.
To oppose all that is unrighteous, resolve difficulties without hesitation, and receive this path of practice is the retribution for patience.
That for six years one transcends all obstacles without a single flaw is the retribution for diligence.
Practicing meditation with firm resolve and understanding all things as being entirely like a mass of foam or bubbles is the retribution of single-minded concentration (*ekāgratā*);

not transgressing the Dharma, food and drink appearing spontaneously, and all who hear one's name returning [to the path], as well as sitting beneath the Bodhi tree to subdue the various Māras, is the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the ultimate limit?
If one subdues Māra along with his retinue, and by turning the wheel of Dharma delivers all beings, this is the retribution for giving.

If one exhorts and transforms all classes of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, enabling them to attain eternal peace and freedom from all afflictions, this is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."

To instruct sentient beings so as to reconcile those who are quarreling, and to establish them in virtuous conduct so that they commit no transgressions—this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
To bring peace and harmony to the three thousandfold world-system when it is in turmoil, so that all share the same flavor of the Path—this is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).

To practice these four dhyānas with a concentrated mind in right reception (*samādhi*), and to carry out the ten wholesome actions without negligence—this is the retribution for single-mindedness (*citta* or *samādhi*).
To eliminate ignorance so that all darkness is utterly exhausted and forever leaves no remainder, thereby attaining brilliant illumination—this is the retribution of wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of purification?

In the past, while traveling through the land of Kāśī, I stayed and wandered for seven years teaching and transforming others; that all their karmic offenses were exhausted and their afflictions eliminated was the retribution for my giving.
That I eradicated these defilements and wandered through the three realms without attachment was the retribution for my upholding the precepts.
That I was able to skillfully eliminate the three poisons so that no thought arose in the mind was the retribution for my patience.
To contemplate the birth, death, transgressions, and blessings of sentient beings with equanimity and compassion is the retribution for diligence;
to cultivate meditative concentration through weariness with afflictions, to attain the eight stages of liberation without forgetting them, is the retribution for single-mindedness;

to be forever free from delusion, to sever craving, to eliminate ignorance, to give rise to the wisdom of the Path, to remove all dharmas so they are not false, and to single-mindedly practice the Perfection of Wisdom, is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the *vajra-pāramitā*?
If one attains the *vajra-samādhi* such that the mind does not waver, this is the retribution for giving.
If one employs skillful means to cast aside ignorance and practices the ultimate virtue, this is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
if one advances toward the meaning of the Path without any grasping and completely abandons all defilements, this is the retribution for patience;
if one protects all sentient beings within the triple world and, in accordance with worldly conventions, transforms and delivers them all, this is the retribution for diligence.

To bring one’s own merits to rest and stabilize them in their proper sequence, and to give rise to them in accordance with reality until their fundamental source is exhausted, is the retribution of single-mindedness;
to know the nature of the minds of all sentient beings and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment is the retribution of wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of providing salvation?

To achieve perfect enlightenment as taught by the various devas, to single-mindedly abandon all evil conduct, and to remain tranquil through meditative concentration; to contemplate worldly dharmas and protect all beings—this is the retribution for giving.
To eliminate the suffering and afflictions of the evil realms and hells, and the calamities of all transgressions—this is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."
To clearly understand the various faculties and achieve perfection in virtuous conduct, causing all that was incomplete to become fully endowed—this is the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).
To dissolve the afflictions and calamities of all classes of sentient beings so that they are forever eliminated without remainder—this is the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).

For all musical instruments to sound spontaneously without being struck, delighting the minds of all and causing them to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment—this is the retribution of single-minded concentration (*ekacitta*).
To constantly practice giving away the vast treasuries of wealth and jewels within the trichiliocosm to countless billions of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans is the retribution for wisdom;
this is the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of spontaneity?
The trees of the trichiliocosm produce flowers and fruits that flourish perpetually through winter and summer; to bestow these upon all who are in need is the retribution for *dāna*.
To eliminate all afflictions and immeasurable pains of toil and suffering, causing long-lasting peace and harmony, is the retribution for *śīla*."
That all sentient beings possess their faculties in full and reach ultimate spontaneity is the retribution of patience;
that the entire trichiliocosm is naturally as level as the palm of one's right hand is the retribution of diligence;
and that all forms and images enter into defilement yet remain truly non-illusory so that all devas receive its grace is the retribution of single-mindedness.
To subdue the four māras with peerless wisdom and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment is the retribution of wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the infinite power of subduing māras?
To practice the bodhisattva path to heal the diseases of the three poisons throughout the entire trichiliocosm and attain supreme perfect enlightenment is the retribution for giving;
to eliminate the myriad afflictions and extinguish all the contentious karmic deeds of Māras is the retribution for ethical discipline;
to transform the various celestial sons and the calamities of harmful ghosts and discordant spirits, causing them all to abide in eternal peace, is the retribution for patience.
That all the officials and followers of the Māra of Death naturally submit, take refuge, and revere the Buddha’s holy teaching is the retribution for diligence;
that there are no five aggregates and the demon of the body is spontaneously liberated without fetters is the retribution for single-mindedness;
and that one attains supreme perfect enlightenment as omniscient according to one's vow is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of non-retrogression?
To sit beneath the Bodhi tree with single-minded concentration and diligent reflection without weariness or satiety is the retribution for generosity;
If one perceives Māra yet remains without fear, personally attaining perfect enlightenment and delivering all beings, this is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
if one’s body is not distracted, its beginning and end are tranquil, and the mind is settled in eternal peace, this is the retribution for patience;
if the mind is joyful, tranquil, and secure, free from all demons, this is the retribution for diligence.
To practice equal giving, such that one's conduct is level, upright, and without distinction, is the retribution for single-mindedness;
for words and deeds to correspond with one another, and body, speech, and mind to be concentrated so as to attain the Way of the Buddha, is the retribution for wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *ekakṣaṇapāramitā*?

To diligently cultivate wisdom for a single moment, attaining the unsurpassed, right, and true path as the most perfect enlightenment, and to guide others according to the occasion through the practice of the mind—this is the retribution of giving (*dāna*).
To eliminate dust and defilement from one's associates and always maintain purity—this is the retribution of ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
The World-Honored One’s intention is to forever destroy the three poisons and cause the Three Jewels to flourish; this is the retribution for patience.
To deliver others through right concentration, extinguishing all defilements so that the three poisons no longer exist; this is the retribution for diligence.
To clearly understand and discern the twelve links of dependent origination, severing all entanglements; this is the retribution for single-mindedness.
To be able to attain a state free from forgetfulness, such that one cognizes all dharmas of the three periods of time—the past, future, and present—is the retribution of wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of equanimity?
To see with the fleshly eye all sentient beings suffering in affliction and distress, and to establish them in great peace—this is the retribution of giving.

To see with the divine eye the births and deaths, the unions and separations, and the good and evil of all beings, and to transform them so they may cross over the world—this is the retribution of ethical discipline."
To exhort and transform others in the stations of the śrāvakas so that they become free from attachment is the retribution of patience;
if, by means of supernormal powers and transformations, one travels back and forth and circulates everywhere to rescue those in distress within the three realms, this is the retribution of diligence;
if, regarding whatever one contemplates, the mind observes such pure conduct and proclaims the Dharma just like Brahmā, this is the retribution of single-minded concentration.
If, by means of knowing the proper time, one makes vows for noble wisdom and expounds the sutras and dharmas so that they reach throughout the ten directions, this is the retribution of wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of samādhi?
To sit in meditation and contemplate without thoughts of clothing or food, dwelling beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*).
To have profound faith in the Dharma, awaken the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), accord with principle, and not lose one's diligence, is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To delight in the awakening of the mind, take pleasure in the meaning of the Path, and keep the mundane world out of one’s heart, is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
To discern the twelvefold divisions of the sūtras and the deeds of the practice of perfect enlightenment in order to transform all beings is the retribution of diligence;
to abandon clamor and distraction, to be free from deviant thoughts, and to cultivate right reception through the concentration of samādhi is the retribution of single-mindedness;
to protect the factors of awakening and nurture sentient beings so that they reach great peace is the retribution of wisdom.
These are the six. "What are the six matters of the perfection of instruction?
If, having attained the Buddha-way, one observes the beginning and the end to transform and enlighten sentient beings, this is the retribution for giving; [the other five follow in the same manner]."
Even if there is no request, to proclaim the Dharma and disseminate wisdom is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
to radiate brilliance through liberation, to maintain it without transgression, and to possess a compassionate nature with magnificent transformations, is the retribution for patience;

and just as when the brothers Kāśyapa and their companions, though three in number, were self-reliant in considering themselves true practitioners of the Way, the Buddha exhorted and transformed them so that they all reached the Ultimate Way—this is the retribution for diligence.

When sentient beings inquire about the meaning of the Dharma, one does not allow doubt or obstruction to arise; by expounding and proclaiming it, one causes each of them to attain understanding—this is the retribution for single-minded concentration (*ekāgratā*).
To discern, dispatch, and definitively resolve matters with holy clarity such that nothing remains unpenetrated—this is the retribution for wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Buddha-way’s Perfection of Crossing Over?
To proclaim the sūtras through the means of ignorance while demonstrating noble wisdom is the retribution for giving.
To act as the Buddha’s messenger to bring peace to those in ignorance and lead them to the radiant light of the Way and its Virtue is the retribution for maintaining the precepts."
To extinguish all defilements, to be compliant and eternally tranquil, and to possess immeasurable eloquence—this is the retribution of patience (*kṣānti*).
That the Dharma is impartial and upright, that one attains concentration without forgetfulness and constantly keeps the ten directions in mind—this is the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).
To universally enter into all things, to practice and fulfill supreme virtue, and to be powerful and majestic—this is the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To be courageous and fearless, to clearly understand the source of the Way, and to set one’s will upon the unsurpassed truth—this is called the retribution of wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of All-Knowledge?
That what the eyes behold through the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) is without obstruction is the retribution for generosity (*dāna*);
that one knows the beginning and end of the thoughts in the minds of the assembly and thereby preaches the Dharma so that their minds become serene is the retribution for ethical discipline (*śīla*);
that one can hear the essential teachings expounded from afar or near with equanimity and tranquility is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).
To preach the Dharma according to the times so that all may attain understanding according to their respective inclinations is the retribution for diligence;
to proclaim the sūtras without losing their proper sequence, so that each finds its appropriate skillful means and suitability, is the retribution for single-mindedness;
to discourse upon right wisdom according to what others delight in, remaining free from attachment while giving rise to all things and composing verses, is the retribution for wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of non-remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-pāramitā)?

If the mind is at peace and one reverently practices the path of the Dharma, giving rise to the ultimate meaning and reaching the state of non-remainder, this is the retribution for generosity (dāna).

If one employs the Way and its teachings as a source of happiness and swiftly brings others who have not yet attained realization to transformation, this is the retribution for upholding the precepts;
to have profound faith in the sūtras and dharmas spoken by all Buddhas as being equal and without distinction, this is the retribution for patience;
to contemplate the matters of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—with equanimity, such that there is forever no obstruction, this is the retribution for diligence.

If, by means of the dhyānas, the liberations, and the samādhis, one enters these meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) according to one's inclination and acts as one pleases while contemplating with a concentrated mind, this is the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one expounds various categories of Dharma for others, such that they all attain understanding and resolve upon the unsurpassed Dharma, this is the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* with remainder?
After his parinirvāṇa, the distribution of his relics and the use of that merit to instruct others so they may attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the retribution for generosity;
contemplating the practice of prohibitions and drawing near to the unconditioned to enjoy it as one pleases is the retribution for ethical discipline."
That all devas come from every quarter to take refuge in and pay homage to the Tathāgata’s vihāra and divine temple is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).

That after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one diligently practices his instructions with tireless vigor, performing the conduct of a śrāvaka without allowing any hindrance, is the retribution for diligence (*vīrya*).
That one gradually advances through the successive stages of samādhi and right reception (*samāpatti*) until reaching nirvāṇa is the retribution for single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To cultivate transcendent wisdom through the faculty of noble clarity, traveling everywhere in vast expansion—this is the retribution of wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of cessation?

To dwell in the world of the Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings, receiving food and offerings while practicing what is correct rather than what is deviant—this is the retribution for giving (*dāna*).

To preach of meritorious rewards, such as when the Brahmin named Pīlata reviled and slandered the Buddha, yet the Buddha maintained a serene countenance without anger or resentment; at that time, three hundred million devas and humans all resolved their minds on the Way—this is the retribution for upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

As for Sundarī (translated in Chinese as Shanmiao), who slandered the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata used this occasion to convert twelve thousand followers of external paths and cause them to attain liberation—this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).

His power is firm and strong, and his mind always regards itself as such; like a Bodhisattva practicing true compassion, even if he falls among beasts as a lion king, should others invade or oppress him, he accepts it in silence to transform the animals—this is the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).

If he divests himself of resentment toward those who treat him unfairly, remaining silent and not contending with them, accepting it calmly without harboring it in his heart—this is the retribution of single-mindedness (*samādhi*).

If he uses meditative reflection to preach and propagate the transformative teachings of the Way, answering questions on their meanings so that none remain unresolved—this is the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the Buddhas’ perfection of crossing over?

If they proclaim the Dharma, making it heard throughout all Buddha-fields so that its sound reaches as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven at the very pinnacle of the upper regions, this is the retribution for giving.

If one emits light that pervades the three thousandfold world system, transforming and enlightening sentient beings so that they all attain peace and security, this is the retribution for upholding the precepts.
If one brings forth the vast and expansive rain of Dharma to transform the Jāṭila-Brahmās and others, causing them to enter the Great Way, this is the retribution for patience.

If one manifests spiritual powers through transformations to display majestic authority, so that those such as Kāśyapa and his peers are gladdened and submit as disciples, this is the retribution for diligence.

To direct one's thoughts toward the Brahmā heavens and observe them with a mind that is not false; to set one's will upon the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) with the desire to deliver all Brahmās—this is the retribution of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To provide timely guidance like the lion’s roar so that none fail to receive its compassion; for this compassion is like space, universally covering all things—this is the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of skillful means?

Formerly, there was a brahmin named Sūsthita who extensively bestowed eighty-four thousand gifts upon each [recipient], all to encourage and assist in the establishment of the Buddha-way. For example, regarding the bhikṣuṇī named Mahāprajāpatī, the Buddha exhorted her, saying:
'Offer this gold-woven cloth to the noble assembly.'"

When these words were spoken, eight hundred bhikṣus all entered the Dharma and Vinaya; this is the retribution for giving. All the Buddhas who have attained parinirvāṇa continue to teach with peace and stability;

thus he opened the way for the outsider named Suma, and while he was amidst the realm of desire, he used six matters to nurture his mind so that he might receive the discipline of the Path; this is the retribution for upholding the precepts.

Although he dwells in benevolence and harmony, it is like the Bodhisattva of old named Kṣāntivādin, who, while practicing patience, had his hands, feet, ears, and nose severed by the King of the Kāśī kingdom; yet his blood turned into milk, his mind gave rise to no anger, and he suffered no injury, cherishing great compassion for him as if for an infant; at that time, he delivered eighty billion devas; this is the retribution for patience.

Exerting oneself to practice diligently, with a great resolve like that of a bodhisattva possessing the five supernatural powers, encouraging five hundred brahmin youths to leave the household life and causing them all to rejoice and accept the teachings of the Way—this is the retribution of diligence (*vīrya*).

If, upon hearing the sūtras, one’s power increases further until reaching the ultimate meditative absorption of right concentration (*samādhi*)—this is the retribution of single-mindedness (*samādhi*).
To proclaim the Dharma freely according to one’s capacity, delivering beings according to their inclinations—this is the retribution of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of sorrowful concern?
If, when practicing giving, one harbors thoughts of anxiety yet constantly makes offerings to the Great Sage with the clarity of wisdom, not seeking any personal gain—this is called generosity.
To summon the vehicle of the Path to come from all quarters, establishing the works of the Path and bringing them to full perfection—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To be like Shenri (in the Jin language, Shouji), who, having previously studied heterodox teachings, gave rise to malice and invited the Buddha [to challenge him], yet through this very encounter received the teaching and entered the Buddha-way—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, to be like the Dragon King Vairocana of old, whose mind was fierce and poisonous as he sent frost and hail upon the five grains and harmed the myriad people, until the Buddha transformed and guided him—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

When he had originally attained the Buddha-way and become the Most Perfectly Awakened One, the Buddha remained silent and contemplated without weariness; Brahmā descended and requested the Buddha’s encouragement and assistance, saying only: "Please deign to preach the Dharma to rescue and deliver those in the three realms"—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

Furthermore, just as a viper harbors a most potent venom, the Buddha entered the fire-chamber to transform it, bringing it into the discipline (*vinaya*), subduing it, and causing it to take refuge—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
“What are the six matters of the *tathatā-tāraka-aparimita* (the Infinite of Transforming True Dharma)?
To settle oneself in peace while rescuing and protecting others, giving away all that one possesses without stinginess—this is called *dāna* (giving).

It is like the Bodhisattva named Padmagarbha, who, through the practice of *vajra*, possesses a mind of great fortitude free from greed or parsimony; yet, regarding all sentient beings who mentally conceive of a self, he says:”

To think, "There is a self," and because of that sense of self, to practice the Dharma with equanimity, and for the sake of those sentient beings, to be willing to lose even one's body and life rather than ever violate the precepts—this is called *śīla* (ethical discipline).

It is like the turtle of old who ferried a group of merchants across [the water] so they would not drown; yet they, harboring evil intentions and lacking gratitude, thought of returning to harm and kill the turtle. The turtle, however, remained single-mindedly peaceful and compassionate, without a thought of anger—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).

If there are fish in the water that drag people down to devour their bodies, or various insects that come to endanger human life, and one rescues those within it with a heart of compassion—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If various beasts come wishing to kill a person, and one is able to endure them all without returning evil for evil—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one recites and studies billions of sutra scrolls and tens of millions of parables, and by means of this noble wisdom delivers others across [to liberation]—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the extraordinary *pāramitās*?
If one sees those who are hungry, destitute, or in distress, and provides for them according to the occasion, this is called *dāna* (giving).

When the brahmin and ascetic named Śrāvakakīrti was partaking of a meal at a great sacrificial offering, [the Bodhisattva] converted him and inspired him to the mind of the Way; this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

Furthermore, when that brahmin diligently provided medical treatments to cure various ailments, [the Bodhisattva] added the medicine of the Dharma and extolled supreme virtue, causing all sentient beings to be reborn in the heavens; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Diligently cultivating physical conduct and resolving to undertake the work of renunciation, being thus valiant even before attaining Buddhahood; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To transcend to the mountain peak through meditative contemplation, and to receive the unsurpassed, true, and correct realization of the three types of supernormal knowledge regarding the past, future, and present—this is called "single-mindedness" (concentration).
To embody and understand the eighteen unique qualities of all Buddhas, and to proclaim the transformative teachings of the Way throughout the eighteen hells—this is called "wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
13. The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment, Chapter Thirteen. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of the four abandonments?"

To guard against the arising of various evils and unwholesome states so that they do not emerge; to gather the combined power of the six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā) to extinguish afflictions (kleśa) and keep them perpetually pure—this is called giving (dāna).
To seek the subduing of the unwholesome and eliminate various evils and improper activities—this is called ethical discipline (śīla).
To understand the source of the non-dharmic as being spontaneous and to transform it so that it enters the Path—this is called patience (kṣānti).
That all unarisen evils are extinguished before they can arise and that the Dharma is made to flourish is called diligence;
to exhort and transform others so that they enter into the true and correct and propagate the work of the Way is called single-mindedness;
to ultimately ensure that all evils and unwholesome states do not arise again by nature, and through such mental practice to nurture the transformation of the Way, is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters concerning the infinite extinction of arisen discursive thoughts?
If one encounters the arising of afflictions and enters into them, yet perceives the Bodhisattva’s skillful means in practicing the truth, this is called giving.
To feel weary of and loathe sensual desires, to find them difficult and impure, and to uphold the practice of pure clarity—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To remain therein, severing defilements and cultivating purity; if one exhausts the roots of evil habits and unrighteousness, and diligently encourages the arising of merit that has not yet been produced—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one understands through wisdom, discerns the afflictions (*kleśa*), and eliminates all sensual desires—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To always dwell in leisure, focusing the mind on meditative reflection and remaining settled in samādhi—this is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā).
To have profound faith in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) of others, to give rise to virtuous merit, and to deliver all beings—this is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *paramitā* of causing unarisen multitudes of virtues to arise?
If one gives rise to various good deeds and does not abandon those who are destitute, accumulating merit and virtue while self-disciplining oneself in every birth, this is called *dāna* (giving).
If one brings forth virtuous qualities with increasing joy, causing them to grow so as to bestow them upon all, this is called *śīla* (precept-keeping)."
To follow emptiness and non-action without exhausting the roots of virtue, thereby eliminating all evils and unwholesome conducts—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To establish conduct through body and speech with skillful means and without conditions, giving rise to the Way and its virtue—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To uphold the teachings of the Dharma, restrain all dependent thoughts, and not forget the concentration of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To give rise to the mind of non-arising through what has been cultivated, to achieve the light of the Way, and to transform all beings by bearing the compassion of the Way—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters by which the perfection of the establishment of virtue (śīla-pāramitā) is initiated?
To give rise to the source of all wholesome merits and virtues, and not to produce unwholesome conduct or that which is meaningless—this is called giving (dāna).
To rejoice in this [virtue] with a mind solely intent upon the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha), and not to dwell on minor deeds that are of no benefit to all—this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
To examine what is appropriate and fitting without harboring resentment, and to eliminate all forms of negligence, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To provide protection that is never false and to cause all to enter the Way is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To revere and follow the power of the Way, being neither weak nor inferior but possessing strength and authority, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To comply with worldly customs while never falling into any of the sixty-two types of wrong views or doubts, and to encourage all others so that they do not harbor delusive thoughts—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the bases of psychic power?
To sever all greedy defilements and contemplate the sūtras, thereby perfecting the bases of psychic power without ever forgetting them—this is called generosity.
How does a bodhisattva fully accomplish this, such that they follow what their mind delights in without harboring any attachment?"
If one joyfully practices giving and provides relief from peril and distress through the meaning of the Dharma, this is called precept-keeping;
if one’s joy is firm and indestructible, and the mind gives rise to no resentment, this is called patience;
if one aspires to leave the household life, renounces worldly glory and pleasure, and finds delight in the Dharma for oneself, this is called diligence.
If one correctly contemplates that the entire triple world is like an illusion or a transformation, this is called single-mindedness;
if one skillfully resolves doubts so that no further web of fetters remains and penetrates deeply into the subtle and wondrous, this is called wisdom—
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the perfection of diligence?
If one protects the bases of psychic power to fly to the ten directions without obstruction, transforming and enlightening all beings, this is called generosity (dāna).

If one applies oneself with earnest resolve to the great enterprise, with a mind of progressive aspiration and joy, wishing for lightness and elevation as one travels throughout the world, this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."

Diligently cultivating the resolve for enlightenment so that it increases day by day without slackening or abandonment, while simultaneously transforming sentient beings—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Attaining skillful means (*upāya*) regarding what ought to be undertaken, leaving the household life to study the Way and taking no pleasure in deviant conduct—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

Resolving the doubts of the multitude, causing them all to be enlightened and transformed, and inspiring them to give rise to the mind of the Way through a heart of joy and gladness—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To provide encouragement and assistance so as to universally enter into all things, causing those obscured by darkness to recognize the true and real, such that those in the ten directions receive its grace—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
“What are the six matters of the perfection of the psychic power of mental formation?
To have a mind that is equanimous, exhausting all defilements and dusts while constantly practicing purity—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To depart from the impure conduct of craving and desire, and to reverently cultivate what is pure and white—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).”
To clearly understand that all things thus produced are subject to extinction and cannot endure for long, and to rely solely upon the Way—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To attain the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*), wherein though there is attainment, one attains nothing attained—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To establish the mind so as to eliminate all constraints, abiding nowhere while constantly following the true and correct—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To sever all fetters and attachments so that the mind is never bound and is equal to space—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the supernormal power of the known consciousness?
To cultivate the activities of consciousness so as to depart from craving and desire, such that there is no further attachment to the dust of sensory objects, is called generosity (*dāna*).
To attain the true and correct, not being treacherous or sycophantic, and committing no transgressions whatsoever, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To encourage and assist in purity so that there is no blemish, and to always be cautious regarding all disputes, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To transcend all obstacles and universally enter into the realm where all sentient beings receive his grace is called diligence;
to be able to awaken to the fact that all hindrances are merely depletions and not to succumb to negligence is called single-mindedness;

to cast off defilements and obstructions so as to be liberated from hindrance, to never lose great eloquence, and to guide those who have not yet attained it so that they all enter deeply, is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the first dhyāna-pāramitā?
Diligently applying skillful means to attain immeasurable merit is called giving (dāna).
To observe all phenomena with skillful means according to the occasion, never failing in anything, is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To receive and master the expedient means of the first dhyāna without losing single-mindedness, maintaining the resolve for concentration and wisdom while constantly contemplating benevolence and harmony, is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one dissolves the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), accomplishes the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and enters everywhere among the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) to transform beings, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To achieve such single-minded concentration that the mind is tranquil and there is nothing produced, yet one perceives the ten directions—this is called "single-mindedness" (ekāgratā).

That the five men’s supreme vows could not remain steadfast and they violated their original oaths, but then bowed their heads in self-refuge and submitted to the Way and its teachings—this is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the second dhyāna-pāramitā?
If, through meditative reflection, one cuts off all delusive thoughts and swiftly attains firm stability, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To clearly understand the infinite and incalculable realms, and to bear the grace of the beneficial precepts of the Path, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To awaken sentient beings so that they can discern for themselves, such that all things are entirely empty and the mind no longer arises—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To dwell in quiet seclusion, practicing self-restraint of the mind without negligence—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To delight in liberation, maintaining non-retrogression, and not being intent on minor matters while remaining in meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To illuminate what is observed, feeling compassion for oneself and pity for others, treating all universally with equality and without partiality—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the third dhyāna-pāramitā?
To practice the third dhyāna with joy, ease, and tranquility, casting aside all evil and unwholesome karma—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To diligently cultivate skillful means to relinquish all music and entertainment, setting one’s will upon the meaning of restraint—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To focus the mind with single-minded devotion, remaining detached from what is liked and finding no delight in external, manifold desires—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To examine within that [body] the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, stillness, and non-self, establishing one’s resolve without any forgetfulness—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That one’s will is firm and reaches everywhere, such that one’s conduct does not run wild—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), so that there is no longer any retribution for sin or merit, nor any karma of existence or non-existence—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the fourth dhyāna-pāramitā?

If, by means of the fourth dhyāna, one cuts off all sufferings of the multitude, resolves upon the joy of the Dharma, eternally eliminates all afflictions, and is no longer subject to various difficulties—this is called generosity (dāna).
To completely cast off all sufferings and attain eternal joy free from affliction throughout the beginning and end of the three realms is called upholding the precepts;
to thoroughly examine all that revolves within the three realms and realize that the perils of birth and death are ultimately non-existent is called patience;
to attain tranquil stillness without ever harboring thoughts of seeking, maintaining mindfulness until realization is reached yet remaining free from expectation, is called diligence.
To attain peaceful meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), with an undisturbed mind and right absorption (*samādhi*), is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
to accomplish pure assistance through the nectar-like medicine of immortality known as the Dharma-teaching, thereby healing all who are blind and ignorant, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the application of mindfulness to the body?
What is the application of mindfulness to the body?

To exhaust all impurities of the body and the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; to uphold pure conduct regarding the body and not conceive of a self—this is called generosity (dāna).
To cast aside all that is fitting for kinship and to feel no lingering attachment is called upholding the precepts;
to delight in the dharma of non-self and not crave the three realms is called patience;
to let go of the mind regarding all that is perceived is [the practice of] non-negligence.
To attain mastery so as not to follow what is contrary to the Dharma is called diligence;

to perceive that all things throughout the three periods of time are spontaneous, fundamentally non-existent, and like illusions or transformations, is called single-mindedness (meditative concentration);

to see that all phenomena contrary to the Dharma arise and cease of themselves, being fundamentally unproduced and entirely without location, yet arising through the encounter of conditions, is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*)?

If one does not manifest [sensation] and the mind has no craving, such that the application of mindfulness to sensation naturally rests and does not pursue various conditions, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To perceive suffering and thus not create fortune or calamity, thereby being free from all afflictions—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To have deep faith in the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) so that the mind gives rise to nothing, and to be capable of enduring all that is unpracticable—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Not to rely on sensations of pain or pleasure, nor to be attached to good or evil, suffering or joy—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To take delight in the cessation of suffering within the three realms, so as to eliminate the afflictions of the three poisons forever without remainder—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To skillfully sever all sufferings and aspire to the Dharma of the Way without ever again experiencing distress—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the cessation of mental activity (cittavipaśyanā)?
To sever all attachments to the five desires that the mind contemplates, and by observing one's own mind to give rise to the mindfulness of the Dharma—this is called generosity (dāna).
To behold those defilements and discipline one's own mind so that it becomes supple and compliant with the truth—this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
To observe all phenomena so that the mind remains settled and to reverently practice the six perfections is called patience;
if one can restrain the mind from its restlessness and prevent it from acting perversely, this is called diligence;
if one perceives the minds of others as stilled of desire and understands them to be fundamentally non-existent, this is called single-mindedness (concentration).
To see with firm conviction and rely upon the conditions that drive [the mind], and to uphold the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the application of mindfulness to dharmas?
To perceive the reality of all phenomena and manifest it clearly so that each person’s mind may be opened is called generosity (*dāna*).

To realize that all objects of observation are fundamentally empty, to thoroughly examine all phenomena as being like illusions, and to perceive that the multitude of things are originally non-existent, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To reverently uphold the scriptures and diligently cultivate the law of cause and effect, bestowing everything upon all beings without increase or decrease, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one perceives those who endanger others yet constantly maintains a heart of compassion, abandoning all harm and setting the will upon the Dharma, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Though wandering among all phenomena and comprehending them all, one remains unattached and free from dependence, with a mind in tranquil concentration; this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To follow the twelve links of dependent origination in their ascending and descending order, understanding that they are boundless and that both beginning and end are entirely quiescent; this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of seeing the truth of suffering?
To behold with one's own eyes that all things in the three periods of time are empty in nature, and to relinquish all sufferings and afflictions without seeking anything—this is called giving.

To see that all sufferings are fundamentally devoid of even a single thing worth enjoying, and thus to realize that birth and death are entirely comprised of sorrow and affliction—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To examine how various matters of suffering arise from one's own conditions and perceptions, and to realize that these hardships are entirely empty and without basis—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To observe that all distresses arise from the subtle, and to understand that one cannot discern them because of a lack of awakening—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To perceive that all sufferings arise from causes and habitual tendencies, and that while they themselves are erroneously obscured, they are fundamentally pure—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To observe in this way so as not to engage in erroneous conduct, thereby severing all suffering so that it has no root and can have no branches or flow—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the truth of origination?
If, with a mind of diligent practice, one abandons the various karmas, the five aggregates, and the six decays, this is called generosity.
If, seeing the five aggregates, the six decays, and the twelve bases of sentient beings, one eliminates all habitual tendencies, this is called ethical discipline."
If, through the perfection of equanimity born of harmony, one accomplishes the practices of all dharmas and the unsurpassed work of the Path, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one relinquishes craving and desire to fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), observing all phenomena and seeing that they arise without any causal basis, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one severs all fetters and all bases of sensation so that there is nothing to be felt, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To observe that the various difficult phenomena are of no benefit, and to eliminate the afflictions of suffering, distress, and falsehood—this is called wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya)?
To attain the end of suffering by following the path of righteousness and practicing wishlessness is called generosity (*dāna*);
to take delight in the practice of cessation and to bring all that is to be exhausted to total exhaustion is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
to eliminate the root of all conceptualizations and hindrances, and to be naturally free from all attachments, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To have undergone diligent toil since the beginningless past, thereby extinguishing all afflictions and attaining long-lasting peace and stability—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To set one’s will upon pure cultivation, dwelling in solitary seclusion, contemplating *samādhi* to subdue one’s own mind—this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).

If one does not seek immediate realization but exhausts all defilements, being free from craving and desire, receiving right concentration with a mind that harbors no distraction—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the Perfection of the Path (mārgapāramitā)?

If one attains the practice of the Ultimate Truth (tathatā) and acts in concert with the Path, remaining harmonious and unperturbed while rescuing others from all calamities, this is called giving (dāna).
To behold the work of the Way and follow the scriptures, not turning back toward heterodox teachings but transforming them through them—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To contemplate the Dharma even when not contemplating the Way, exhorting and assisting others to enter the Dharma and abide in the True and Real—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To maintain the dhāraṇīs of the Dharma, grasping the source of the triple world, proclaiming the scriptures and adhering to the Way of the Teachings—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one provisionally dwells in the Way and does not follow worldly conventions, remaining upright and true without falsehood, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one can understand the Way according to the various forms and types [of beings], comprehending all things and transforming each accordingly, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the faculty of faith?
To believe that the severing of all evils is fundamentally quiescence, and to eliminate unwholesome conduct in order to manifest the source of the Way—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To practice with steadfast faith and delight in all dharmas, such that the source of all virtues is entirely non-arising—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To harbor supreme faith and attain joy and gladness, being free from anger and resentment—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To realize that nothing exists and to delight in true reality, ultimately upholding all dharmas—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To possess the faculty of liberation as the source of the Way, and to have faith, effort, diligence, and the various faculties in a state of tranquil concentration—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To be able to maintain one's faith and keep the mind fixed upon the factors of the Path (mārga-aṅga) without longing for heterodox thoughts—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the faculty of diligence (vīryendriya-pāramitā)?
To diligently cultivate with firm resolve and steadfast will, practicing skillful means without ever succumbing to greed or stinginess—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
Not to rely on the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) yet not to abandon clarity, remaining tranquil in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
That all bodily actions toward every form of being are entirely free from offense or harm—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To set one’s will upon the profound and remote, aspiring to the great and vast vows of infinite compassion, is called diligence;
to listen according to the proper time and immediately practice what is heard without negligence or abandonment, is called single-mindedness;
and to thoroughly master all the teachings learned—comprehending the affairs of both this world and the next, as well as the work of transcending the world—is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the faculty of mind (manendriya-pāramitā)?
If one perceives the True Truths and beholds the afflictions of the impurities associated with household life, thereby abandoning one's dwelling, this is called giving (dāna).
To contemplate conditioned phenomena with detachment from craving and to eliminate all attachments by not dwelling on the unconditioned—this is called precept-keeping.
To examine both adverse and favorable conditions, to refrain from practicing amidst manifold sufferings, and to have no mind of craving—this is called patience.
To be able to maintain all dharmas through total retention (*dhāraṇī*), never forgetting them until one reaches the root of the Way and its virtue—this is called diligence.
To practice the meaning of tranquility so that one enters into all states of arising with a mind that does not arise—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To follow suchness with discernment and not succumb to falsehood, contemplating that all phenomena have no fundamental basis—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the faculty of concentration?
