To eliminate the afflictions through the faculty of concentration, reaching the profound void where no further troubles remain—this is called giving.
To cast aside all distractions, attain the samādhi of concentration, and reveal it to all—this is called ethical discipline."
If the mind is tranquil and has never been disturbed, and one attains the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and right reception (*samāpatti*), this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If the will finds no pleasure in the affairs of various causes and conditions, but instead delights in the joy of the Dharma as the unsurpassed Dharma, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If the mind is single-minded and free from dualistic thoughts, and through concentrated intent and right reception guides and benefits all beings, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To be powerful and influential while maintaining a will that is neither cowardly nor weak, to subdue the mind and exercise self-restraint through the practice of samādhi and meditative concentration—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
What are the six matters of the perfection of the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya-pāramitā)?
To set one’s will upon the sagely clarity of all that exists, thereby completely eliminating all defiled practices, is called giving (*dāna*).
To achieve clear penetration into the most remote and profound mysteries so that the mind has nothing to rely upon, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To be able to endure all hardships for the sake of sentient beings, revolving through birth and death life after life without ceasing, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To thoroughly understand the meaning of the Way and grasp its essential points while realizing fundamental purity is called diligence;
to possess supreme, sagely clarity and remain tranquil and detached, yet proclaim the primordial source for the sake of sentient beings, is called single-mindedness;
and through liberation by wisdom to honor non-action, attaining universal penetration so that those within the three realms receive its grace, is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the power of faith?
If one has faith and does not violate or lose it, like the prince Siṃha, who made a covenant with the multitude and never failed in his faith—this is called generosity;

To abide in the foundations of the precepts without any laxity—just as in the past there was an elephant calf that grew its body by eating—so too does the Bodhisattva partake of the Dharma of gentleness and compliance; being able to contemplate this so as to achieve the path of Buddhahood is called *śīla* (morality).

Even if someone were to come and crush one’s bones and marrow, one continues to practice a heart of loving-kindness, just as the Mahāsattva Sumati saved all wriggling creatures; though there may be those who cause harm, his mind remains unchanging—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).

Diligently practicing vigor without ever withdrawing or regretting, exhausting its very root-source as if draining the great ocean, and acting in such a way as to eliminate lust, anger, and delusion—this is called *vīrya* (diligence).

If one delights in meditative reflection according to the Dharma, and through the progressive advancement of practice eliminates all discursive thoughts, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If the noble wisdom one cultivates is free from grasping, and one's conduct accords with the Dharma without contradicting the teachings of the Way, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the power of diligence?
To practice profound patience and employ timely skillful means to liberate all beings is called giving (*dāna*).

If, by means of one's power, one achieves the most excellent state and performs what ought to be done—just as the son of King Kuyaya subdued his enemies through his strength—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

If, upon hearing of emptiness and non-existence, one accords with and accepts it—just as the conduct of the Queen of King Susima was extraordinary, supple, gentle, and harmonious, such that all submitted to her without exception—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice what is upheld with diligent cultivation, reaching the ultimate truth and attaining great penetration without delighting in indolence or negligence, this is called vigor (*vīrya*).
To practice meditative reflection so that there is nowhere one does not enter, rescuing and liberating all beings without laxity, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To achieve accomplishment through the application of logic (*hetuvidyā*), thereby conforming to the meaning at all times—just as in the past the youth Uttara led his companions—is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the power of mental resolve?
If one is in the celestial realms and does not abandon the five celestial pleasures, yet the mind does not transgress desire nor manifest attachment to them, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If one beholds the jade maidens of the various heavens and perceives their suffering and peril, remaining without attachment, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
Though dwelling in celestial palaces, not coveting the heavens nor delighting in jeweled halls or the spontaneous hundred flavors—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To act as a celestial being with one’s will fixed on liberation, departing from all sweet pleasures to find joy in the Dharma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one is among the various devas or stays within great assemblies, the mind remains undisturbed and the will is concentrated upon the Dharma—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To proclaim the sutras for the sake of devas and humans, with a mind that is detailed and orderly and free from fear—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the power of concentration?
To give all that one possesses without stinginess, remaining serene and joyful—just as King Mādhava abandoned his kingdom and renounced kingship to become a śramaṇa—is called generosity (*dāna*).
To carefully guard one’s physical conduct so as to be free from verbal faults, nourishing the mind so that it does not pursue worldly things—is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To act and perform deeds in accordance with peace and stability, rather than following what is unrighteous—is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To observe all phenomena and perceive them as they truly are, free from erroneous thoughts—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To regard all phenomena with the fourfold assembly of learners, setting their minds upon supreme, true, and correct awakening, and to perceive all phenomena as empty and non-existent—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Not to rely on worldly dharmas but to maintain a vow for the mind, just as a potter successfully fashions various vessels—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the power of wisdom?

When someone comes seeking a head, one gives it immediately without opposing their wish; just as in the past, when the King of Kāśī would grant whatever was requested to those who came begging—this is called giving.

To rescue and protect others while not being greedy for one’s own body—just as when a yakṣa cut off the royal road, the Bodhisattva at that time did not spare his own life to battle and subdue the spirits, so that for the sake of all, he cleared the royal road and enabled the merchants to travel back and forth in safety—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
In the past, the Bodhisattva entered the sea three times, desiring to deliver them from all perils and lead the multitude safely back home; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

Regarding the giving he undertook, he ensured it reached its proper destination; crossing the sources of many rivers, he entered the sea seven times to procure vast treasures to relieve the poor and destitute; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To employ meditative contemplation to bring the mind and intentions under control, wishing to be reborn wherever one desires—whether in the heavens, among humans, or before the Buddhas of the ten directions—is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To follow the sagely brilliance and understand that [the world] is like a mirage, skillfully protecting oneself and exhorting others to follow the noble path so as to proclaim the Dharma, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the awakening factor of mindfulness?

To abandon unwholesome thoughts and apply oneself with diligent effort to wholesome thoughts, and through reflecting on merit to give rise to unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment—this is called generosity (*dāna*).

To rely on the thoughts of the mind to contemplate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and to examine oneself so as not to let the mind run wild—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one’s resolve is focused on gathering all dharmas together, preventing them from scattering and keeping them supple and harmonious, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one’s resolve is to diligently practice without expectation or attachment, cherishing the aspiration for the Way and pitying all beings with a concentrated mind, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To be strong and powerful, gathering and sustaining all powers so that they do not become weak or inferior, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

Having already attained liberation from mental conceptions and being compliant with the power of meaning, such that the significance of its sublime virtues is difficult even for the sagely and wise to reach—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the awakening-factor of dharma?
To select all dharmas, uphold pure conduct, and cast off all defilements is called generosity (*dāna*).
To seek liberation in accordance with the truth, proclaim all dharmas, and thereby transform the afflictions of the triple world is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To abandon the notion of self, to be free from attachment and longing, and to contemplate only the unsurpassed, true, and correct Jewel of the Path is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice what is righteous and seek out the sūtras—the treasury of the six pāramitās and the three vehicles—is called diligence;
to universally seek all dharmas as being without form or appearance, serene and profound in their emptiness and having no fixed location, is called single-mindedness (concentration);
to examine all that exists and find that it cannot be grasped or maintained, its fundamental source being spontaneous and natural, is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the awakening-factor of diligence?
If one can awaken to the realization that all wealth and undertakings cannot be preserved, and with a mind free from attachment, renounces all worldly possessions—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To practice with diligent application without ever seeking personal pleasure, and to aspire toward the Dharma with a resolve for supreme truth—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To diligently cultivate practice so as to understand the three realms, seeing that all things above and below heaven are like illusions and transformations with nothing to rely upon—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To discipline one’s own mind and transform sentient beings, so that all are fully enlightened and each attains their proper place—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To contemplate through meditative absorption so as to sever all fetters and attachments, seeking their beginning and end yet finding no root source—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To be clear that there is nothing upon which to rely and not to receive [teachings] from others, to understand all arts and sounds, and to enter the seventh stage (*bhūmi*)—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the awakening-factor of joy?
To have a serene and pleasant countenance and to love the Dharma without weariness—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To guard the three matters of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To have a mind that is supple and kind, never giving rise to anger, is called patience;
to be mindful of the Buddhas of the ten directions without any deviant thoughts is called diligence;
for the mind to be tranquil and peaceful, with nothing arising at all, is called single-mindedness (concentration).
To clearly and thoroughly understand all things as empty is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the awakening-factor of faith?
To have one's bodily conduct grounded in sincere faith such that the inner and outer correspond is called *dāna* (giving);
to harbor sincere faith in the mind without any deviant thoughts is called *śīla* (precept-keeping);
to remain amidst birth and death without giving rise to greed or envy is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To maintain one's profound faith without ever severing it, and to penetrate the Great Principle without obstruction or hindrance—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To gather all forms of faith without dispersing them, to attain unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment, and to liberate all beings—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To observe all that is exhausted so as to leave nothing to be extinguished, and to delight in the true and correct while rescuing those in the three realms—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of the awakening factor of concentration?
To practice diligence without slackening or abandoning it, and upon attaining concentration to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions—this is called giving.
To attain tranquility and remain free from all desire and craving, not coveting honor or beauty while constantly setting one's will upon the Great Way—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

To abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), receive the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and follow the Bodhisattva path of the Eightfold Noble Path without grasping at anything—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To maintain an equanimous mind that realizes all things are empty, understanding that they are originally natural and indestructible—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To cause all those who have gone forth to see that the sixty-two views are like a net that entangles the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense-bases (*āyatana*), so that through the realization of their original non-existence they naturally dissolve away—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To attain the hearing that all phenomena are ultimately unborn and originally non-existent, such that one understands all things as quiescent, empty, and unimpeded—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the awakening-factor of vigilance (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

To be able to relinquish all that is dear and cherished without any greed or regret; to be able to rescue the multitude from calamities and bring them to the ultimate limit of the Dharma—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To guard body, speech, and mind so as not to transgress the ten unwholesome paths and to practice the ten virtues—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

To quiescently examine the twelve links of dependent origination among sentient beings and, because they lack awakening, for the Bodhisattva to explain them without any attachment—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To distance oneself from all fundamental and derivative攀缘 (pān-yuan, objective conditions) and discursive explanations, yet to practice and uphold the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) without ceasing—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To contemplate with the mind that sentient beings fall into the evil realms due to committing defiled deeds, and to feel sorrowful distress and compassion for them until tears rain down—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To sever all that arises so that nothing further arises, and to see that all afflictions and difficulties—the entirety of all phenomena—are fundamentally non-existent: this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of right view?
To understand right view and abandon the root of all false actions and that which is unbeneficial—this is called generosity.
To be thoroughly proficient so as never to be deceptive, always practicing until one reaches ultimate faith—this is called ethical discipline."
To realize that one’s own conduct is already pure and to subdue the mind so as to return to the Great Way for the sake of liberating all beings—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To be able to exercise self-restraint, to take pity on others throughout the three realms, and to diligently practice in accordance with the hardships of birth and death—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To set one’s will upon the Unsurpassed, to abandon the three periods of time, and to remain free from arrogance while humbling oneself and submitting the self—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To attain the retribution of the True Dharma, to abandon all false views, and to practice the dharma of the bodhisattva such that there is nothing one does not penetrate—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of right mindfulness?
To sever all conditioned activities through equanimous reflection so that there is no further action, and to cultivate the roots of merit and goodness—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To maintain right mindfulness, constantly contemplating the Dharma of the Path, and not abandoning desire while remaining like a lotus flower—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).

That which is called "ground" refers to the master of the ground; to be capable of enduring it through its causes and conditions, and to receive the teachings of the Buddha by discerning the emptiness of the body—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To cast off all marks through equanimous mindfulness, to abide amidst all gatherings without forming attachments, and to accumulate merit and virtue—this is called diligence.
To encourage and assist all virtuous merits while realizing they are fundamentally empty and beyond discrimination—this is called single-mindedness.
To cultivate right view regarding the present life, future lives, and the supramundane Dharma, which is true, ultimate, and pure—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of right effort?
To refrain from evil speech with the tongue and instead provide virtuous instruction to others, revealing the Dharma to rescue all beings—this is called giving.
To practice with purity and freedom from defilement while proclaiming the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To proclaim the words of ultimate truth without transmitting worldly teachings that lack benefit is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To remain in the world while constantly guarding one’s speech and taking no pleasure in mundane talk is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To always practice with single-minded diligence, with a mind free of conceptualization, tranquil and serene, and to maintain non-dual conduct through meditative concentration and right reception—this is called "single-mindedness" (ekāgratā).
To speak with utmost sincerity, discussing the Way and explaining its meaning without engaging in idle talk—this is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of right action?
To practice right action without fault or calamity, protecting oneself through virtue and reverently upholding the Triple Gem—this is called generosity.
To attain one's aspirations and be fully endowed with all virtues, while refraining from any unlawful or unbeneficial conduct—this is called ethical discipline."
To accord with what is appropriate without inversion, fully understanding impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To not engage in any future courses of action that involve present unwholesome karma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To practice and uphold the ten wholesome paths and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) without ever becoming attached—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To adhere to right livelihood without ever entertaining deluded thoughts or setting one's mind upon the basis of the heterodox—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of right livelihood?
Furthermore, to transform others through skillful means according to the circumstances of the time, acting appropriately to establish right livelihood, is called generosity (*dāna*);
to dwell in the life sustained by the practice of extinction (*nirvāṇa*) without craving for one’s own body is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and seeing that sentient beings are fundamentally neither pure nor virtuous, yet giving rise to compassion with the desire to lead them into the Way, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one knows that all phenomena ultimately return to extinction, yet the Way itself cannot be exhausted, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To be among sentient beings without clinging to life, and to enlighten and transform all sentient beings through the Way, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Not establishing one's livelihood through food or clothing, but setting one's will solely upon the Dharma, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of right concentration?
To universally observe that all conditioned phenomena are fundamentally unconditioned, yet while remaining within the unconditioned not to realize its final cessation—this is called giving.
If one regards good and evil, merit and defilement as equal and without duality, such that all dharmas are likewise, this is called precept-keeping;
if one’s virtuous conduct is uninterrupted and advances day by day until reaching the stage of non-retrogression, this is called patience;
if one’s wholesome and joyful retribution is immeasurable and one is mindful of bestowing it upon all people throughout the ten directions, this is called diligence.
To perceive that the root and source of all dharmas are thus truly non-existent from the beginning is called single-mindedness;
to revere the quiescent state wherein both the beginning and the end are entirely empty, such that there is nothing to be lost and nothing by which one can be harmed, is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of right concentration?
If one delights in right view and does not follow false doubt, practicing right view without any false karma—this is called generosity.
To establish the practice of equanimity and true reality, upholding the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas—this is called ethical discipline."
If one perceives through right concentration that peace and liberation come from not engaging in unwholesome actions, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To abide in equanimity by honoring the fundamental nature of a bodhisattva, remaining diligent day and night without depending on anything external, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To embrace peace and security according to one’s aspirations, such that the wholesome deeds one performs are received with profound composure, this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To sever attachments through the practice of samādhi and to be free from a mind of right or wrong—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes one of the six types that were formerly missing from the Eightfold Path.
The Bhadrakalpika Sūtra, Volume Four;
The Bhadrakalpika Sūtra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Fourteen: The Perfection of Tranquility (Śānti-pāramitā) "What are the six matters that constitute the perfection of tranquility?
They are as follows: [The text continues with the enumeration of these six matters]."
If one can sever the nature of contention and strife so that it is always harmonious and well-adjusted, this is called generosity (*dāna*);
if body, speech, and mind are characterized by profound faith and joy, not transgressing against any phenomena and being in accord with the Way, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
if, through the absence of the hindrances and coverings, one experiences the five aggregates and the six decays with correct and unobstructed reception, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That his samādhi-concentration cannot be moved or shifted, and that his mind of lust, anger, and ignorance cannot defile it—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That the practice of noble wisdom is beyond discrimination, and that he delivers all beings according to the proper time and circumstances—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That his vows reach everywhere and pervade all things, and that he is unimpeded regarding the phenomena of the three periods of past, future, and present—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of contemplation?
To hear dharmas never heard before and thereby transform and enlighten all sentient beings—this is called giving (*dāna*).
Not falling into various views and being fundamentally free from heterodox doubt, thereby crossing over all defilements and manifold sins—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
Being able to transform and enlighten countless sentient beings, causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta and feel compassion for those in peril and distress—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That which the mouth proclaims are the Buddha’s correct and true practices, constantly accomplishing them and transforming others—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one can sequentially and thoroughly master the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If, within wisdom, one realizes that all things are empty, and being free from conceptualization and aspiration, understands that nothing exists, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters that constitute the perfection of the joy of the light?

If one can, at the appropriate time, distance oneself from the calamities and afflictions of old age, sickness, and death, and proclaim the unsurpassed, true, and correct Dharma, this is called giving (dāna).
To extinguish the afflictions of craving and desire through wisdom, so that the unsurpassed Great Way naturally brings them under subdual, this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
If, through noble wisdom, one is universally and completely settled, such that there is no perverse karma and all actions are those of a bodhisattva, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one brings universal peace through radiant brilliance, with the mind fixed upon the stages of the Way so as to pervade everywhere, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, through luminous radiance, one universally receives all things, understanding that the root-source of all dharmas has no location whatsoever, this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).
To employ noble wisdom so as to know all dharmas and the twelve divisions of the scriptural canon is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of liberation through arrival?
That one’s resolve is liberated, supple, and serene, and that one always delights in rescuing sentient beings from calamity and suffering—this is called giving (*dāna*).
That one eliminates all obstructions and hindrances in every dwelling place so that there is no darkness or obscuration—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).

That when receiving anything, one casts off all defilements and constantly cultivates the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and because of such actions, one perpetually practices virtue—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To universally pity all beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, with a heart of joy and tranquility that gives rise to no [discriminative] thoughts—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To be constantly able to adapt to circumstances and endure with patience;
to remain unaffected by any suffering or pleasure—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Constantly teaching by means of the Dharma without contravening the Way, and ensuring that everything one does is truly authentic and not false—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of entering the noble assembly of bhikṣus?
If one can transform and establish all vows, with the will set upon the aspiration for the Way, this is called generosity (*dāna*);
to establish all things according to what they delight in and transform them through the Way, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and when one’s aspirations are tranquil and serene, and the mind is not agitated, transforming others through such moderation, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To have conduct that is extraordinary, surpassing the multitude and not conforming to the mundane is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To ensure that the teachings received by the mind are always authentic, to maintain all dharmas through *dhāraṇī* without negligence is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).

To practice tranquilly and with focused intent until reaching the gates of liberation, yet not realizing the fruit prematurely within the states of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
There are eight assemblies of beings, which are likewise equal and without difference.
What are the six matters of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) regarding the meaning of the eight classes of beings?
If one proclaims the meaning [of the Dharma] as the resolution of what is non-meaningful, yet cannot apply the mind to realize the true and correct meaning, this is called giving (*dāna*).
To proclaim the teachings that accord with the inclinations of all beings, including the gods and humans of the triple world, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one expounds the meaning without blemish, constantly cultivating pure compassion and benevolence, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To preach with perfect sincerity and full extent, proclaiming the Way and its teachings to others so that they may all receive the benefits of the Path up to the palace of Akaniṣṭha Heaven—this is called diligence.
To gladden all beings with an equanimous mind through the meaning of the Dharma—this is called single-mindedness.
To abide in a state free from the dharma of anger and to transform others through the Dharma—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of the liberation through understanding the Dharma?
If one attains all dharmas without loss, follows the wisdom of the Path, and does not contradict the True Dharma, this is called giving.
To eliminate the notion of self and not conceive of a body, such that the mind is naturally unattached within the three realms—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
For words and deeds to correspond without contradiction, and for the actions of body, speech, and mind to be constantly in accord with meditative concentration—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice diligently day and night without interruption, perfecting the dharmas of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, and the knowledge of deliverance—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To abide eternally in the Way and the Dharma, not following what is contrary to righteousness; to transform sentient beings through the four kinds of benevolence—this is called single-mindedness.
To constantly practice supreme virtue with equanimity, not engaging in minor details that do not benefit all beings, and having no divergent thoughts—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of discerning accordance with principle?
If one proclaims and transforms others by teaching the twelvefold accordance, destroying the defilements of evil and eliminating the five turbidities—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If, through profound stillness, one transforms those who are deluded, leading them to extinction (*nirvāṇa*) and the liberation of all beings—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To follow conventional worldly discourse in explaining matters and thereby instruct others so that they reach all beings is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to be able to relinquish the activities of lust, anger, and delusion, such that there are no longer any manifold perceptions or deviant thoughts, is called diligence (*vīrya*);

to contemplate tranquilly in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and right reception (*samāpatti*), without giving rise to manifold or unbeneficial thoughts, is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).
To practice the holy path to reach supreme wisdom, thereby returning to liberation that is without attachment or bondage—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of eloquence that accords with principle?
To proclaim various kinds of eloquent wisdom for the sake of the multitude is called generosity;
to have speech that is supremely wondrous, harmonious, gentle, and lubricating, such that none far or near do not turn toward it, is called ethical discipline;
to be able to accord with the minds of all who come to listen and cause them to apply their hearts [to the teaching] is called patience.
That his teachings are universal and boundless, heard throughout the ten directions, is called diligence;
that his fame and virtue are far-reaching, renowned above and below heaven, with merits fully perfected and never interrupted, is called single-mindedness;
that he reaches the ultimate treasury of Dharma which is unborn, entering the triple world yet attaining nirvana, is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of non-satiety?

To preach the sutras and practice the Way for the sake of those who are greedy without ever becoming weary; to keep in mind the deliverance of all those who are covetous and envious—this is called giving.
To take pity on sentient beings and guide them, showing them the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—without ever becoming weary at first, is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).

To personally apply diligence without harboring anger or resentment, even to the point of breaking one’s own body and bones to establish a mind that is all-pervasive, universal, and impartial so that the Dharma may spread, is called *kṣānti* (patience).

To travel everywhere by means of supernormal powers of flight, applying oneself with earnest devotion to transform the ignorant and deluded who are ready for deliverance, is called *vīrya* (diligence).
To enter into samādhi and right concentration according to their wishes, instructing them so that they may preserve the practice of the Way—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To listen to the sūtras according to the number of those who wish to hear them, joyfully listening at the appropriate time and immediately expounding the Dharma for them—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of giving?
If there are teachings that can be bestowed as gifts to provide encouragement and assistance, so that all beings everywhere each find their proper place, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To bestow through speech, body, and mind with gentleness and harmony, transforming people through the Dharma, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To delight in bestowing kindness and not oppose those who seek it, maintaining a serene and joyful countenance—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To regulate one's thoughts through giving, to practice skillful means, to eliminate all that is unwholesome, and to purely cultivate merit—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
For the mind to be clear and transparent, free from defilement, with pure aspirations and a settled mind that has compassion for all beings—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To use these merits from what one has bestowed upon others to encourage and assist them toward the Buddha-way, and likewise to transform sentient beings so that they may give rise to the Great Resolve—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā)?
To uphold the prohibitive precepts with compassion as the foundation, and always to bestow fearlessness upon all beings—this is called generosity (dāna).
To be fearless and free from resentment, guarding the three matters of body, speech, and mind so that no transgression occurs—this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
Constantly harboring a heart of compassion and pitying all beings without any intent to harm, like a loving mother nurturing her infant—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Employing skillful means to uphold the precepts and awakening through a sense of shame so as not to do anything that is of no benefit to others—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

Bestowing kindness upon sentient beings, training the mind in heedfulness, regarding all things as impermanent, and focusing one’s will without indulgence—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To uphold the precepts out of such compassion, to constantly practice with diligence, and to inspire and assist all who have not yet attained realization toward the Buddha-way—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of patience?
If one is gentle and mild, with a mind set on joy, universally bringing peace to all—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If, for the sake of sentient beings, one endures various afflictions and hardships without regarding them as toil throughout incalculable eons—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To seek through the long and arduous cycle of birth and death, yet not perceive any basis for attachment regarding its beginning or end, is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to always maintain harmony and joy while seeking skillful means without negligence or despondency is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to take pity on sentient beings who are in peril and distress and to subdue them is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To practice patience through this, always acting with benevolence and harmony, harboring no malice in one's heart, and encouraging others toward the Buddha-way—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the Perfection of Vigor?
To take pity on worldly beings and provide medicine according to their ailments so that each may find their proper place is called generosity (*dāna*);
to set one’s will upon skillful means (*upāya*), never inflicting harm, and always practicing a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
to encounter all obstacles and yet achieve liberation through appropriate giving is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To remain in various places without losing the proper timing and to act entirely in accordance with the Dharma is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to practice with such assiduity day and night without ceasing and without any impairment is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
and to use this diligence to exhort others toward the realm of the Buddha, causing them to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind and to follow the right practice, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of tranquility?
If one directs a mind of loving-kindness toward all people and feels compassion for sentient beings, this is called giving.
To take pity on all sentient beings within the three realms and to bring them down into the profound Dharma is called upholding the precepts;
to feel compassion for the ignorant and deluded masses of the mundane world, showing them what is appropriate and guiding their minds with the Way, is called patience;
if one leaves the household life to study the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, maintaining a mind fixed in tranquility without indulgence, this is called diligence.
To contemplate the gift of Dharma in order to enlighten and transform the masses, and to proclaim the Dharma for those who have not yet attained understanding—this is called single-mindedness.
To possess a pure and undefiled nature, following the path toward *nirvāṇa* without falling into premature extinction—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of wisdom?
If one bestows the Dharma of the scriptures upon others, causing them to resolve upon the path, this is called generosity.
If, in whatever one preaches, one remains detached from clothing and food and does not crave gain or offerings, this is called ethical discipline."
If one bestows the gift of Dharma without relying on worldly occupations and without succumbing to indolence, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To enter into all *dhāraṇīs* and all dharmas, encompassing them all without exception so that each is made perfectly clear, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To contemplate with discernment the great difficulties of the three periods of time while expounding the gift of Dharma, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one proclaims the meaning of original purity and original non-existence within the Way of the Teachings (Dharmapatha), providing guidance and instruction without losing its source, this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the retribution of the eye?
If one regards all people with love and respect through one's fine eyes and does not harm them, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If, when observing anything with those eyes, one fully understands that nothing is of benefit except for the Dharma which alone can be relied upon, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To see that which is vast and far-reaching, without limit, reaching no boundary and being inexhaustible—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
For the eye to be tranquil and free from attachment, seeing that all forms are empty and originally non-existent—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To behold with joy and delight, causing those who see it to rejoice and take pleasure in the Dharma—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That all who come to see him find their minds and bodies humbled in submission, and that they all leap with joy until reaching the ultimate goal—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the retribution of the ear?
To hear with the ears without error or omission, always abiding in the Dharma and not engaging in worldly thoughts—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
For the ears to be pure and free from defilement, understanding that all sounds are fundamentally quiescent—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If, when hearing, the sound is clear and penetrating and one harbors no distorted conceptions—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
When the ear perceives that which is subtle and immeasurable, this is called diligence (*vīrya*);
when one examines what is distant and hears it all with the ear, yet knows it to be entirely empty and of no benefit to people, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
when one hears that there is nothing and listens to that which is without solidity, like an echo, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the nose-retribution?
If the nose is clear and penetrating, realizing all things are empty and there is nothing to smell, this is called generosity;
When the faculty of the nose is stilled and free from discursive thought, and one’s resolve for the Way remains undiminished, this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To be serene and tranquil, knowing contentment and sufficiency, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To perceive fragrances as appropriate and fitting, without transgression or failure, and remaining free from sensual desire, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That the nose has nothing to which it is attached, does not crave various fragrances, and remains free from negligence—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

That the nose perceives whatever it smells as being defiled and impure, recognizing that it benefits nothing but only causes the wasting away of the mind of training (*śikṣācitta*)—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the retribution of the tongue?
Though the tongue obtains flavors, one does not take pleasure in them with greed; remaining free from worldly delight and finding sweetness in the suitability of the precepts—this is called giving.
Speech that is clear and distinct, proclaiming only the teachings of the Dharma—this is called ethical discipline."
If one correctly conveys the words and expressions of countless beings to their fellow practitioners, this is called patience (*kṣānti*);
if one brings to mind boundless wisdom and explains it for others, this is called diligence (*vīrya*);
if one extinguishes the habitual attachment to the five flavors and the sharpness of the tongue, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
That the tongue has something to speak, constantly propagating the Way of the Buddha and radiating it far and wide—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of bodily retribution?
To possess an abundance of wealth and resources through the mastery of the scriptures and to bestow them upon the world is called *dāna* (giving).
That countless people all look up to one and respectfully receive one’s words is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).
That one’s person is made noble and honored because of serving and obeying the Buddha, thereby possessing majestic virtue, is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To possess a body that is strong and influential such that none fail to rely upon it, and for all sentient beings to collectively receive its support and protection—this is called diligence.
To have a form that is supple and beautiful, with a face always serene and joyful and a radiant complexion—this is called single-mindedness.
To be pure and stainless, capable of much, and to transform and enlighten sentient beings—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the mind’s retribution?
When one’s mind is impartial, universally compliant, and enters into all sentient beings, this is called giving.
If whatever the mind contemplates is largely filled with joy and nothing but the practice of the Dharma, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To be liberated from what is to be transcended, delighting in present meaning rather than what is meaningless, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one’s mind awakens swiftly, attaining universal penetration without any obstruction, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To follow and practice that which is to be revered, constantly adhering to the Way and the Dharma with harmonious compliance, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
for its resonance to pervade all phenomena and to evaluate all practices against the fixed Dharma is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of encouraging and assisting others with compassion?

To instruct and transform others by giving to them—just as in the past there was a man named Śiṣyaka who protected all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, exhorting and transforming them all to enter the Great Way of the Buddha and guiding them therein—is called generosity (*dāna*).

To diligently cultivate precepts so as to bring peace to all others, and through this merit to bring about its corresponding fruition—just as a flock of birds gathers together and spits out water to extinguish a blazing fire—is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

To harmonize with those in sorrow and apply oneself to the cycle of birth and death while remaining as steadfast as Brahmā, compassionately mindful of the common people and enduring all manner of toil—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To diligently instruct others, like a physician who encounters two lives whose lifespans have not yet ended and, out of a heart of pity and grief, attends to them without ceasing; whereupon the physician travels twenty-eight thousand *li* to reach their location and provides medicine to treat their illness—such is the way a Bodhisattva treats all beings; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To regard others with compassionate mindfulness through meditative reflection, just as the Rishi Kapila established cities and towns out of pity for sentient beings—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one uses wisdom to bring universal peace to the world, causing all who uphold the scriptures to have their lives endure in the heavens, or if they receive celestial bodies throughout the ten directions, such that all enemies and thieves are eliminated as they flow away with the current even unto the abode of the dragons—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Compassion for Oneself?
To perform beneficial deeds for oneself and, simultaneously, to bring peace and accomplishment to all people—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To personally accord with what is appropriate by accumulating the roots of myriad virtues and refraining from causing harm—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
Its physical form is majestic and dignified like a most exquisite flower, and its color remains thus; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To rise early and sleep late for the sake of one’s own person, never being indolent or remiss in rescuing the multitude from peril and distress; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
One’s body is constantly diligent, mindful of one's own purpose, vowing to be born in the heavens before the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To undergo seven cycles of being incinerated by the kalpa-fire, formed and then destroyed, ending and then beginning again, yet to traverse this world without confusion—just like King Kāśirāja—is what is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Dharma-Regulation?
Adorning oneself with various colors and ornaments through the merit resulting from past giving—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
The Dharma does not abide in inversion; being without attachment and relying solely on the scriptures—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To be able to eliminate the perceptions of sentient beings as being stained by lust, anger, and ignorance is called patience;
to practice the path of the Buddha’s sutras through the perfection of conduct, without dualistic action yet employing skillful means, is called diligence;
to attain a mind of equanimity that forever eliminates attachment and leaves the mind free from seeking is called single-mindedness (concentration).

Radiant light vibrates and shines throughout the ten directions; all dharmas are clearly analyzed and distinguished, and the dharmas of superior, middling, and inferior are truly non-dual—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Appropriateness?
To give gifts with the result that one attains great wealth and causes the Way of the Sūtras to flourish is called giving.
To observe the prohibitions with the result that one is born in heaven, yet constantly contemplates the practice of the Dharma without longing for heavenly bliss, is called upholding the precepts."

That the fruit of patience is to have no fear of words or phrases—this is its meaning; that one always focuses with single-minded diligence on the desire to deliver all beings—this is called vigor (*vīrya*);
that whatever one contemplates in meditation serves to assist those born [in the world]—this is its meaning, and it is named concentration (*ekāgratā*);
and that if one gathers wisdom to increase noble insight so that it is never diminished or lost—this is its meaning, and this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six aspects of the perfection of boundless liberation through the boundaries?
To practice with diligent effort without harming one's body is called giving.
To find joy in liberation by severing the karma of manifold conceptualizations and cravings is called ethical discipline;
to attain the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti) without any loss or failure is called patience;
and for all that one practices to be auspicious and universally complete is called diligence.
That which can be attained through meditative contemplation, resulting in the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
that which is cultivated through holy illumination, diligently receiving instruction and attaining the *vajra-samādhi*, is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of joyful exhortation?

If one practices giving without being intent on sleep, without giving rise to the notion of a self, and like those of great renown who possess ninety-six great groves situated at all great treasuries, whereby the king bestows gifts to transform the multitude so they receive the merit of alms-gathering; or like the son of a sinless king, who, though leaving his residence, never speaks falsely, and as he was in his original state, rescues the world from peril and distress without committing evil deeds—this is called giving.

To provide for one's parents, teachers, and friends, honoring them with body and mind without ever becoming indolent, and regarding their scriptures until reaching the Buddha with no net of doubt—this is called precept-keeping."

If one protects others with gentleness and flexibility, like the Dragon King who sacrificed his own body and did not harm his own blood vessels; if, like the Dharma Master of old, one practices with diligent and earnest effort for thirty-two thousand years, performing deeds without sorrow or distress, never becoming weary or indolent as one transforms all beings—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) out of compassion for sentient beings, abandoning all evils, and to feel pity for the people of Jambudvīpa who are afflicted by the five subtle pleasures, contemplating them with loving-kindness and using ancient parables to clarify and explain this—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To possess ultimate, holy, and brilliant wisdom, such as the six great supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of emptiness?
If one can attain the samādhi of the practice of emptiness without giving rise to conceptualizations or vows, this is called generosity;
His mind is vast and open like empty space, beyond measure; this is called upholding the precepts.
Being able to attain the stage of non-retrogression, receiving the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment, and beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called patience.
Diligently practicing day and night without slackening or ceasing, with strength and power advancing daily; this is called vigor.
When the mind is always focused and concentrated, undisturbed, upright, and never forgetful, this is called "single-mindedness" (ekāgratā).
When one is firm and unassailable, such that all actions are forever free from manifold afflictions, this is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā-pāramitā*)?
If one constantly and timely rescues those in peril and distress, as well as all who are destitute, while remaining entirely free of conceptual thought, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To be prudent in all actions and to guard body, speech, and mind so that the three are not transgressed, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
Constantly cultivating humility and reverence without harboring arrogance or contempt is called patience;
performing meritorious deeds without negligence and using them to encourage and assist those who have not yet attained is called diligence;
renouncing the household life with a resolve for the Dharma, emulating the various teachings so that the aspiration for the Way advances daily without interruption is called single-mindedness.
To be free from the three poisons oneself and further cause others to sever the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion so that they take refuge in the Triple Gem—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the wishless (apraṇihita-pāramitā)?
If one can swiftly attain the fundamental state of wishlessness and, out of compassion, take pity on the afflictions of the three realms, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To be free from conceptual observation and without arrogance, attaining that which is non-attainment so as to accord with the transformation of the Way, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To abide within the three realms without attachment, yet to guide and transform sentient beings through birth, aging, sickness, and death, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To have internal practice that constantly guards body, speech, and mind so as not to commit any transgression or fail in any duty—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To cultivate skillful means (*upāya*) to remove all defilements and unbeneficial practices until reaching liberation—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To don the armor of virtue with a vast aspiration, rescuing all beings from the perils of cyclic existence—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the practice of the distinct perfection of giving?

To sit at the site of enlightenment and daily consume only one grain of hemp and one grain of rice, seeking out those who are destitute and desiring to provide for them without considering it a hardship—this is called generosity.
If, within one's own person, one practices diligence and meditative concentration without negligence, this is called upholding the precepts;
to attain the vision of the Buddha and, through training, become fully equipped with all dharmas and various practices, this is called patience;
to embrace and master all dharmas, realizing that they are fundamentally non-existent and beyond conceptual discrimination, this is called diligence.

To be united with liberation and to simultaneously rescue all beings from the perils of birth and death so that they may maintain the aspiration for the Way—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
For the mind to be serene and enter into profound stillness, such that the mind gives rise to no further conceptualizations and realizes its natural state—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of liberating others?
In the past, there was a merchant who, having renounced his own profit, cut from his own food to offer pure-hearted and pure-conduct worship to the Buddha; this is called generosity (*dāna*).
When the Dragon King Manasvin appeared and circled his body, his mind remained free from transgression as he stood in attendance; this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
When Śakra and Brahmā descend to see that the Buddha is silent and does not expound the Dharma, they encourage him to preach the Dharma; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
At that time, he surveys the ten directions with the Buddha-eye, advancing or withdrawing according to the occasion to guide and benefit all sentient beings; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
For seven days he contemplates a tree with single-minded focus, desiring to cause all beings to possess a mind of repentance and reform; this is called single-mindedness (*citta-ekāgratā*).
To turn the wheel of Dharma upon seeing [beings] exhorting and assisting one another, with the eightfold voice flowing forth and pervading the ten directions—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of meditative concentration through diligent application?
To see the Buddha at dawn, attain the Way, and reflect upon his diligent labors is called *dāna* (giving).
To go forth to teach and deliver the five men, witnessing his manifested transformations and immediately accepting what he taught upon hearing it, is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).
To cast off self-importance, to comply with the Dharma and Vinaya, and to transform those who have not yet reached realization, is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To transform and enlighten them with the ambrosia of the deathless medicine is called diligence;
for the five men to eliminate their divergent thoughts at that moment is called single-mindedness;
to sprinkle and drink the ambrosia of the Way upon those in poverty, thereby extinguishing lust, anger, and delusion and delivering five hundred million devas and humans, is called wisdom.
"These are the six.
Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Powers. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, as well as its depth, shallowness, distance, and proximity? They are as follows:"
To attain discernment from that state and thoroughly understand its beginning and end is called giving (*dāna*);
to recognize and realize that the three realms are empty and equal without distinction is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and to clearly comprehend all things through analytical discernment, thereby attaining universal entry into the ground of benevolence and harmony, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That the practice of his vast vows and deeds of supreme virtue is powerful and influential is called diligence;
that he destroys all defilements and the twelve links of dependent origination so that no distinction remains is called single-mindedness;
and that in what he reveres and follows, he knows the proper time and does not fail the holy teaching is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of knowing the past, future, and present?
If one can completely eliminate all karmic deeds performed by the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind, this is called giving.
If one can extinguish all conditions, retributions, birth and death, and calamities or blessings, this is called upholding the precepts;
if one abandons the causes—the five aggregates and the six sense-fields—and the opposition of causal conditions such that no further karmic activity arises, this is called patience;
if one leaves behind both sin and merit so that birth and death within the three realms are naturally eliminated, this is called diligence.

To be serene and detached, suddenly severing form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness so that they are understood to be utterly non-existent—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To follow and practice what one reveres such that nothing arises, with a mind so tranquil that it takes the Way as its source—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of knowing the various kinds of the world?
If sentient beings sever various kinds of manifold and confused practices without indulging their own whims, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

If they sever various kinds of aggregates (*skandha*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and practice and cultivate the six *pāramitās*, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
Though existing amidst all phenomena, not reckoning the existence of a person and realizing all things as empty and non-existent—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

Roaming through all categories of teachings to provide medicine according to the disease, causing the three poisons of sentient beings in the triple world to be eliminated—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Abiding within the four great elements, removing greed and not reckoning it, guiding the masses of delusion to eliminate all that exists—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To dwell within various modes of contemplation and discern that all consciousnesses and mental recollections are empty—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections].
What are the six matters of the perfection of skillful means regarding knowing that the faculties of beings in the world increase and decrease, and that their speech differs from one another?
To understand that the four great elements are a composite which, when assembled or dispersed, does not constitute a self to be reckoned as a body—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To awaken to the emptiness of the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind, such that their activities commit no transgression—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To understand that the mind is spontaneous and that all things are fundamentally non-existent, such that there is nothing it does not penetrate—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one can understand the lifespans, pleasures, pains, virtues, and evils of men and women, and contemplate these six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) as being utterly without foundation, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one can discern faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom—these five faculties (*pañca-indriya*) being the source for practicing the Path—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

If one can penetrate and comprehend all that is distinguished, including the various different thoughts of others' faculties and fully understanding these faculties of all sentient beings, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of liberative art (upāya-pāramitā) regarding understanding the world’s likes and dislikes through various practices?
To transform others according to their inclinations and preferences by administering medicine according to the illness, this is called generosity (dāna).
To gather and exhort all with a compassionate heart so that none are harmed is called upholding the precepts;
to eliminate at will, according to the occasion, all transgressions and evils committed is called patience;
to sever the net of doubt and exhaust all indolence and negligence is called diligence.
To cause all that has arisen and that which has not yet arisen to be forever extinguished is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
to accord with what is desired so as to bring about tranquility, and to dissolve it through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of skillful means for universally entering all conditioned activities and liberating beings from the bonds of desire?
If one can understand the root source of all sufferings and incinerate them, blazing forth the Way and its teachings, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To know the origin of all afflictions and swiftly abandon the various calamities—the defilements of lust, anger, and ignorance—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To thoroughly understand the Way and bestow peace and security to eliminate all afflictions is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to be sincere and swift in reaching the unsurpassed Way and to find eternal joy in the bliss of the Dharma is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to discern the various practices and their destinations, as well as the origins and ends of the five realms of existence, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To know through practice the realms of existence and non-existence, as well as birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, is called wisdom;
these constitute the six [perfections].
What are the six matters concerning the perfections of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, all doors of liberation, meditative concentration, and right reception?
If one bestows this Dharma as a gift for the sake of peace and security, refraining from all evils and treating others with kindness, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If one practices impartial giving toward both the poor and the noble without distinction or partiality, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one takes pity on others, encouraging and assisting them through the Dharma so that they may enter what is appropriate for the Path, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To take pity on oneself and realize that one's spirit is merely lodged within this body, which is fundamentally not one's own self and thus not to be reckoned as having a body—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To understand that all things are empty, to eliminate reputation and craving, and to be without self-aggrandizement—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To understand impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and to transform the multitudes by means of the absence of "I," "mine," "person," or "other"—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of mindfulness regarding past lives?
If one recognizes the events of countless eons experienced in former lives and uses this to instruct others, this is called giving.
To know the five destinies through which one passes—whether in the heavens, among humans, in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals—is called upholding the precepts;
to discern the destinations of transgressions and blessings, of good and evil, and to fully subdue the mind therein is called patience;
to clearly understand the defilements of worldly toil, sensual desires, and all impurities, yet to remain unattached to them, is called diligence.
When the essence of one's mind understands that all things are empty, quiescent, and devoid of conceptualization, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
when one eliminates all karmic actions and perceives the fundamental source of the faculties of all sentient beings, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of the Heavenly Eye?
To perceive with the heavenly eye the misfortunes and blessings, the good and evil, and the destinies to which beings go, is called generosity (*dāna*).
To practice what should be followed, to refrain from transgressions and calamities, and to constantly resolve upon the practice of the Way, is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To perceive that what is seen is vast and far-reaching without limit, and to discern the faculties of sentient beings, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To see all things without weariness regarding their virtues, and to transform and enlighten those who are blind and ignorant, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To examine the obscurations of the multitudes—whether there be a path or no path, and the destinations of right and wrong—is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To manifest radiant light so that beings may find refuge and thereby attain liberation is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the exhaustion of all outflows?
To behold all that is pierced, leaking, flawed, and useless, and to abandon it in order to practice the Way—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To take no pleasure in the various outflows (*āsrava*) of lust, anger, and delusion, but to set one's will upon the Dharma—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Not to cultivate any defilements but to constantly practice purity—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To transform the minds of the multitude and clarify all perceptions, and to remain free from negligence regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the coverings (*āvaraṇa*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*), is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To realize and comprehend all outflows (*āsrava*) and their habitual tendencies through the Way and its teachings, thereby attaining extensive penetration, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To enter into the cycle of birth and death while remaining diligent in regard to the outflows, transforming sentient beings and causing them to resolve upon the Way, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
"These are the six.
Chapter Sixteen: The Four Fearlessnesses. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of the First Fearlessness, which consists of understanding this Dharma through the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment?"
To attain the path of Buddhahood, which is pure and exhausts the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To keep the mind fixed on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while aspiring to the great vow for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To contemplate all things with the truth of reality as being entirely empty and free from false views—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To fully understand all that arises within the three realms, penetrating everything through the absence of roots—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To bring forth universal wisdom to transform the gods, humans, and those in the three evil paths of the three realms—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To roam among the eight classes of beings proclaiming the transformative teachings of the Way, causing each to find their proper place and be free from fear so that their aspirations are fulfilled—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six; this is the first fearlessness.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the equal realization of the exhaustion of all outflows?
The Buddha is without outflows; since all outflows are exhausted, there is no difficulty whatsoever—this is called giving.
To have no place of abiding because all dwelling places have been severed, and to be free from the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
That what is born and the unborn both arise nowhere—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That the renown of one's passage through the world is profound, empty, and boundless, such that its origin cannot be apprehended—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To harbor vows with the intent to transcend the eight worldly dharmas of all existence is called single-mindedness;
to abide in liberation, immediately attaining non-retrogression and reaching unsurpassed truth, is called wisdom.
These constitute the six [perfections], which is the second fearlessness.
"What are the six matters of the third *vaiśāradya* (fearlessness) regarding the unsurpassed true essentials of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which are to be received and practiced?
To cultivate that which leads to the realization of universal emptiness—knowing that what arises must perish and that unions end in separation—is called generosity (*dāna*).
To exhaust the three poisons and all heedless practices so as not to run wild is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
That which is called "extinction" refers to the exhaustion of all places of birth so that there is never again any arising; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To eliminate all faults such that the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind can no longer find opportunity to commit transgressions; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To establish the aspiration for the Path in order to deliver sentient beings, thereby removing the roots of various worldly activities and that which is unbeneficial; this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one reaches the gates of liberation where birth and death have already ended, such that wisdom cannot be exhausted—this is called wisdom.

These are the six aspects of the third fearlessness, "The Inability to Dispel the Mind Regarding Internal Correspondence to the Truths. What are the six matters of the fourth fearlessness, the *pāramitā* of "The Inability to Dispel the Mind Regarding Internal Correspondence to the Truths"?
To attain samādhi within the inner True Dharma such that no one can stir the mind, and for those who are unsettled to naturally exhaust their defilements—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To realize the state of non-arising and to maintain the dharma of wisdom so that it cannot be exhausted—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To eliminate notions of impermanence, to understand that all dharmas are empty, and to resolve that the Way is eternal—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That which is called "internal matters being incapable of obscuring" means that by exhausting the root of all transgressions, this is termed diligence (*vīrya*);
that which is "incapable of hindrance, causing all that is unaccomplished to be fully accomplished" is termed single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);

and because the sagely brilliance is entirely spontaneous and incapable of being obscured or hindered, such that the Buddha-way—being profoundly deep—is able to resolve all capacities, whether inferior, middling, or superior, and decisively and clearly penetrates the root-nature of the faculties of sentient beings, this is termed wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six [perfections], and this is the fourth fearlessness.
What are the six matters of the Great Compassion Pāramitā?
To harbor great compassion and pity for all classes of sentient beings, with a mind free from resentment—this is called giving (dāna).

To have a mind of equanimity, desiring to deliver sentient beings, never showing partiality toward those afflicted by birth, old age, sickness, or death—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To always practice the observance of the Dharma toward sentient beings, responding to them with benevolence so that they may find joy and peace—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To go forth and return, moving about everywhere to rescue sentient beings from the afflictions of toil and suffering—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To transform and guide others according to their inclinations—whether of superior, middling, or inferior capacity—is called single-mindedness;
to roam through the three realms from beginning to end across immeasurable eons, delivering beings from the perils of birth and death, is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters concerning the perfection of the purification of the eye?
If one can clarify the earth element and the water element, with a mind as immovable as the earth element and washing away mental defilements like water, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If one can establish the fire element and the wind element to incinerate all evils, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To burn away birth and death until nothing remains, so that all defilements are extinguished and one harbors no resentment—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That what the eyes behold is seen without exception, as light shines afar—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
