To act with earnest devotion, seeing all things without the thought of right or wrong—this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To observe the ten directions as vast and boundless, and to provide salvation without weariness, is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the pure celestial eye?

To see various physical forms with the divine eye—whether they are upright or deformed, beautiful or ugly, tall or short, broad or narrow, white or black, fat or thin—and to go forth to transform them according to their needs, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

To know their bodily conduct, names, mental nature, and the lands from which they were born, and to perceive the places where their bodies come and go and circulate, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To observe their bodily conduct and to discern right from wrong, union from separation, success from failure, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To observe how heaven and earth are destroyed and then reconstituted to give rise to gods, humans, and all things is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to perceive the retribution of sins and blessings, good and evil, the mundane and the supramundane, and light and darkness is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);

to perceive the various sequences—whether distant or near, deep or shallow—and the three gates of liberation: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of the wisdom-eye?
To accomplish the wisdom-eye so as to universally perceive the fundamental origins and the sources from which all sentient beings arise—this is called giving.
To be able to achieve and attain liberation, free from all fetters, is called upholding the precepts;
having attained this, to establish one’s mind and abide in the meaning of the Way is called patience;
to be steadfast in what is achieved and to establish it universally, observing the ten directions with complete clarity, is called diligence.
That which one perceives is like the ultimate truth, examined as being neither false nor delusive; this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To harbor a mind of joy without giving rise to [distraction], not falling into the calamities of transgression, and having an inexhaustible resolve for the Way—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the purification of the Dharma-eye?
If one is able to attain the eighteen unique qualities of all Buddhas, this is called generosity;
if one brings these eighteen Buddha-dharmas to oneself and goes to rescue those in the eight difficult realms from the eighteen poisons of suffering, this is called ethical discipline;..."
To perceive the causes and conditions in their various grades of high and low, deep and shallow, and subtle and fine, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To contemplate that all that exists within the three realms is fundamentally and entirely of its own nature, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To remember and discern the beginning and end [of afflictions] and to administer medicine according to the ailment to treat the three illnesses, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To see things as they truly are, without falsehood, and not with a foolish gaze, but to universally enlighten and transform all people—this is called wisdom.
This constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Buddha-eye’s purity, the perfection of the infinite?
To behold all things with the Buddha-eye without obstruction and awaken those who are unawakened is called generosity (*dāna*);
to observe and take pity on the afflictions of the three sufferings of all sentient beings is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
to deliver sentient beings so that they encounter no calamities and attain eternal, long-lasting peace is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To behold that which is immeasurable, profound, bottomless, and beyond analogy is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to observe its root as one would its branches and fruit, and when they have ripened and are about to fall, to reach out and pull them back is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
to see that the beginning and the end arise from conditions, and through understanding their fundamental non-existence, to realize there is nothing produced, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of mastery (vaśitā-pāramitā)?
If one attains self-reliance and achieves the ultimate goal without ceasing midway, this is called giving (dāna).
To attain one's wishes wherever one goes and never to violate one’s solemn vows is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*);
to establish practice with sovereign mastery, to reach the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*), and to relinquish all attachments is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to be harmonious, gentle, and compliant, and to discern and understand through all-encompassing wisdom is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That all things are exhausted yet wisdom cannot be exhausted—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To understand that all phenomena are the essential and sacred illumination of holy wisdom, thereby transforming those who have not yet attained it—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Amusement?

To give gifts while remaining free from expectation—just as [the Buddha] manifested five hundred canopies in empty space to cover the assembly of bhikṣus; or as when the brahmin village named Thūna had its well-water spontaneously become sweet—this is called giving.
When entering a city, the people are universally at peace and lute-like musical instruments sound of themselves without being struck—this is called morality."
That those with impaired faculties—such as the blind, the deaf, the mute, the lame, and the diseased—are all freed from their various afflictions by his radiance, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That he emanates brilliant light that illuminates immeasurable Buddha-lands in the ten directions, bringing benefit to all beings, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
That within and without the city of Vaiśālī, he manifests eighty-four thousand transformed bodies of the Buddha in each location, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
At that time, by conforming to the needs of the eight classes of beings to proclaim the Way of the sutras so that each may attain understanding, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Taking Refuge That Is Difficult to Attain?
To maintain one’s dignified deportment and ritual propriety with composure and order, and to possess vast merit capable of encompassing emptiness—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To thoroughly understand that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a profound and transcendent virtue that is difficult to withstand—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).

To practice with firm resolve and skillful means according to the times without losing their proper measure; to have aspirations free from contradiction, administering medicine according to the ailment to transform and guide others; to protect all karmic activities and be able to tame a venomous serpent while holding it in one's hand; and through the power of utmost sincerity to be forever without fear, and by means of spiritual footprints and mantras to regard such tasks as no difficulty—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

For example, when Maudgalyāyana swiftly understood how to transform and subdue Māra, the Buddha accompanied him to deliver the multitudes of that land; yet, unaware of his own return, he came back to the Jeta Grove and spilled the water from his alms bowl, defiling the ground of the Buddha—this is called diligence.
Furthermore, as the Buddha’s disciple Śāriputra said:
"In a single moment, forty-nine thoughts arise to form the karma of birth and death," to which the Buddha replied that they are incalculable.
This is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā). As the Buddha said:

"Once there was a city where the people therein had committed grave offenses; they disregarded the Way and its teachings and slandered those of high virtue. In a single night and half a watch, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, preached the sūtras for them, causing them to cast off their heavy sins. Through diligent practice and thorough mastery, they attained the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā)."
"This is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
Chapter Seventeen: The Eighteen Unshared Qualities. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Pramuditarāja:
"What are the eighteen unique qualities?
There are eighteen matters regarding the dharmas of all Buddhas.
What are the six matters of the perfection of non-destruction?"
To provide timely guidance and instruction so that one’s virtuous conduct is complete and free from deficiency is called giving (*dāna*);
to eliminate partisan factions and act without partiality so as to be without fault is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and for one’s speech to be ultimate and essential, free from error, while body, mouth, and mind are tranquil, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
That their karmic retributions accord with the original intent, such that there is no duality from the initial aspiration until the Way, is called diligence;
that according to their vows each attains their proper place without violating the original essentials, is called single-mindedness;
and that through the gate of liberation attained by a sincere heart, one forever gains entry into peace and security without any hardships, is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of unattached and non-illusory speech?
To teach and transform others by proclaiming that which is pure and mature, rather than that which is fragmented or trivial—this is called giving (*dāna*).

To attain the three types of supernormal knowledge and insight regarding the past and future, maintaining constant purity of mindfulness so that one's conduct is free from defilement—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To harbor no intent to harm others but always embrace benevolence and compassion—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To explain the Dharma according to the inclinations and preferences of others' minds, thereby causing them to rejoice—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To proclaim what is subtle and wondrous for those who are peerless, causing the hearts of others to be joyful as if honeyed nectar were added to them—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To proclaim that which eliminates the various fetters and doubts that entangle one like a net—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the resolve for liberation?
To relinquish the mind so that merit is uninterrupted and naturally settled is called giving;
to encourage and assist the mind with all virtues so as to cause the aspiration for the Way to arise is called ethical discipline;..."
To practice boundlessly, adhering to the ultimate meaning so as to be forever free from transgression—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To attain all virtuous practices and the true Dharma—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To constantly know the events of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—never neglecting or forgetting them—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Because he grows up silently and naturally from that tree, contemplating the Dharma with focused mindfulness and not losing his fundamental nature—this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of mental concentration (citta-samādhi-pāramitā)?
That which is called the impartial mind that gives rise to nothing yet causes the Way and its teachings to flourish is termed giving (*dāna*);
that which is proclaimed as relying upon and dwelling in accordance with them without losing the Way and its teachings is termed ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and that which relies upon them to transform others through the Dharma, bringing great joy to many, is termed patience (*kṣānti*).
To practice the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and the path of true correctness for the sake of others is called diligence;
to restrain one’s own mind, to deliver others with kindness, and to guide them is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā);
to act according to the needs of all at all times, such that their aspirations and practices are boundless and each is made joyful, is called wisdom (prajñā).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of contemplation on tranquility and the unconditioned?
When one’s vows have been fulfilled and one is as auspiciously serene as a state of calm, this is called generosity;
To rely upon others while remaining tranquil and at peace is called upholding the precepts;
to practice compassion and examine and protect all karmic actions as if they were a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is called patience;
to universally protect all sentient beings within the three realms and demonstrate the boundless conduct of the bodhicitta is called diligence.
To provide sustenance and to proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all ignorant and deluded multitudes is called single-mindedness;
though one preaches the Dharma through the transformations of body, speech, and mind, causing them to commit no transgressions and remain unattached to the three realms is called wisdom—
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of non-differentiation?
If one does not give rise to thoughts of various categories but maintains the mind fixed upon the Path, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
If one gives rise to such thoughts as to manifest and exalt the Way and its Virtue, never departing from the True and Real, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one is without intentionality and does not engage in discursive thought, maintaining a mind that is always fixed and concentrated, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Never violating the nature and conduct of oneself or others, and protecting all things, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Diligently practicing what should be practiced, understanding the proper timing, and not losing the sacred rhythm, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To be able to thoroughly penetrate and master the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies, and to circulate through all their fundamental sources, is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Delightful Practice?
If one’s mind delights in protecting its own heart while taking pity on others, this is called giving (*dāna*);
if one reflects upon the past and present worlds with a mind that takes pity on oneself and feels compassion for all beings, this is called morality (*śīla*);
if one further rejoices in expounding the sūtras rather than engaging in worldly affairs, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Constantly practicing at all times for the sake of all supreme, true, and perfect bliss is called diligence (*vīrya*);
if one takes delight in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha, severing all craving and unwholesome conduct, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
if one eliminates the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths and sets one’s will upon the sweet Dharma of the Way, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six aspects of the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) that is non-wasteful?
To apply diligent effort in practicing and following the path of the Dharma, such that one's virtue is not diminished and everything is fully perfected—this is called giving (dāna).
If one delights the mind by compassionately regarding all beings and practices giving and diligence without harboring a harmful intent toward others, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If, when being instructed, one demonstrates the Dharma and is fully capable of receiving it, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If, through the illumination of the Dharma, one observes all things without causing harm, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To expound upon all that is taught by speaking of its fundamental source, and to recognize past lives so as to comprehend their boundless limits—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To understand the principles and meanings such that they are immeasurable—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-forgetfulness?
To know through the consciousness of one's mind the countless billions of kalpas of past lives, reaching back to their infinite depths, is called generosity (*dāna*).
To remember the accumulation of merit and the gathering of virtue throughout distant, incalculable kalpas is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one examines and knows [all things] as being thoroughly pure and forever free from defilement, this is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to recognize and understand what is cherished, from the initial resolve through all practices of the past and present, this is called diligence (*vīrya*);
and for the mind to enter into every thought-moment, contemplating the advancement and retreat, the beginning and end, of all phenomena, this is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To sever all diverse perceptions and to recollect past lives, discerning all that was previously experienced, is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramitā) through which one does not lose the focused mind?
To receive the meditative attainments (*samādhi*) of the four immeasurable minds—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—is called generosity;
to be able to fully receive and establish the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), wherein there is no perception of bodily pain or thought, is called ethical discipline;
to practice the supreme virtue by cultivating the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) such that there is nothing to be abandoned, is called patience.
To attain the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and fly to the ten directions to transform and teach all beings is called diligence;
to practice meditative contemplation and attain the majestic *samādhi* of concentration is called single-mindedness;
and to receive the wisdom of the Way through holy clarity without falsehood is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the wisdom that is never lost?
If one receives the faculty of wisdom and, through immeasurable knowledge, knows the fundamental nature of sentient beings—this is called giving;
To possess firm and powerful strength, attaining the power of wisdom up to the ten powers of a Buddha—this is called precept-keeping.
To attain the factors of enlightenment, awakening others through transformation and guidance so that those who have not awakened may reach clear understanding—this is called patience.
To understand with a clear mind, receiving and accepting the meaning of the Way and practicing in ways beyond measure—this is called diligence.
To analyze and understand the twelve links of dependent origination, knowing that causes are interconnected due to a lack of awakening, is called "single-mindedness.
To employ this noble clarity to attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is called "wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of liberation through non-forgetfulness?
To have physical strength that is firm and a mind like a diamond, never losing hold of the ultimate essentials—this is called giving (*dāna*).
To remain the same in mind whether dwelling among the great assembly or in solitude, never forgetting anything—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To roam amidst the turbulence and clamor of the multitudes without becoming deluded is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to understand the dispositions, actions, and thoughts—both good and evil—of others and sentient beings is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to securely establish the unsurpassed Great Way and the wisdom that is never extinguished is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To eliminate all bases of existence through the wisdom of non-arising, so that nothing remains and one’s resolve is fixed solely upon the scriptures—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation?
To act with ultimate sincerity and without hypocrisy so that one’s wishes are immediately fulfilled is called giving (*dāna*);
to perceive only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while delivering the multitude from the hardships of conditioned birth-and-death is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
to examine the defilement of desire and perceive its beginning and end as arising from causes and conditions is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To fully equip oneself with all the stages from stage to stage, establishing the karma of the ten abodes as the locus of fruition—this is called diligence.
To give rise to the mind that contemplates and practices the Way, thereby attaining the state of abiding—this is called single-mindedness.
If one puts on robes and fastens them upon the arms, employing skillful means to eliminate all evils, remaining without forgetfulness and not deviating from liberation—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of wisdom that turns through the clear illumination of knowing bodily conduct?
Diligently cultivating one-pointedness of mind and right conduct in bodily actions, guarding body, speech, and mind without weariness—this is called generosity.
To transform one's nature so that one refrains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, committing no transgressions, is called the precept of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To practice the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) so that there are no obstructing karmas in those dwellings, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To single-mindedly apply oneself with focused concentration to establish the roots of all virtues and bestow them upon all beings, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To cause countless people to obtain their retributions and the blessings of the ten directions is called single-mindedness;
to manifest spiritual powers through physical instruction and travel by flight to all places where the Buddhas preach is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of noble wisdom through the progressive advancement of verbal conduct?
To proclaim and expound the unsurpassed Dharma with one's speech, having experienced and resolved upon all dharmas without ever becoming weary or indolent—this is called giving (*dāna*).
For one’s voice to reach everywhere, entering all hearts and causing their conduct to become pure and transparent—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To transform and enlighten the assemblies so that they all attain unexcelled, true, and correct awakening is called patience;
for the sound of the Dharma teachings one proclaims to pervade and reach throughout the ten directions is called diligence;
to constantly recall supreme conduct without allowing it to be wasted, and to contemplate with single-minded devotion and firm faith in the ultimate truth, is called concentration of mind.
That which is proclaimed is never false, bringing great peace and security to all sentient beings; this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the progress of mental activity?

If the mind and consciousness are correctly focused and do not dwell on the perverse, and if the mind maintains its practice and mindfulness, remaining ever fundamentally pure, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To use the hearing of the Dharma to guide those who are ignorant and deluded, transforming all their attachments, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To be able to lead and benefit others through the karmic activities of existence and non-existence, establishing the practice of equanimity, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one studies the Dharma while discarding the notion of self and does not become conceited, this is called diligence;
to abandon folly and fix the will upon the Great Illumination so that there is no darkness or obscuration, this is called single-mindedness;
and for one’s conduct to be profound, subtle, preeminent, and limitless, this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of unimpeded knowledge regarding what was seen in past lives?
To contemplate all fruits, the various seeds, and the four great elements as fundamentally non-existent from the beginning—this is called giving (*dāna*).

To examine that the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and the elements of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are fundamentally without location is called upholding the precepts;
to observe that the six sense-fields (ṣaḍāyatana) arise from extremely subtle roots through the conjunction of conditions is called patience;
to contemplate that the origins of good and evil, or calamity and fortune, all stem from attachment to the body is called diligence.
To sever all worldly afflictions, constantly practice purity, and remain free from all defilements—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To examine sentient beings and realize that the twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally unarisen—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is unimpeded regarding the beginning and end of all things as seen in the future?
To see the convergence and dispersion of the five destinies in the past as being like the flourishing and decline, or the success and failure, of spring and autumn—this is called giving (dāna).
To be able to discern the sixty-two types of false views and not fall into inversion—this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
To contemplate that the fundamental source of humans is devoid of any inherent basis for either union or separation is called patience;
to examine which medicine should be used to treat sentient beings is called diligence;
to observe that the arising of their various realms and their advances or retreats each have their own conditions and actions is called single-mindedness.

To clearly understand the law of retribution and, upon seeing those who can be transformed, go to them to deliver and guide them so that they may give rise to the aspiration for the Way—this is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the Perfection of Knowing the Present Without Limitation?
To observe the conditions of the causes and effects they have created, and to transform all living beings while establishing merit—this is called *dāna* (giving).
To perceive the origins through which one understands the three liberations, and to uphold the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) until their fulfillment—this is called *śīla* (precept-keeping).
To practice and follow these instructions so as to be entirely free from greed and desire, and to aspire to the Way and its teachings, finding joy in the Dharma—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To contemplate that all forms—whether subtle or coarse—are entirely extinguished and impermanent, with nothing remaining, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To perceive the realization that the three realms are like an illusion, fundamentally non-existent and without contradiction or loss, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To behold the source of birth-and-death as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), where the mind does not dwell in duality regarding the finite or the infinite, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
This constitutes the six [qualities]. A note in the Dan-ben (Dānapāla) edition states:
"Among the eighteen unshared qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), there was formerly one textual passage missing.
Chapter 18: The Chapter on Expedient Means (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*). The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy (*Priyarāja*):
"What are the six matters of the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*) through clear understanding?
If one is able to apply oneself with single-minded diligence to skillful means and enter [the world] according to the occasion, this is called giving (*dāna*).
To transform those who are defiled and impure, thereby causing them all to become pure, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To employ all merit performed to encourage and assist all sentient beings is called patience;
to go wherever one travels without causing harm or committing any fault is called diligence;
to resolve with joy to teach and instruct sentient beings by means of the four ways of attracting others is called single-mindedness.

To enter immeasurable gateways, proclaim the essentials of dhāraṇī, and guide others toward benefit; to transform those within the three realms and cause them to enter the Great Way—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of maturity?
If one can skillfully and impartially guide and advance all dharmas, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

To embrace the teachings of the Dharma with a correct mind free from conditions, possessing profound and subtle wisdom characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; if one perceives the eightfold path and eliminates the eight difficulties, and sets the will upon the Eightfold Noble Path to realize that all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To contemplate various views and their delusive discriminations without falling into false views is called patience;
to observe those in the five destinies who should be enlightened and to go forth to save them is called diligence;
to see those who may be guided and to immediately employ skillful means to deliver them is called single-mindedness (concentration).
If one perceives conditioned phenomena and enters into them, dissolving all attachments so as to attain nirvāṇa, this is called wisdom;
these are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of seeing spontaneity?
The merit attained is void and has no basis of reliance, shining forth vast and expansive; this, like single-mindedly taking refuge in the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, is called generosity (*dāna*).

When the body is free from weariness and devoid of greed or attachment, just as when the moon is full and its brilliance illuminates the stars, a person with clear vision perceives it with true discernment; this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one can perceive that all phenomena are entirely like empty space, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To perceive all phenomena through meditative contemplation, such that as they arise they are immediately extinguished and fully discerned—this is called diligence.
To see no giver yet provide salvation, while observing one's own inadequacies—this is called single-mindedness.
To observe the activities of body and mind and proclaim the teachings of the Dharma, benefiting all beings without duality—this is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) regarding the causes and conditions of karma in the realm of desire?
To see that the desires one has cultivated are defiled karmas, and to realize that while they were originally entirely pure, obstacles have now been established—this is called giving.
To perceive that all dharmas are inherently quiescent, yet to realize that one brings about calamity or fortune through a lack of understanding—this is called upholding the precepts.
To contemplate that which is profound and remote, reaching the ultimate limit where there is no boundary—this is called patience.
To observe for oneself that the conditions of sin and merit are entirely exhausted and nothing endures for long—this is called diligence.

When conditions and objects have ceased, yet one perceives what ought to be practiced, and spontaneously abides in the correct and true through the appropriateness of skillful means—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
When both demerit and merit are exhausted and are no longer further created, such that the difficulties of the three realms are seen as having no place of arising—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of karma conditioned by the practice of form?
To see that all conditions of form arise from bodily actions, and that when the mind fails to understand, it recklessly gives rise to the source of retribution—this is called giving (*dāna*).

To observe that all perceived forms possess causes and conditions, and that they do not necessarily arrive recklessly, yet the body and mind become deluded—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To examine the places of rebirth—whether in the heavens or among humans, or in the three evil realms—as the retribution for one's merits and faults, is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to observe these places of rebirth while maintaining mindful reflection, is called diligence (*vīrya*);
to constantly regard the retribution with joy and gladness, is called single-mindedness (*ekacitta*).
To protect the lofty and serene while remaining tranquil and unattached toward the lowly—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the formless karmic activities?
If one is equanimous toward form and does not fall into the realm of desire, refraining from conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*) in the sphere of purity, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

To perceive the fivefold practice of karma—namely, the categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*)—is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one is able to exhaust the opposition of causes and conditions so that neither calamity nor fortune arises, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Diligently cultivating supreme practice so that all things are made equal and free from partiality—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one possesses profound faith and cultivates those practices with purity, free from defilement—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Seeing always as clearly as walking by daylight and never encountering darkness, neither destroying anything nor failing to save anything—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of dwelling in pure and white observation?
If, by beholding the place where one stands, one desires to attain this dwelling on the ground of pure and white loving-kindness, this is called giving.
To be able to attain the karma of auspicious responses while not giving rise to the threefold actions of body, speech, and mind is called upholding the precepts;
to diligently practice the Dharma of the four debts of gratitude without interruption is called patience;
and for one's contemplation to be vast and expansive, with the resolve for enlightenment towering and boundless, is called diligence.
To accumulate merit and virtue so that the practice of sagely illumination increases day by day is called single-mindedness;

to examine what is pure and white, thereby eliminating the various conceptions of good and evil as well as the conception of dharmas regarding the birth and death of sentient beings, is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the lineage of dharmas?
To perceive that all phenomena are suffering and yet, due to a lack of penetration, one creates calamity and fortune—this is called giving.
To see the middle way wherein the mind abides nowhere, being neither in existence nor non-existence—this is called ethical discipline."
If one perceives desire and passion and swiftly eliminates them so that they do not grow, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To maintain right nature without ever deviating from the unsurpassed, true, and correct [path], this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To be fully endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and never sever the lineage of the Buddha, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
When the mind achieves the eightfold equality and attains all dharmas without realizing them, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
*Bhadrapāla-akṣaṇa-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The Sūtra of the Wise and the Holy, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen: The Eightfold Equality. Chapter Nineteen: The Eightfold Equality.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"What are the six matters regarding the eightfold equanimity that leads to the ultimate perfection?
If one faithfully believes in the eightfold equanimity, joyfully and resolutely maintains it, and does not fall into the eight deviations, this is called generosity (dāna).
To uphold the dharma of the path through the eightfold noble practice and not for worldly glory is called *śīla* (precept-keeping);
having abided in the noble practice and maintained impartial karma, to attain mastery such that one is neither harmed nor deceived is called *kṣānti* (patience);
to reach the state of an Arhat without rising from a single sitting, traversing the three realms so as to no longer undergo birth and death, is called *vīrya* (diligence).

To proceed from the eightfold path to the fruit of stream-entry, and to become a once-returner, a non-returner, or a true person of no further attachment—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To transcend the various currents, to discern their manifold distinctions, and to embrace this meaning of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Embracing the Dharma of the Path (Mārga-vidyā-dharmapada-pāramitā)?

To attain illumination progressively by means of the path, thereby exhausting and eliminating the hindrances (āvaraṇa)—namely, lust, anger, ignorance, darkness, sleep, and restlessness—this is called giving (dāna).
To exhaust all craving and desire so that there are no longer various defiled or impure practices, this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
To go back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human world until all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted is called patience;
to practice begging from house to house to bestow blessings upon all, thereby attaining peace in every lifetime, is called diligence;
and to maintain the body, speech, and mind through a single practice is [patience].
To abandon all sources of useless karma is called single-mindedness;
to be unattached and to understand that the three realms are fundamentally empty is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the *paramitā* of the subtle dust of coming and going?
Though one exists within the triple world, seeing that its forms and desires gradually tend toward extinction—this is called giving (*dāna*).
Seeing the difficulty posed by the afflictions and the cravings of desire, yet never transgressing in mind—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To examine their transgressions and faults so as to diminish them and ultimately cause them to cease—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To observe with clear penetration that karmic offenses are formed through one's conduct—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To see all cravings and desires incinerated until nothing remains—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To thoroughly understand and clarify the root of birth and death throughout one's life, thereby removing attachment and love so that no further afflictions remain—
this is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of non-returning?
To be able to distance oneself from attachment to the realm of desire, practicing the four methods of benevolence and the four equanimities without weariness—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
That one’s mind is free from the hardships of further defilement, exhausting its very source so as never to return to this world—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To be born among the twenty-second heaven, the Heaven of Bestowing Goodness, and there practice the Way without abandoning its tasks—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To diligently cultivate day and night with the mind fixed upon the Dharma, and if one is born in the twenty-third heaven, the Heaven of the Nature of Bestowing Goodness—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If one is born in the twenty-fourth heaven, the Heaven Free from the Bonds of Attachment, and there remains composed with a mind free from seeking—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one approaches the path of the true practitioner through the six supernormal powers and thereby attains the treasury of wisdom, this is called wisdom;
these are the six. What are the six matters of the unattached perfection (pāramitā)?
To reach the stage of Arhat through the complete eradication of forgetfulness and negligence is called generosity (*dāna*);
to no longer require the maintenance of the quality of non-forgetfulness as it is naturally perfected is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and to attain liberation through profound faith such that the mind harbors no doubt is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To reach the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, and death through the liberation of wisdom is called diligence;
to exhaust all calamities and the hardships of the three miserable realms, personally attaining verification, is called single-mindedness;
to achieve simultaneous liberation and escape from the cycle of birth and death so that it is forever exhausted without remainder is called wisdom.
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the *pratyekabuddha-pāramitā*?
To contemplate few affairs while dwelling in the mountain stillness; not craving one's own body or life, and not seeking the clamor of crowds—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To cultivate the deeds of a true person by selecting the Dharma, and to be upright and sincere, appropriately attuned to the timing of things—this is called precept-keeping.
To dwell alone and maintain one’s resolve without indulgence—this is called patience.
To attain liberation, cross over the three realms, and depart from them so that there are no further fetters or bonds—this is called diligence.
If one cultivates stillness until reaching a state of detachment where the mind has no attachments, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To attain the fundamental source of the one grade of karma that is upright and true, remaining constant and in accordance with the Dharma such that there are no dualistic karmas, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection?
To practice salvation with a mind always characterized by equanimity and free from flattery—this is called generosity (dāna).
To attain a nature of harmony and constantly practice tranquility to heal and treat the mind—"
To transform and guide beings according to their individual dispositions is called upholding the precepts;
to apply an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and refrain from harming them is called patience;
to practice the profound and essential dharma of emptiness, the unsurpassed Great Way, and the meaning of ultimate truth, thereby attaining omniscience, is called diligence.
Not relying on the voices of others, yet returning to and dwelling in the equanimity of the samādhi of minor precepts—this is called single-mindedness (citta-ekāgratā).
Not wearying of birth and death, using wisdom to guide and enlighten all sentient beings—this is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the wisdom of exhaustion?
To cultivate what is appropriate through the wisdom of exhaustion so as not to fall into deficiency is called giving;
to use the truth of goodness to heal all practices so that body, speech, and mind are pure is called morality."
To practice the removal of defilements with pure radiance and to be free from conceptualization—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To sever all delusions and delight in the true reality (*bhūtārtha*), proclaiming what is appropriate and following the teachings of the Buddha—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To be without stinginess regarding anything one possesses, being able to rescue others from distress and diligently cultivating the true reality—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To be able to cast off all unwholesome karma and all ignorance, thereby attaining the lofty and holy penetration of the six supernormal powers and reaching all-knowledge—this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of wisdom that is non-arising?
When the fundamental retribution of craving and desire is about to arise, to understand through clear comprehension that all is empty and that wisdom is non-arising—this is called generosity.
To cause there to be no outward form and no returning, and to realize non-arising—this is called ethical discipline."
To have no association or entanglement with worldly dharmas, but to practice the Dharma purely, is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To single-mindedly cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—without any forgetfulness or loss, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
It is by means of this that one is able to perceive the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-prajñā*).
To perceive that all things are entirely non-existent is called single-mindedness;
to sever all discursive thoughts, to be free from all defilements, and to harbor no delusive imaginings is called wisdom.
These are the six. "What are the six matters of the establishment of the *pāramitās*?
If the True Dharma remains or even if the True Dharma has vanished, one does not abandon the Way for the sake of obtaining clothing, food, sustenance, or fame; this is called giving (*dāna*).
To abide in the teachings of the Dharma without relying on or seeking anything, with a mind equal to space—this is called upholding the precepts.
To be able to bring joy to those of the four castes while not relying on those four—this is called patience.
If one diligently cultivates the fruits of skillful means and seeks the fruit of the truly correct, unsurpassed path—this is called diligence.
When among the asuras, constantly studying the scriptures and not abandoning the Three Jewels—this is called single-mindedness;
when all in the world hear their Dharma and immediately receive and practice it without any deviant thoughts—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the divine eye?
If one perceives all forms with the divine eye, yet the mind remains unattached and realizes their emptiness, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

If one is able to clearly perceive the formless and, through the exercise of skillful means (*upāya*), does not fall into the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
If one understands and penetrates the formless nature of phenomena, and with a mind that has attained equanimity, is free from both hatred and love, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To examine the sufferings of birth and death, the cycles of coming and going, and the various hardships without being bound by fear, this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To perceive non-thought as equal to all thoughts, such that there is no obstruction internally or externally and nothing to which one returns, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one perceives with tranquility and the mind is serene and detached, like space that cannot be measured, this is called wisdom;
these are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the divine ear (divya-śrotra)?

If one can hear the speech and voices of all sentient beings—the sounds of celestial music, song, and dance, as well as the cries of those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—and directs a heart of compassion toward them, this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To enable others to hear even the most subtle sounds, and to realize that all words are entirely empty and devoid of substance, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
To ensure that all actions accord with the work of the Path and do not follow the sixty-two views of external teachings, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To proclaim with the mouth and contemplate with the mind as this practice, employing skillful means according to the exigencies of the time to transform others through wisdom—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).

To hear that all things are empty and that no phenomena exist, to inquire into and receive the Way of the sutras, and to grasp, recite, and maintain them—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To comprehend all sounds and know them to be utterly extinguished, returning to the silence of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six aspects of the perfection of mastery over the minds of others through the power of one's own mind?
If, by means of one’s own mind, one perceives the various realms and seeks to rescue them from the afflictions of the three worlds, this is called generosity (*dāna*).

When the mind universally perceives the meaning of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and this mind remains equanimous without dwelling upon conditioned phenomena, this is called upholding the precepts.
When one contemplates that the karma of causes, conditions, retributions, and responses is fundamentally without objective correspondence, this is called patience.
When one observes the affairs of the past and future worlds and clearly perceives their beginnings and ends in advance, this is called diligence.
To view present phenomena with equanimity, seeing them all as like illusions and transformations—this is called single-mindedness.
To universally perceive that the beginning and end of all practices have no such beginning or end, and that there is nothing therein to be grasped as essential—this is called wisdom.
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of recollecting the past?
To perceive the births, the successive experiences, and the right and wrong of one's past conduct is called generosity;
to achieve what has been done and employ it to assist toward supreme, perfect enlightenment is called ethical discipline."
Not coming again repeatedly, but causing all things to be extinguished so that nothing arises, is called patience (*kṣānti*);
by means of this name, realizing there is nothing to possess, yet perceiving and seeing the fundamental nature of all things, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
proclaiming the Way of the Sūtras through various categories to transform the three realms and benefit those in peril and distress, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda) for flying through the air?
To attain supernatural power so as to soar and travel throughout the ten directions is called giving (dāna).
To always act in accordance with the meaning of the Dharma through skillful means, understanding that the five aggregates are empty and not to be destroyed, is called upholding the precepts;
to give rise to great compassion, feeling pity for sentient beings and desiring to deliver them, is called patience;
to be fully perfected in one's conduct, like the full moon shining among the stars without any loss or deficiency, is called diligence.

If one can exercise self-restraint over the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense-fields (*āyatana*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to suppress and subdue the will, this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);
if one does not remain in indolence but exerts oneself to cultivate progress until entering the ultimate state of the sages, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
these constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayapāramitā)?
Having seen those [outflows] for oneself, not reckoning them as 'self' or 'other,' and being without any outflows—this is called generosity (dāna).
Observing all outflows to know their origin and ensuring they do not arise again—this is called ethical discipline (śīla)."
To perceive that all outflows (*āsrava*) are fundamentally rootless and entirely extinguished is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To physically attain the observation that all outflows are exhausted such that there is nothing further to exhaust, and not seeing any destination to which birth and death return, is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To cause the roots of all outflows to naturally and eternally cease without remainder is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To extract these various outflows through the power of diligence, such that no location is found and no destination is perceived, is called wisdom;
this constitutes the sixth.
What are the six matters of the perfection of majestic deportment?
To employ dignified deportment so that countless people all adopt ritual propriety and rejoice with harmonious minds is called generosity (*dāna*);
to bring universal joy to all sentient beings such that none fail to receive the teachings of the Dharma with delight is called ethical discipline (*śīla*);
to observe with focused diligence and without negligence, keeping only the Great Way in mind, is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To move and come with calm composure, without abruptness or violence, is called diligence;
for one’s dignified demeanor to be flawless and ritual propriety to be fully complete is called single-mindedness;
to perceive profound and far-reaching karma as luminously rootless and to be fully endowed with virtuous conduct is called wisdom.
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of compassion?
If there are those with evil minds who harbor perverse poison, and one sustains and rescues them by providing food and clothing—this is called giving.
To see those who are cruel or harmful, and when they encounter calamity or distress, to rescue and protect them by showing them the Way of the Sūtras—this is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
To be able to endure all instances of arrogance and self-importance from those of external heterodox schools who harbor various aspirations—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To expound and propagate the principles of meaning for the sake of the multitude, like a lotus flower in a pond—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To expound the meaning of virtuous and wholesome deeds so as to bring about self-subduing is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);

if there is a sacrificial rite, to go there because it has arisen and preach the Dharma for them, speaking with such thorough discernment that even the naked ascetics (*nirgrantha*) are transformed, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These constitute the six.
"What are the six matters of the perfection of the emptiness of practice?
To give without weariness and without becoming weary; to transform others so they enter the Way rather than engaging in worldly affairs—this is called generosity (*dāna*).
To act with mastery, attaining autonomy through one's own effort rather than following the teachings of others—this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
To practice with single-minded devotion without turning back or falling into minor attachments is called patience (*kṣānti*);
to carry out practices to their ultimate conclusion without seeking realization midway, thereby completing all meritorious virtues, is called diligence (*vīrya*);
and to constantly practice that which should be followed without relying on anything, bringing such cultivation to maturity, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
To establish practices according to what others prefer and thereby guide and benefit all beings is called wisdom;
these are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of relinquishment?
To cast aside the practice of clinging to life and not being attached to the body, acting with freedom and without obstruction—this is called *dāna* (generosity).
To abandon present attachments of body, speech, and mind, and to have no mental clinging toward the cycle of birth and death in the five realms—this is called *śīla* (ethical discipline).

To settle within the realm of conditioned phenomena while practicing in accordance with the Dharma, and to never transgress the four immeasurables and the six perfections—this is called *kṣānti* (patience).
To relinquish and abandon lust, anger, and delusion, casting off all other sufferings, views, and the sixty-two matters—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
To cause the practices of sentient beings to reach maturity, and to abandon those practices without arrogance—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

To free sentient beings from the sorrows and grief of lamentation, keeping the mind fixed on the ultimate Dharma and remaining compliant with the teachings of the Vinaya—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six. What are the six matters of the perfection of nirvāṇa?
To understand emptiness through clear comprehension and not by means of false conceptualization, such that one reaches nirvāṇa and attains the state of non-arising—this is called giving.
To establish the mind upon the Great Way so that it abides nowhere is called upholding the precepts;
to relinquish the security of one’s own body and not cling to life or limb in order to transform and enlighten sentient beings is called patience;
to shake the trichiliocosm with the power of the divine feet such that no devas or humans are struck with alarm or fear is called diligence.
When one’s mind is in meditative contemplation, settled in samādhi, and in right reception, being without attachment and free from negligence—this is called single-mindedness (ekāgratā).
After entering parinirvāṇa, when one’s bodily relics are dispersed and spread throughout the ten directions so that all receive its grace—this is called wisdom (prajñā).
These constitute the six [perfections].
"What are the six matters of the Perfection of Transformation?
To distribute the *śarīra* relics so that they may be obtained everywhere and spread throughout the world is called giving (*dāna*).
For the *śarīra* to manifest auspicious signs, majestic spiritual power, and radiance such that all who see them are filled with joy is called ethical discipline (*śīla*)."
When sentient beings see these transformations and their hearts are filled with joy, thereby giving rise to the mind of the Way—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
When the various devas see his majestic merit and loftiness, and they exhort him and rejoice in his stead—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
If, upon seeing the relics of the Sage’s feet emitting light, the hair on one's body stands on end and tears immediately flow forth—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
If one beholds the śarīra and establishes a vow of utmost sincerity, such that it manifests light and majestic virtue with the five colors shining brilliantly, this is called wisdom;
these constitute the six.
What are the six matters of the *pāramitā* of disseminating the Dharma teachings?
If one attains the refuge and offerings of the multitude, providing for all their deficiencies, this is called giving (*dāna*).
If one constantly guards one’s own mind so that nothing arises, and since there is nothing that arises, there is nothing that ceases, this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).

If one perceives the three realms as being devoid of intrinsic existence, and views the Buddha, the Dharma, and all sentient beings as entirely spontaneous (*svabhāva-śūnya*), this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To cause the scriptures, the Way, and the teachings to flow through the heavens and pervade the world is called diligence (*vīrya*);
for all the hosts of Māras to see them and shrink back in awe, unable to withstand their majestic countenance, is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*);

and if the Dharma teachings are made manifest and spread so that those in the ten directions love and respect them, each harboring joy, and gradually attain the state of extinction (*nirvāṇa*), this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
These are the six.
What are the six matters of the perfection of the distribution of relics?
To seek various articles of offering for the relics and to serve them with reverence day and night is called giving.
That countless multitudes all rejoice together, take refuge, and pay homage is called upholding the precepts;
that he further manifests radiant spiritual power, drawing those from far and near to observe him so that their minds are transformed one by another, is called patience;
that gods and humans alike leap for joy, recognizing his supreme dignity and thereby giving rise to the aspiration for the Way, is called diligence.
If, upon seeing the relics, one finds no other pleasure but to contemplate the Buddha-way which is beyond compare, this is called single-mindedness;
to praise the relics for attaining wondrous eloquence, being without obstruction and thereby entering into wisdom—
this constitutes the sixth.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy:

"These two thousand one hundred perfections (pāramitās), along with the remaining ninety perfections that eliminate the nine worldly afflictions, transform the ninety-six heterodox schools and cause them to enter the true and correct path."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"These two thousand one hundred perfections (pāramitās) involve preaching the Dharma to transform those of the lustful nature;
these two thousand one hundred perfections involve preaching the Dharma to enlighten and transform those of the wrathful nature."
Two thousand one hundred *pāramitās* of the infinite, through preaching the Dharma, awaken those of the deluded class;
two thousand one hundred *pāramitās* of the infinite, through preaching the Dharma and providing instruction, transform those of the equal-part class.
These eight thousand four hundred *pāramitās* are each transformed into ten, totaling eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.

The Buddha is the King of Physicians; his Dharma serves as the supreme, excellent medicine for all sentient beings within the three realms. It cures the three poisons and eliminates the veils of the aggregates (*skandha-āvaraṇa*). For those who are equally afflicted by these factors or who are rebellious and incorrigible, he guides them through his manifestations so that none fail to attain liberation. Without practicing these eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*, one cannot succeed in removing the eighty-four thousand varieties of defilements and afflictions for hundreds of thousands of kinds of people, nor can one reach the eighty-four thousand gates of *samādhi*. Therefore, he establishes the eighty-four thousand dharmas of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to guide these hundreds of thousands of kinds of people, eliminating their eighty-four thousand varieties of defilements and afflictions and reaching the eighty-four thousand gates of *samādhi*. This is called the Buddha-way; it penetrates deeply into the infinite and leads to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The Buddha said to King Nanda:

"By means of this Dharma, I sat beneath the Bodhi tree, subdued the hosts of Māra, and attained supreme perfect enlightenment. Thereby, I understood the Dharma and established equanimity; sitting cross-legged upon the ground, I immediately attained a state of sublime and wondrous majesty."
The Brahma King, with reverent haste, descended and prostrated himself, seeking refuge and compassion, saying:
"In accordance with my ancient vows for the sake of all sentient beings, they have now all assembled together, desiring to hear the sutra."
The Brahma King shed tears and earnestly exhorted him: "Only deliver all those who have not yet crossed over and are deluded!

Now that you, Buddha, have become such a subtle and wondrous Great Sage and have attained Supreme Perfect Enlightenment, you sit in tranquil stillness; yet you remain silent within yourself, contemplating this thought: 'In this world of five turbidities, with its ninety-six paths and sixty-two views, beings are deluded, violent, and for the most part lack repentance and do not accept the Way and its teachings; it would be better to remain silent and enter Parinirvāṇa.'"

The Buddha sat beneath the tree, his majestic radiance illuminating the ten directions. The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, beholding from afar this awesome brilliance—the countenance and meritorious achievements of which were nowhere not resplendent, and whose virtuous path and auspicious karma shone most brightly—realized that it was fitting for these teachings to be propagated.

The assemblies of all the devas were filled with joy; he established a great radiance of profound stillness, true and holy, reaching the boundless. His brilliance shone resplendently, his majestic virtue manifesting everywhere; supreme and pure, most honored throughout the three periods of time, it pervaded all Buddha-realms in the ten directions. His mind was thoroughly liberated, shaking the three thousandfold world-system; his wisdom of the Way was vast and far-reaching, difficult to see or hear, transcending all depths as his renown spread everywhere.
Beholding this majestic spiritual power, the wondrous and immeasurable radiance, the countenance of sublime virtue, and wisdom like the void—extraordinary and beyond compare.
At that time, Brahmā King again addressed the Buddha:
“With bated breath and single-minded devotion, I reverently take refuge.”
He spoke this verse:

"The Great Light is manifested at the site of enlightenment; subduing Māra and extinguishing the dust of affliction, it causes the three thousandfold world-system to tremble and eliminates the sufferings of all evil realms."
With body upright and sitting in peace, Unswaying like Mount Sumeru, he radiates brilliance that illuminates the Buddha-fields;
Dwelling beneath the tree, there is none who does not receive his grace.
Sitting with composure, his faculties are tranquil; Like a lion, he abides in fearlessness.
Beholding for himself the desire for quiescence, he sat upon the supreme couch and spread forth his radiant light;
manifesting his majesty beneath the King of Trees, he widely disseminated the Great Way and established peace.
He eliminated worldly dharmas that are of no benefit and extinguished the calamities of the three miserable realms.
Beholding his countenance, one never tires; his mind contemplates with sincere compassion.
Reflecting deeply, he proclaims the honored discourse, equally expounding the level path of the Dharma.
He selects the karmic deeds of the three periods of time and illuminates all dharmas of the three categories.
Acting in accordance with the timely expression of his intent, he manifests the Way like the full moon.
Possessing the thirty-two marks of physical excellence, he is the Great Holy Father of the world.
Not abandoning the world for the sake of personal bliss, the peerless Brahmā has come.
Observing the world within the three fires, awakening the mundane with the water of Dharma, he constantly protects against the burning of the flames; at that time, he rains down nectar.
Examining diligence without interruption, those who were deluded find the correct path.
The Eye of Wisdom teaches non-duality; out of compassion for the age, he instructs.
His virtue is like the great ocean or a massive mountain; for the sake of the multitudes, he launches the vessel of enlightenment.
He ferries across those submerged in the current and transforms those on the perilous paths of heterodox learning.
Bound by craving and clinging to the body, Harming themselves with wrong views and enslaved by passion, They cannot escape the long prison;
Lead the multitudes so they may be transformed and liberated.
Giving rise to perversity, they dwell long in slumber; Following after sensory dust, they find no joy in the Path.
Having attained meditative concentration and firm vows, why do you not beat the Dharma drum?
People are destitute and fall into hell; wandering through the five realms of existence, they constantly fail to reach the inexhaustible. For what reason do you not proclaim the sacrifice?
Countless beings harbor faith; dwelling in tranquil equanimity, they partake of the nectar of immortality.
Through the rain of Dharma that extinguishes the flames of sorrow, they grasp the awakening that can bring down the bounty of grace.
Knowing the sores and maladies of the three periods of time, they do not perceive the mental afflictions of the dust of the world.
Having obtained pure medicine, why do you not provide relief and healing?
You dispel the darkness and ignorance of sentient beings and have perfected the great virtue of the Horse-Treasury;
with the light of wisdom illuminating the great trichiliocosm, why do you not radiate glory throughout the Buddha-lands?
Out of compassion for gods and men who have fallen into the four rushing torrents,
why do you not rescue them from this calamity and protect those who have fallen into the great abyss?
Seeing the various thoughts [of beings], the Buddha beheld the gods and men standing with palms joined.
Free from flattery and having cast aside what is not peaceful, why do you not manifest the Jewel of the Path?
With the Buddha-eye you observe the three realms; Brahmā exhorts the Honored One among Men:
out of compassion for those with various wrong views, please turn the Wheel of Dharma to extinguish their fever.
The Honored One sits upon the lion throne; all devas and humans have gathered here.
Standing thus, they seek moistening grace; pray, turn the wheel of Dharma for their sake.
Chapter Twenty: The Names of a Thousand Buddhas. The Bodhisattva King of Joy again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes indeed, World-Honored One!
Is there now within this assembly any Great Being who has attained this concentrated mind,
and who has entered these eight thousand four hundred perfections (pāramitās)?"
"And how does one enter the eighty-four thousand dharmas of the *pāramitās* and the eighty-four thousand gates of all *samādhis*?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva King of Joy:
"In this assembly there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained these concentrations and *pāramitās*, and who further attain entry into these eighty-four thousand gates of all *samādhis*."
Not only these bodhisattvas, but also those who shall study this [path] and become the one thousand Tathāgatas who attain supreme perfect enlightenment within this Bhadrakalpa—
excluding four Tathāgatas— are likewise those who have previously attained unsurpassed, true, and correct awakening, and have also attained this samādhi.
The Bodhisattva King of Joy addressed the Buddha again,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”

Out of your singular compassion, you should proclaim the names and clan titles of these bodhisattvas; for this will bring great solace and security, showing pity for the devas and the people of the ten directions. You should protect the true scriptures so that the Way and its Dharma may endure for a long time, and provide a gift for future students of the bodhisattvas, manifesting the light of the unsurpassed, right, and true path so that they may achieve success through it.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall now proclaim for you the names of the thousand Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva Joy-King and the great assembly received these instructions and listened attentively.

If there are those who hear, receive, uphold, recite, and study this with a focused and diligent mind, clearly understanding its meaning; if they practice without negligence, offer it with harmonious devotion, abandon the sufferings and afflictions of the various evil realms, and long abide in peace within the prohibitions and precepts; if they maintain faith and accord with joy in the path of the sutras, practicing purity and attaining the fruit of fulfillment—this is the profound and wondrous patience, the root and source of the Dharma-patience, which protects all worlds for many billions of kalpas.

Those who have committed various evil deeds and do not understand the retribution of the fruits of sin and merit, upon hearing the names of the Buddhas, shall have all their sins eliminated and be free from all afflictions.
If one should hold these names of the Buddhas and all their honorable titles, they will attain supernormal powers and a concentrated mind of single-mindedness.

If there are ordinary people who, having attained the opportunity to see or hear this, encounter it through these guides of the multitude who govern and practice the sūtras; who have embraced immeasurable merit and blessings for billions of years; whose explained meanings are fluent and whose wisdom of sound is penetrating; and who, by virtue of encountering and seeing this samādhi-concentration, possess pure conduct and a mind free from hesitation; whose arising wisdom does not cling to the three realms; and who have attained dhāraṇī and maintain it within their hearts—such as these shall practice this samādhi-concentration.

In the first assembly where he preached the sutra, seven billion six hundred million disciples gathered; in the second assembly, seven billion four hundred million; and in the third assembly, seven billion two hundred million—all of whom attained the realization of the Way.

In the lineage of the Noble One, his father was named Śikṣā, his mother was called Madhuvīryā, and his son was Brahmā.
His attendant was Dharmakīrti; his chief disciple of wisdom was Mūlamati, and his disciple of supernormal powers was Āryaka.
In the first assembly, forty billion disciples gathered to hear the sutra; in the second, thirty billion; and in the third, twenty billion, all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, the human lifespan was three thousand years; the True Dharma remained for ten thousand years, and his relics were combined to establish one great stupa-temple.
"The land where the Tathāgata Susthitu was born has a city named Tranquil Majesty; that Buddha’s radiance illuminates four hundred li.

The attendant was named Jueji; the foremost disciple of wisdom was named Shangyu; and the disciple of supernormal powers was named Zhikai.

At the first assembly, forty-six thousand disciples gathered to hear the sutra; at the second, twenty-five thousand; and at the third, forty-three thousand—all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
When this Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was five million years; the True Dharma remained for eighty thousand years, and his relics were combined to establish one great stupa.
As for the land where the Tathāgata Ākāśa was born, the city was named Priyavāsa, and that Buddha’s light illuminated one hundred and twenty *li*.
In the lineage of the Noble One, his father was named Mūladatta, his mother was called Devasena, and his son was named Varuṇa.
His attendant was named Jñānabandhu; his chief disciple in wisdom was named Uttaramati, and his disciple in spiritual power was named Dharmottara.

In the first assembly, ninety billion disciples gathered to hear the sutra; in the second assembly, eighty billion; and in the third assembly, seventy billion—all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
