“The land where the Tathāgata Aparimitabuddhi was born has a city named Sugandhā. That Buddha’s radiance illuminates three hundred and eighty li.
He is of the Brahmin caste; his father’s name is Jātanetra, his mother’s name is Nāgadattā, and his son’s name is Suvibhakta.”
His attendant was named Bhadradatta; his chief disciple of wisdom was named Cittasvara; and his disciple of supernormal powers was named Mahāviṭapī.
In the first assembly, he preached the sutra to seventy billion beings; in the second, fifty billion; and in the third, forty billion, all of whom attained the realization of the Path.

When that Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was one hundred million years; the True Dharma remained for sixty billion years, and his relics were distributed and spread throughout the ten directions.
As for the land where the Tathāgata Śubhavarṇa was born, the city was named Vaiśālī; the light of that Buddha illuminated five hundred and twenty li.
He was of the Jūni clan; his father’s name was Rāva and his mother’s surname was Rāvi; his son was named Svastika; his attendant was named Uttara;
his chief disciple of wisdom was named Puṇyaprajña; and his disciple of spiritual power was named Abhaya.

In the first assembly for preaching the sutra, seven hundred million disciples gathered; in the second, nine hundred million; and in the third, one billion—all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, the human lifespan was three thousand years; the True Dharma remained for sixteen thousand years, and his relics were combined to establish a single great stupa.
"The land where the Tathāgata Āryamati was born has a city named Sukṣetra. That Buddha’s radiance illuminates five hundred and sixty *li*.
He is of the Brahmin caste; his father is named Īśvara, his mother is named Viraja, and his son is named Śūra."
The attendant was named Ānanda; the foremost disciple of wisdom was named Iṅgīta; and the disciple of supernormal powers was named Sudatta.

In the first assembly where he preached the sutras, twenty-two billion disciples gathered; in the second, twenty-one billion; and in the third, twenty billion; all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
When that Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was twenty-eight thousand years; the True Dharma remained for sixty thousand years, and his relics were combined to establish one great stupa.
As for the land where the Tathāgata Prabhāsa was born, the city was named Vaidūryaprabhā, and the light of that Buddha illuminated three thousand three hundred and twenty li.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste; his father’s name was Vatsa and his mother’s name was Āśaya; his son was named Priyaprabha.
His attendant was named Udyāna, his chief disciple of wisdom was named Nandaka, and his disciple of psychic power was named Vinayamitra.

In the first assembly for preaching the sutra, eight billion two hundred million disciples gathered; in the second assembly, eight hundred and seventy million; and in the third assembly, eight hundred and sixty million; all of them attained the realization of the Way.
When that Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was ten thousand years; the True Dharma remained for three thousand years, and his relics were widely distributed throughout the ten directions.
As for the land where Tathāgata Firm Vow was born, the city was named Day-Wandering (Riyou), and the light of that Buddha illuminated forty *li*.
He was of the Brahmin caste; his father’s name was Devānāmpriya, his mother’s name was Priyavādinī, and his son was named Ratna.
His attendant was named Mṛdughoṣa, his chief disciple of wisdom was named Vākpradatta, and his disciple of supernormal powers was named Mṛduka.

In the first assembly for preaching the sutra, ten billion disciples gathered; in the second assembly, nine billion seven hundred million; and in the third assembly, nine billion five hundred million, all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, the human lifespan was one hundred million years; the True Dharma remained for four billion years, and his relics were combined to establish a single great stupa.
“The land where the Tathāgata Śrī was born has a city named Mātṛvatsalā. That Buddha’s light illuminates two hundred and eighty *li*.
He is of the Brahmin caste; his father is named King of Brocade, his mother is named Flower-Source, and his son is named Immeasurable Hand.”
His attendant was named Yangyou; his chief disciple of wisdom was named Fashi; and his disciple of supernormal powers was named Shengyou.

In the first assembly for the preaching of the sutra, fifty billion disciples gathered; in the second, eighty-two billion; and in the third, eighty-six billion—all of whom attained the realization of the Way.

"When the Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was fifty thousand years; the True Dharma remained for one hundred million years, and his relics were widely distributed throughout the ten directions.
As for the land where the Tathāgata Chengying was born, the city was named Aiyang, and that Buddha’s radiance illuminated forty li."
He was of the Brahmin caste; his father’s name was Puṇyabāhu and his mother’s name was Bhadrā.
His son was named Priyanāman.
His attendant was named Gaurīya, his chief disciple of wisdom was named Candrabhadra, and his disciple of supernormal powers was named Vṛkṣamati.
In the first assembly, eighty billion disciples gathered; in the second, seventy billion; and in the third, sixty billion, all of whom attained the realization of the Way.

During the Buddha’s lifetime, the human lifespan was one hundred million years; the True Dharma remained for eight hundred million years, and his relics were combined to establish a single great stupa.
"The land where the Tathāgata Nīlotpala was born has a city named Mahāpuṣpatejas; that Buddha’s radiance illuminates four hundred and eighty li.
He was of the kṣatriya caste; his father’s name was Dhāraṇī, and his mother’s name was Priyadattā."

The Buddha’s name was Gongfu (Merit and Blessing). His attendant was named Nansheng (Invincible). His chief disciple of wisdom was named Yuefa (Delighting in the Dharma). His disciple of supernormal powers was named Yaozhi (Medicine Clan).

In the first assembly, one hundred thousand disciples gathered to hear the sutra; in the second, ninety-nine thousand; and in the third, ninety-eight thousand. All of them attained the realization of the Way.
When this Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was five hundred years; the True Dharma remained for fifteen thousand years, and his relics were combined to establish a single great stupa.
As for the land where the Tathāgata Hūṅkara was born, the city was named Saṃjñeya, and the light of that Buddha illuminated three hundred li.
In the lineage of the Noble One, his father was named Ānanda, his mother was called Dānaśīlavatī, and his son was named Kalyāṇabhadra.
His attendant was named Maṇiratnabandhu, his chief disciple in wisdom was named Śaikṣamitra, and his disciple in supernormal powers was named Anumati.
In the first assembly for preaching the sutra, sixty billion disciples gathered; in the second, fifty billion; and in the third, ninety billion, all of whom attained the realization of the Way.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, the human lifespan was twelve thousand years; the True Dharma remained for thirty thousand years, and his relics were widely distributed throughout the ten directions.
"The land where the Tathāgata Anśī was born has a city named Manojña; that Buddha’s radiance illuminates one hundred and twenty *li*.
He is of the Brahmin caste; his father is named Amitaratna, his mother is named Saṃpatti, and his son is named Bhūmidatta."
His attendant was named Jianqiang; his chief disciple of wisdom was named Yueyao; and his disciple of supernormal powers was named Shizi.

In the first assembly where he preached the sutra, nine billion six hundred million disciples gathered; in the second assembly, nine billion four hundred million; and in the third assembly, nine billion two hundred million—all of whom attained the realization of the Way.

When the Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years; the True Dharma remained for eighty-four thousand years as well, and his relics were widely distributed throughout the ten directions.
"In the land where the Tathāgata Prajñākarma was born, the city is named Puṇyavati. The radiance of that Buddha illuminates four hundred *li*.
He is of the noble class; his father’s name is Aśoka, his mother’s name is Priyasāgara, and his son is named Saumyabuddhi."
His attendant was named Sudatta; his chief disciple of wisdom was named Vartamānārya; and his disciple of supernatural powers was named Puṇyapriya.
In the first assembly, there were incalculable billions of noble disciples; in the second, eight hundred billion; and in the third, seven hundred billion, all of whom had realized the Way.

When that Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was eighty thousand *koṭis* of years, and the True Dharma remained for five hundred million years; the Buddha’s relics were distributed like medicinal herbs.

At that time, Anzhu (Aniruddha) was majestic and difficult to surpass. If anyone hears the names of even one hundred and one of these [Buddhas], they shall before long attain the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha; how much more so for those who make offerings to these thousand Tathāgatas?

The learning of the various disciples is not even worth mentioning; as for the various bodhisattvas, they have attained the stage of non-retrogression and the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and as those in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajāti-pratibaddha), they deliver and liberate incalculable beings throughout the ten directions.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Chapter on the Resolve of Two Thousand Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva Joy-King again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent!"
World-Honored One!

We pray that you will deign to show us compassion and explain the origins and details of these thousand Buddhas of this kalpa—how they first began their practice to become Bodhisattvas, under which Buddhas they initially resolved their minds on the Way, how they accumulated merit and virtue, self-disciplining themselves in every lifetime to make offerings to all Buddhas, and how they eventually attained perfect enlightenment to deliver all beings.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Joyful King:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall explain for you the beginning and end of the arousal of the aspiration [for enlightenment].
The Bodhisattva Joyful King and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:

"In a former life, when Krakucchanda Buddha was still a sentient being, he beheld the Tathāgata Candramati. His heart became suddenly radiant, as if seeing light in the darkness; he realized that the Way was supreme and most honored within the triple world. He then sought out a precious canopy to offer to that Buddha, first giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment with diligent and tireless effort, thereby attaining perfect awakening himself and delivering all beings."

"In a former life, when the Buddha Konaṃda was practicing the path, he beheld the Tathāgata Siṃha and offered him a precious necklace and sumana flowers. By thus first giving rise to the mind of enlightenment and accumulating merit and virtue, he attained perfect awakening for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When that Kāśyapa Buddha was in his previous lives, he was born into the family of a brahmin as a young boy. Upon seeing the Tathāgata Sītamṛdu, his heart was filled with understanding and joy; he removed the exquisite and precious sash he was wearing and offered it to the Buddha. He first resolved upon the path of enlightenment and practiced the dharma of a bodhisattva without ever becoming weary or negligent, thereby attaining perfect awakening himself and delivering all beings."
The Buddha said:

"Now that I have attained Buddhahood and am named Śākyamuni, in my past lives I was a skilled physician. I specialized in treating human ailments and thereby acquired medical fees, precious objects, clothing, and utensils."

I beheld a Buddha of antiquity whose name was identical to mine, also titled Tathāgata Śākyamuni; recognizing him as the Most Honored One, I took garments and offered them to that Buddha. For the first time, I resolved upon the Way and practiced the four immeasurable minds, the four debts of gratitude, the six perfections, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, without seeking realization midway, thereby attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

He beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara manifesting the reception of his prediction, desiring to rescue all sentient beings within the three realms and personally attaining perfect enlightenment to deliver them all.

"When the Tathāgata Maitreya was in a former life as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he saw a Buddha named Anantapratilabdha. Thereupon, he gave rise to the aspiration for the Way and invited the Buddha and the assembly of sages, providing them with sweet delicacies. He offered radiant jewels to bestow upon all, practicing benevolence and compassion wherever he went for those who had not yet attained [enlightenment]. He traversed through birth and death for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges without regarding it as toil, until he himself attained Buddhahood to deliver all beings, at a time when the human lifespan reached eighty-four thousand years."

"When the Tathāgata Siṃha was in his former lives, from the time he first resolved his mind [for enlightenment], there was a Buddha named Huāngyù Yīn (Radiant Sound). Because of that initial resolve, he offered a five-inch square of five-layered rag-robe to that Buddha; by serving the World-Honored One and practicing the Bodhisattva path, he attained Buddhahood for himself."

"When the Tathāgata Prabhāśobha was in a former life, he was once a merchant who entered the sea and obtained rare treasures. At that time, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Amitaprabha; seeing the World-Honored One, his heart was filled with joy, and he offered a bright moon pearl to that Buddha. Relying upon that resolve for the Way, he practiced the Dharma of a Bodhisattva, thereby attaining Buddhahood himself and delivering all beings."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Muni first resolved his mind on the path under the Tathāgata Rucita, he was an ordinary person of immeasurable wealth. Upon seeing the Buddha, his heart opened; he offered a jeweled canopy to that Buddha and, practicing the Dharma of a Bodhisattva through that resolve for enlightenment, made this vow in his heart:
'By these merits, may they flow throughout the ten directions so that all beings may be protected and sustained.'"
"Through unflagging diligence, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and delivered all beings.

In a former life, when the Tathāgata Sunetra first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Citraratna, he beheld the Buddha and his heart was suddenly enlightened; he offered flowers and incense, and because of that aspiration for the Way, he practiced the Dharma of a Bodhisattva. He upheld the four immeasurable minds, the four debts of gratitude, the four analytical knowledges, and the six perfections (pāramitās). Out of compassion for the ten directions, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment and delivered all sentient beings from peril and distress, providing them with vast peace and security."

"When the Tathāgata Sunakṣatra was in a former life, he first conceived the aspiration for the Way under the Tathāgata Ananda. At that time, acting as a householder, he beheld the Buddha with joy and offered him a magnificent, multi-storied pavilion adorned with necklaces. Having made this offering to the Buddha, he cultivated the Bodhisattva path through his resolve for enlightenment, desiring to deliver the ten directions and, having attained Buddhahood himself, to liberate all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Puṣpa was in a former life, he beheld the Buddha Daoyu (Guide and Controller) and first resolved his mind on the Way. At that time, he was originally impoverished and distressed; because of that resolution, he realized the emptiness of the three realms. He then took off a garment worn by a corpse and offered it to that Buddha, dedicating himself to the Bodhisattva path with the desire to deliver sentient beings. He sought to enrich all beings with the seven riches so that they would no longer fall into poverty and distress. Protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions, he eventually attained Buddhahood and delivered all beings."

"Regarding the second Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Puṣpa: in a former life, he first conceived the aspiration for the Way under the Buddha Atiśīrṣa. He offered a single willow twig for rinsing the mouth to that Buddha; by virtue of his resolute intention and his practice of the Bodhisattva path, he liberated sentient beings and attained perfect enlightenment himself, rescuing all from perilous calamities and the hardships of the triple world."

"When the Tathāgata Daoshi was in a former life, he saw the Buddha Zhicheng when that Buddha first resolved his mind on the Way. At that time, Daoshi was an ordinary man; he offered all the fine beds, seats, and implements he possessed, as well as red sandalwood, to that Buddha. Because of that resolve for the Way, he practiced the Dharma of a Bodhisattva, desiring to rescue the ten directions and, having attained Buddhahood himself, to deliver and liberate all beings."

“Most Tathāgatas, in their past lives, first gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment under the Buddha Kīrtivighuṣṭa. At that time, wishing to enter the city, they saw the Buddha emerging from it; because they bowed their heads in refuge and made offerings, they presented excellent bamboo with a sincere heart, thinking to themselves:
‘May all sentient beings walk as straight as this bamboo, never harboring crooked intentions.’”
For this reason, he constantly encountered the Triple Gem and attained perfect enlightenment himself to rescue and deliver those throughout the ten directions.

When the Tathāgata Mahābala was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Ācāryamati. At that time, he was born as the son of a perfumer’s family and sold various fine incenses. Seeing the Buddha entering the city, his heart was filled with great joy; he offered the Buddha a wooden *kamaṇḍalu* and held exquisite, extraordinary, and diverse fragrances in his hands. Attending upon the Honored One as his attendant, he made the vow: "May all sentient beings enter the gateway of the Way. Because of this, he subsequently attained perfect enlightenment and delivered all beings.

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Nakṣatrarāja first resolved his mind on the Path under the Buddha Dānāśaya, he was living in that land in poverty and destitution, working as a hired hand tending cattle for others. Seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy and offered seasonal flowers to him. Practicing the bodhisattva path with diligent and tireless effort, he attained perfect enlightenment by himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Xiuyao was in his past lives, he first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment before the Buddha Miaoxiang. At that time, serving as a charioteer, he beheld the World-Honored One; he made offerings, followed, and took refuge in the Unsurpassed Great Sage. With a humble and reverent heart, he conversed with the Buddha. For this reason, he eliminated the hardships of the triple world and attained Buddhahood himself, whereby all beings received his grace."

"When the Tathāgata Renowned Glory was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Lamp-Light. Upon seeing the Buddha preaching the Dharma, he offered banners and streamers to that Tathāgata; that very night he lit lamps and practiced diligently day and night, thereby attaining Buddhahood for himself. He delivers beings from the perils of the three realms and the afflictions of the five destinies; all rely upon his auspicious merit and find peace without exception."

"When the Tathāgata Yingmiao was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Lianhua. At that time, while he was out plowing and sowing, he saw the Buddha and, filled with joy, abandoned his plow and oxen to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet. He offered *vimukti* flowers to the Buddha, vowing: 'May all sentient beings till the field of the Way and virtue, so that they may personally attain Buddhahood. From this, he practiced the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, the three liberations, and the six perfections, until he attained perfect enlightenment and delivered all beings."

“When the Tathāgata Mahāprabha was in his former lives, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Mahādīpa. At that time, he was the most impoverished and destitute in that land; entering a vast wilderness, he saw the Buddha and his assembly of monks. He offered money to the Buddha as an offering to the Most Honored One, and while in the wilderness, he burned incense and lit lamps, making this vow: ‘May the minds of sentient beings in the three realms be empty and their intentions pure, just like this wilderness; may there be universal illumination throughout the three periods of time, free from the darkness of the three poisons. For this reason, he attained Buddhahood by himself and brought all beings to liberation.”

"When the Tathāgata Jieyin was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Fanyin. At that time, he was a leather-worker who offered the Buddha exquisite sandals, vowing: 'May all beings readily obtain vehicles, and thereafter may they all achieve the gallop of the five supernatural powers. By virtue of this merit, he attained Buddhahood himself and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Jyotirasa was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Vigatamānasa. At that time, having become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he offered eighty-four thousand rows of trees as a gift to the Buddha and had a vihāra constructed for him. Walking back and forth within it with diligent and tireless effort, he eventually attained Buddhahood and liberated all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Sūryagarbha was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Aparimitajina. At that time, he was the son of a brahmin of great lineage; he offered *kuyika* flowers to that Buddha, and by virtue of this cause, he attained perfect awakening himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Candrasvāmī was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Nāmaghoṣa. At that time, he was the son of a goldsmith and offered a fine jeweled staff to that Buddha. Because of this, he attained perfect enlightenment and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Prabhāsa was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the Path under the Buddha Anantaprabha. At that time, he was born into the most impoverished class of that land; while carrying grass to sell in the marketplace, he saw the Buddha and felt great joy. Having nothing else to offer, he presented the grass to the Buddha, vowing that the merit thereof might flow throughout the ten directions, leading him himself to attain Buddhahood and deliver all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Suvimalaprabha was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Rucirarāja. At that time, serving as a garden superintendent, he saw the Buddha with joy and offered a campaka flower to the Supreme Honored One. Practicing the Dharma of a Bodhisattva, he thought to himself:
'May the minds of all sentient beings become as supple as this flower.'"
"By means of diligence, he attained Buddhahood himself and delivered all beings.

In a former life, when the Tathāgata Aśoka was first inspired to seek the Way under the Buddha Vimuktārtha, he was born as the son of an elder in the household of a nobleman. He took the most excellent flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, aspiring for the Great Way, the unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment. By virtue of this cause, he attained perfect awakening and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Oṣadhiprabha was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path to enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Guṇavarmā. At that time, acting as the son of an elder, he offered a bright moon pearl and red lotus flowers to that Buddha. Through unremitting diligence, he attained perfect awakening for himself and delivered beings from the afflictions of the three realms and five destinies."

"When the Tathāgata Jvālāprabha was in his former lives, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Sudarśana. At that time, acting as a merchant, he frequently entered the great ocean and offered a fine bed and bedding made of red sandalwood to that Buddha. By practicing the bodhisattva path through this merit, he attained buddhahood for himself and delivered all beings from the calamities of birth and death throughout the three periods of time."

"When the Tathāgata Grasping Flowers was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Pleasing Majesty. At that time, he was born as the son of an elder; he washed fine garments with milk and burned exquisite, renowned incense to offer to that Buddha, desiring that the merit thereof should flow forth to the ten directions so that all might receive salvation. By virtue of these causes and conditions, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Kṣemaprabha was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Anigūhitatejas. At that time, being an ordinary person, he saw the Buddha and, with joy, prostrated and took refuge in him. He then offered a bright mirror and various rare and precious jewels to that Buddha, practicing the Dharma of a Bodhisattva; by virtue of these causes and conditions, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Present Meaning was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Immeasurable Sound. In ages past, he was a Wheel-Turning Sage King; seeing the Buddha, the Most Honored One of the Unsurpassed Great Way, he offered that Buddha various necklaces and multi-storied vihāras, vowing: 'May the virtues of sentient beings be like space; by this cause, may they attain perfect enlightenment and deliver all beings.'"

"When the Tathāgata Diṅkāra was in his former lives, he first resolved his mind upon the Way in the presence of the Buddha Pradyotana-rati. At that time, he was the son of a perfumer; he gathered various flowers and incenses to offer to the Holy Honored One. Subduing his mind and restraining his thoughts, together with his family and a retinue of sixty billion, he made offerings to that Buddha. He inquired after and received the Dharma, practiced the Bodhisattva path, and thereby attained perfect enlightenment himself, delivering all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Prabhāvega was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Samantakīrti. At that time, he was a rishi dwelling in the mountains who offered a fine white woolen cloth to that Buddha as a carpet for his walking meditation. Knowing the Buddha to be most venerable, he practiced the Bodhisattva path and attained perfect enlightenment himself to deliver all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Bhiṣaj was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Vigataraṇa. At that time, he was the son of a physician; he offered medicinal pills, various incenses, flowers, and other items to that Buddha, vowing that all sentient beings might be cured of the diseases of the three poisons. By this cause, he gave rise to the aspiration and practiced the Bodhisattva dharma, eventually attaining perfect enlightenment himself and delivering all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Subhakṣema was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Mṛdusvara. At that time, he was the son of an oil-maker; he offered a lamp lit with oil to that Buddha, vowing that all beings throughout the ten directions might each receive the light of the Way. By virtue of this cause, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and came to deliver all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Udayana was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Vipulaśrava. He offered that Buddha a fine, exquisite white cotton cloth, spreading it over the place where the Buddha walked; thus encouraging and supporting the act of giving, he gave rise to the aspiration to practice the bodhisattva conduct out of compassion for all sentient beings, and thereby attained perfect enlightenment himself to deliver all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Yi-su was in his former lives, he first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment under the Buddha Vigatarajas. Born into a family of physicians as a medical apprentice, he saw the Buddha with joy and offered him several medicinal pills. By virtue of this practice, he attained the state of a bodhisattva, realized perfect enlightenment for himself, and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Śikhidatta was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Samantadarśin. At that time, he was the son of a householder who crafted ornaments and necklaces; he offered the Buddha a carriage for protection and precious necklaces, serving and making offerings to him. Practicing the Dharma of a Bodhisattva with diligent and tireless effort, he attained perfect enlightenment and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Dṛḍha was in a former life, he first conceived the aspiration for the Way under the Buddha Anabhibhū. At that time, having become a Cakravartin King, he beheld the World-Honored Buddha and offered eighty-four thousand couches, mats, seats, tables, and banqueting stands made of the seven treasures to that Buddha. Thereby, he gave rise to the aspiration for the Way and practiced the dharma of a Bodhisattva, eventually attaining perfect enlightenment himself and delivering all beings."

"When Śrītejas Tathāgata was in his previous lives, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Tejorāja-prabha. At that time, he was a merchant who entered the great ocean and offered a moon-pearl to that Buddha; the radiance of this pearl illuminated forty li. By virtue of this diligent effort, he attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Dṛḍhapadavikrāmin. At that time, as the master of carriages and wealth, he beheld the Buddha with joy and offered a willow branch for the Buddha to rinse his mouth and teeth. By virtue of this pure practice, he attained perfect enlightenment by himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Guṇadhvaja was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Mṛduyaśas. He offered the Buddha a water vessel and a large cauldron to be used for bathing, so that bodily impurities were removed and his body became pure and clear. He established the light of universal practice and the virtue of giving, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment himself and delivering all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Kṣema originally lived in a past life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Anuttara. At that time, he was the son of a jeweled necklace-maker; he adorned necklaces as offerings for that Buddha and bestowed upon him purple-gold sandals, couches, and incense. He made a vow that all sentient beings might attain meditative concentration, and by virtue of this cause, he personally attained perfect enlightenment and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Jianzhong was in a former life, he resolved his mind on the Way upon hearing the Buddha Daqingyue. He made offerings to that Buddha with pure, fine cotton cloth; he warmed the bathhouse for the holy assembly to bathe and presented various incenses. By virtue of giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and practicing the bodhisattva path, he attained perfect awakening himself and brings salvation to the ten directions."

When the Tathāgata Brahmaghoṣa was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Mṛdughoṣa. At that time, he served as a king’s overseer tending sheep. When the Buddha Brahmaghoṣa had first attained perfect enlightenment and was staying in a marshy wilderness, [the king] beheld the Tathāgata and felt great joy in his heart. He divided the parched flour he was eating and offered half to the Tathāgata. By virtue of practicing the unsurpassed Great Way of a Bodhisattva with unremitting diligence, he personally attained perfect enlightenment and delivered all beings.

"When the Tathāgata Dṛḍha was in a former life, he took a handful of the most diverse and precious jewels from the presence of the Buddha Acalagati and scattered them as an offering over that Buddha. Having been born into the family of a great teacher, he resolved his mind toward enlightenment through this act of giving; by virtue of this merit, he attained perfect awakening for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Supreme Joy was in his former lives, he first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity. At that time, he was the crown prince of a king named Amusement in the kingdom of Śāketa. When the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment, he radiated a brilliant light that universally illuminated the ten directions; through the causal practices of a bodhisattva, he personally realized perfect enlightenment and delivered all beings across."

"When the Tathāgata Saṃkusumita was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Tejorāja. At that time, he was a Wheel-Turning Sage King who offered fine garments, rare jewels, and extraordinary treasures to that Buddha, bestowing them as blessings upon all beings. By virtue of this diligent effort, he attained for himself the unsurpassed Great Way of Perfect Enlightenment and liberated all."

"When the Tathāgata Damingshan was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Wangdao. He offered a flower of *anoka* to that Buddha, accumulating merit and virtue while self-disciplining himself in every birth. Out of great compassion, he took pity on all beings, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment and delivering all."

"In a former life, when Vajra Tathāgata was practicing the path as a bodhisattva, he was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as Śakra, Lord of Devas, under the guidance of the Buddha Sthira. There, he rained down a profusion of divya-māndārava flowers as offerings to that Buddha. By virtue of this practice, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

“I recall that when the Tathāgata was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Vimuktarāga. He offered a canopy adorned with purple-golden jewel necklaces to the Buddha, scattering them over the Buddha’s body and thereby generating the aspiration for enlightenment; thus, he attained perfect awakening himself and delivered all beings.”

"When the Tathāgata Abhaya was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Abhaya. Having a nature that was stubborn yet fond of laughter, he made offerings to the Buddha with music, beating drums and singing praises; through this, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Ratna was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Anantaghoṣa. At that time, serving as a high minister, he offered excellent flowers and incense to that Buddha. Through the causal practice of a bodhisattva, he attained perfect awakening by himself and brought all beings to liberation."

“When the Tathāgata Padmanetra was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Samantadarśin. He offered to that Tathāgata the jeweled belt with which he himself was adorned as a bed for reclining, desiring that through the merit of all sentient beings, they might personally attain perfect enlightenment and deliver all beings.”

"When Balin was formerly in his past lives, he first conceived the aspiration for the Way in the presence of the Buddha Mahendra. At that time, acting as a king of physicians, he offered a single āmalaka fruit to that Buddha. By virtue of this practice, he attained perfect enlightenment and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Padmaprabha was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Sarvatejas. At that time, serving as a goldsmith, he offered a jewel-ornamented flower to that Buddha. By virtue of this and through the full practice of these deeds, he attained perfect awakening and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Aishufo (Love-Subduing) was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Huikong (Teaching-Offering). He had once been the son of a gambler; by offering a fine incense burner to that Buddha, he accumulated merit through these practices and thereby attained perfect enlightenment himself to deliver all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Mahātejas was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Prabhāśirṣa. At that time, acting as the son of a nobleman, he offered fine garments to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of practice, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Brahman was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the presence of the Honored Buddha Praśānta. At that time, serving as a high official, he offered that Buddha rock honey, sugarcane, and molasses. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Aparimitaprabha first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Viśuddhaprabha, he was working as a merchant for others; he offered a fine parasol to that Buddha, and by virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Nāgadatta was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Siṃhahanu. At that time, he was the son of a master garland-maker; he offered a precious vessel of flowers to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Dṛḍhapada was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Vimati-jaya. At that time, he was born as the son of a jeweler; he offered precious pearls, necklaces, couches, and seating mats to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Avitatha-darśana was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Sudarśana. At that time, his family served as physicians who treated the living and cured diseases; he offered excellent medicinal compounds to the noble assembly to heal their various ailments. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Vīryadatta was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way upon encountering the Buddha Amitābha. At that time, he was a Cakravartin King who constructed hundreds of thousands of monasteries, pavilions, and chambers; using red sandalwood, he fashioned various couches and spread fine mats to offer to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Bhadrabala was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Yaśaḥprabha. At that time, being an ordinary person, he offered food of a hundred flavors to that Buddha and his holy assembly, and constantly provided meals for ten koṭis of disciples. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment and liberated all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Xinle (Ānanda) was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Hongcheng (Mahāyaśas). At that time, he was the son of a wealthy and noble brahmin; he offered the Buddha a beautifully adorned, exquisite vessel and a rare, wonderful fan made of pearls. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment by himself and brings liberation to all."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Avinivartana first resolved his mind on the path to enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Śāntendriya, he served as a messenger and offered five bilva fruits to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect awakening himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Siṃhadhvaja was in his former lives, he first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Viśuddhasvara. At that time, being an ordinary man leading an ox to plow a field, he offered a single amalaka fruit to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect awakening for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Jñānottara was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Anabhibhūta-cakra-vartana. At that time, serving as a shoemaker, he offered a harītakī fruit to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Dharmasvāmin was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Anantaghoṣa. At that time, he was a strongman who sought to offer a fine banner to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Priyarāja was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Jnanasmita. At that time, he served as a perfumer and offered excellent blended incense to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Wondrous Guide was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Divine Power and Majesty. At that time, being a young child, he offered three kinds of fruit to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Aiying was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Gongxunwang. At that time, serving as the Crown Prince Mingzhi of a kingdom, he offered flowers to the Buddha; by virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Subhakṛtsna was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Anantapraśaṃsā. At that time, acting as a merchant, he offered a bowl of sweet honey. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Bahukarman was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Mahābala. At that time, he was a poor man of the country who offered to that Buddha a walking path sixteen feet in length. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Saṃghanāmakara first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment in a former life under the Buddha Dyutiviśuddha, he was the son of a perfume merchant; because he sprinkled perfumed water upon the place where that World-Honored One walked, he accumulated merit through this cause and condition, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment himself and delivering all beings."

“Observing the Tathāgata’s past lives in succession, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the presence of the Buddha Unobstructed Vision. At that time, while dwelling in the mountains, he fashioned a decorated canopy from fine silk and cotton cloth and offered it to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation.”

When the Tathāgata Vṛṣṭisvara was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Siṃhagati. At that time, he was a potter and offered a water jar to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect awakening and brought all beings to liberation.

When the Tathāgata Sudhyāyin was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Samantadarśin. At that time, he was the son of a flower-gatherer; he offered a single lotus flower to that Buddha and, by virtue of this accumulation of merit, attained perfect enlightenment himself and delivered all beings.

When the Tathāgata Kāyika was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Dānottara. At that time, serving as the son of a nobleman, he offered a *sumana* flower garland to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation.

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Vigatamala first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Sudarśana, he was lying down at night in a vihāra; he offered the Buddha a hand-towel for wiping his hands. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Yaśas was a son in a dyer's household, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Sucandravimala. He gathered *āmalaka* fruits, filling his hands with them, and scattered them as an offering over the Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When Mahāyaśas Tathāgata was in his former lives, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Manojñaśabda. At that time, he was the most impoverished person in that land; he offered a *kusuma* flower—exquisite, soft, and wonderful—to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect awakening and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Maṇiratnacūḍa was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path to enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Ratnaviśuddha. At that time, acting as a young boy, he scattered various incenses from his cupped hands as an offering to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect awakening for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Dṛḍha was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Path in the presence of the Buddha Jvalanaprabha. At that time, he was a divine and wondrous son of heaven; he offered a fine celestial fan to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Siṃhakrama was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Dhyānottara. He had once been an umbrella-maker; during the height of the summer heat, he offered an umbrella and sandals to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Śrīkṣa originally lived in a past life, he first resolved his mind on the path to enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Ratnaviśuddha. At that time, acting as a shepherd tending sheep in the wilds, he saw the Buddha along the road and was filled with joy; he immediately took some tree bark and offered it to the Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When Cheqsheng was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Juejue. He had once been a shepherd who, having filled a fine bowl with milk, offered it to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Jñānakoṣa was in his past lives, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Prajñāśrī. At that time, while still an ordinary person, he prepared a Dharma seat and made offerings for one day to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Supratiṣṭhita was in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Saṃbodhana. At that time, he was the son of a tanner and offered a full armful of hides to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Ākāśa was practicing as a bodhisattva, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Caritramati. At that time, serving as a hired laborer, he offered the Buddha fine water and gruel; he also set aside the food he had prepared for himself to present as an offering to the Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Yinchengle (Anurādha) was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Buddha Shangen (Kuśalamūla). He presented that Buddha with a gift of clothing, offering a superior upper garment and a fine, black, high-quality lower robe, rather than using fine cotton wool. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Immeasurable Enlightenment was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Awesome Sound. He offered to that Buddha a tree suitable for sitting; by virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Suprasanna was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Path in the presence of the Buddha Prabhāsa. At that time, he gathered various fruits and offered five stalks of blue lotuses to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment by himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Āryamati first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Susthita, he was a bhikṣu dwelling in seclusion. He purified the walking-path of that Buddha; by virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Prabhāsa was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path in the presence of the Buddha Amitatejas. Residing in a city, he offered the Buddha a seat and bedding worth hundreds of thousands of coins. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Dṛḍhapratijñā was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Pratyayacintin. Acting as a flower-garland maker, he offered flowers to that Buddha; by virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect awakening and delivered all beings."

"When the Tathāgata Śrī was formerly in a previous life, he first resolved his mind on the path of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Kīrtivimala. At that time, while carrying firewood along a road, he encountered wind and rain; consequently, he entered a vihāra and saw a disciple of the Buddha. He offered a particularly exquisite flower to that Buddha, and by virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and delivered all beings."

"When Chengying Tathāgata was practicing in his past lives, he first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment in the presence of Xunhua Tathāgata. At that time, having just finished bathing after he had made his resolve, he offered fine incense to the Buddha, personally presenting it with his own hands. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Blue Lotus was practicing the path of cultivation, he first resolved his mind on enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata Wondrous Flower Radiance. At that time, he was born as the son of a noble householder; being intelligent, courageous, and wise, he offered a red lotus flower to that Buddha. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Āṅkuśa was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Durjayottama. At that time, he was a master of incense markets and various commercial affairs; he smeared red sandalwood upon the ground where the Buddha walked. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings to liberation."

"In a former life, when the Tathāgata Ansheng was still a sentient being, he first resolved his mind on the Way in the presence of the Buddha Ruoxiang. At that time, as a royal envoy dispatched on a mission, he presented three Dharma robes to that Buddha along with his retinue. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment for himself and brought all beings across to liberation."

"When the Tathāgata Prajñākarma was in a former life, he first resolved his mind on the path under the Buddha Sudarśana. Together with a great assembly, he offered a large banner and canopy to that Buddha with a harmonious mind and single intention. By virtue of this accumulation of merit, he attained perfect enlightenment and brought all beings to liberation."

At that time, the World-Honored One briefly recounted the origins and conclusions of a thousand Buddhas, so that the entire assembly gathered there might understand their essential points and praise their virtues; he then spoke in verse:

"The blessings established in the presence of the various Buddhas—the merit of their practice was so slight as to be hardly worth mentioning—yet the fruits they obtained as retribution were such as these. What person of clear understanding would not resolve to develop the mind of the Way?"

One might still be able to measure the limits of space, and one might also calculate the volume of the waters of the great ocean; yet, for one who possesses even a slight degree of faith, joy, and inclination toward the Buddha, the retribution of that merit is beyond all measure.

Not falling into the eight difficulties and not encountering obstructions, one thereby attains the peace and bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, meeting the Buddha, the most supreme field of merit, one should serve him with reverence and diligence, practicing without negligence.

Whether I am currently present or have entered parinirvāṇa, those who take up my Buddha-relics, even as small as mustard seeds, and with faith and joy offer them veneration—their merit shall be bottomless and their virtue inconceivable.

Regarding the realm of empty space and the realm of sentient beings, one gives the merit of a Buddha by generating the mind of omniscience; who would dare to fathom the limits of these four dharmas? Only the Buddha possesses unique wisdom, for none can exhaust their boundaries.

It is like a person who is impoverished, destitute, and in dire straits, who rejoices upon finding a great treasure forty *li* in circumference; if one awakens the mind of the Way, its merit is just like this.
Abiding therein, one rescues and relieves all sentient beings; that Honored One of Ten Powers provides eight kinds of delights, and thus one is graced by the protection of five hundred Buddhas.

I have previously seen eighty thousand preeminent Buddhas, who proclaimed the four delightful meanings, elucidated and distinguished eighty-four meanings, and [expounded] up to sixty thousand gateways of dharmas.

He expounded the seventy-six stages of the path of wisdom; the Buddha, through his understanding, elucidated the eighteen modes of practice. These ten auspicious intentions and five skillful means constitute the root of these ten practices, which transform into one hundred and ten billion.
That which even the various pratyekabuddhas cannot attain, let alone the assembly of śrāvakas who rely on sounds;

furthermore, the eighty secondary marks and the primary signs, as well as the majestic deportment and meritorious achievements attained by all Buddhas, are inexhaustible and beyond comparison. For this reason, the Buddha is called inconceivable.

If there are those who resolve their minds upon the most supreme path of the Buddha, though they dwell in the world, they engage in the practice of eternal peace; having entered among common people as great treasures, wherever they go, they have no dependence and nothing to which they are bound.

Having subdued all demons and attained the nectar of immortality, he relieves and satisfies the multitude of calamities through the karma of the seven treasures; may he remain in the world to surely deliver beings from the mundane, just as a great rain universally moistens the world beneath heaven.
Although you may encounter countless hundreds of thousands of sufferings, before long you shall achieve merit, renown, and majestic virtue.
All the world ultimately returns to this non-existence; therefore, do not consider the practice of the Path to be wearisome, for you will be able to endure all the afflictions of various sufferings.

If one falls into the evil realms due to the retribution of transgressions, yet by virtue of meritorious deeds and noble qualities must surely be reborn in the heavens, what wise person would engage in dispute with a fool?

One who is deluded by ignorance has a mind at peace through wisdom; while wisdom leads to the fruit of the Path, folly remains unaware of it. Therefore, one should practice the Path and endure all things with patience.

The fool delights in strife and disorder, while the wise have no cause for contention; by this, he abandons all improper actions and cultivates the practice of refined cultivation and clear wisdom, thereby being able to relinquish these things and not relying on gain or sustenance.

One should always diligently cultivate and uphold this samādhi, contemplating the virtue and wisdom of each and every Buddha, enduring the hardships of countless billions of kalpas; the meritorious achievements of the Buddhas are inconceivable.

Though undergoing manifold sufferings, they remain steadfastly practiced in the wisdom of the Path; taking patience as their armor and practicing meditative concentration, they raise the banner of diligence and delight in planting the seeds of the precepts, with wisdom as their medicine, possessing peerless power.

Having subdued all Māras and attained the fruit of the nectar of immortality, the followers of Maitreya practice as spiritual friends; they exhort and deliver beings boundlessly without causing them harm, dwelling in the emptiness of houses and taking tranquility as their sustenance. The practices they cultivate are the virtues of omniscience; therefore, they always resolve upon a state of non-negligence.

Chapter on Praising the Past, the Twenty-third. At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy:

Chapter 24: Entrustment At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“Receive this fundamental Dharma, from which all Buddhas of the past and present are born. Human life is difficult to obtain; the Way of the Sūtras is difficult to encounter; and the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to meet.”
Thus one knows the difficulty: after a thousand Buddhas have passed, for sixty-five kalpas there will be no Buddha in the world, and the interval will be desolate and cut off;
after passing the kalpa of Great Renown (*Mahāyaśas*), for eighty kalpas there will likewise be no Buddha;

after passing the kalpa of Constellations (*Tārakā*), three hundred kalpas will elapse during which the teachings of the Dharma will be darkly severed and Buddhas will not arise again, until the kalpa of Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*) when a Buddha shall finally appear.

Therefore, know this: it is a tragedy for those in the world that a Buddha is so difficult to encounter. Cast into blinding darkness, they do not recognize the Way of the Teachings, and thus they drift and fall through the cycle of birth and death without end.
If they are in hell, they suffer the agonizing pain of being scorched and roasted for countless billions of years;

as hungry ghosts, they are impoverished by hunger and thirst, utterly exhausted, unable to escape from the torments of birth and death, their distress so intense that liberation seems impossible even after incalculable time.
Among the animals and beasts, they prey upon one another, suffering such poisonous harm for many kalpas.

From darkness they enter further darkness; from suffering they enter further suffering. Emerging from hell, they enter the realm of hungry ghosts; emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they enter the realm of animals. Whether as insects in the earth, insects in excrement, insects in grass, or moths—were one to describe each of them, it could never reach an end. Their pain is beyond words; they are truly pitiable and tragic.

"The Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of such beings as these; yet they fail to open their minds and accept the teachings shown to them. They let their minds run wild and unrestrained, like a blind man stumbling into darkness, or like a madman drowning in water, or like one lost in a valley who fails to see the many perils before him."

The Buddha, through great compassion, proclaimed the Great Way and disseminated the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*; by means of immeasurable teachings, he transformed sentient beings. He subdued the afflictions of the eighty-four thousand fetters and the perils of the four Māras; disregarding selfhood, he caused them to give rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment and to practice the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas. Thus they were rescued from the suffering of birth and death, freed from the three evil destinies, and having delivered themselves, they were liberated from the afflictions of the triple world.

"Furthermore, in future generations, those among the fourfold assembly who study [this] shall find joy in hearing the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas; yet they will be unable to recite it or hold it in their hearts. They will delight in the discourse of miscellaneous phrases and will not be intent upon the meaning of the profound and wondrous Dharma of emptiness, even when hearing of the most profound wisdom that is vast and boundless."

Furthermore, they take what they have habitually practiced as supreme; upon hearing the Great Way, they claim it is not worth listening to. Desiring something easy to understand, they explain its merits and faults by clinging to and reciting worldly fables, immortals, secular classics, and miscellaneous sayings, claiming these to be most subtle and wondrous. They all study and listen to them with immeasurable joy, celebrating themselves. Yet, burdened by the karmic merit of past lives, when they hear the profound Dharma being expounded and repeatedly explain its meaning, the terminology becomes so repetitive and profound that they cannot comprehend it; they then fall asleep or lie down and refuse to listen. It is precisely because of this that the True Dharma is extinguished.
The Buddha said:

"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, I delighted in the proliferation of diverse phrases and dwelt upon conceptual constructions. Consequently, I was unable to personally attain or reach the Great Way through the six perfections. It was only upon reaching the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha that I attained complete and pervasive clarity. Abandoning all conceptual constructions, my mind became free from attachment, and I was able to realize the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), whereby Dīpaṃkara Buddha granted me the prediction of enlightenment."

Understanding the emptiness of the three periods of time through unimpeded dharmas, he surveys the present world of the five turbidities, where opposition abounds and compliance is rare, with transgressions beyond measure. It is like planting a tree by sowing its seeds in the earth; at first, they cannot be seen and no one perceives them.
